Woman at centre of Cornell University rape inquiry in 'constant fear', lawyer says

BBC News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 13:52:33 GMT

The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her lawyer has said.

Speaking to the BBC ahead of a hearing in the civil case on Friday in New York, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said: "She feels under fire."

The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former school and the fraternity over the alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.

When the case went viral, a series of "I am Jane Doe" solidarity posts appeared, but there was a separate campaign aimed at unmasking her and defending the men, who have all denied any wrongdoing.

The men, who are also being sued by the woman, have not been charged with any crimes.

With initial proceedings now under way in the civil case, Giuffra told the BBC that these last few weeks have been "a very hard time" for his client, who isn't doing a lot beyond "surviving".

Her decision to sue was rooted in a desire for closure and to take power back, he said.

Giufrra visited Jane Doe this week and found that she hadn't been sleeping well – relying on medication to get rest.

Now in trauma therapy, he says she doesn't feel safe in her own home following malicious threats that were directed at her and her family.

After her address was published online without her consent, someone called in a fake emergency that led to police in full tactical gear drawing assault rifles on her father, her friend and her brother at their family home.

"It's just constant fear," he said.

He added that despite this her resolve hadn't been shaken and she remains determined to overhaul the university system at Cornell, and across the country, to protect survivors.

Cornell University, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, acknowledged it fell short in its handling of Jane Doe's case.

After facing intense pressure, the college's president announced that fraternity parties would be suspended until the end of the academic year to allow for a thorough review to determine whether and how they can safely continue.

The school also said it would add sexual assault investigators to its police force.

Giuffra, however, says he is surprised that Cornell has not reached out to him and believes they have been focused solely on "damage control".

He says any agreement with Cornell to resolve the civil lawsuit will need to include "steps to ensure there are no more Jane Does" and if there are, that they are going to be supported.

The BBC contacted Cornell for comment who directed us to the university's previous statements and comments on its internal investigation in 2024.

New York's governor Kathy Hochul appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.

Giuffra expects it will take a long time to do a proper investigation but is concerned that they will be going after evidence that is now "stale".

"A lot of the communication was on Snapchat, Snapchat goes away," he told the BBC.

"The best time to get evidence is around the time of the crime and that just didn't happen."

However, Giuffra believes he can win the civil case against the university, the men and others, where the burden of proof is lower than a criminal case.

Civil cases require a preponderance of the evidence, that it's more likely than not it happened, while criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

Recent high profile cases have shown the way juries evaluate consent can be unpredictable.

"I wouldn't have taken the case if I didn't think it was a strong case that I could win and get her some closure."

Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

BBC News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 13:30:32 GMT

Do you have three days' worth of food and water in your home?

That is what the government has told all of us to have on hand to get through a national emergency, as well as some other basic items.

Its "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need to get through a rocky few days.

On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".

As one expert warns the UK is "light years" behind our neighbours when it comes to preparing for major disruption, we've drilled down into what you need and why.

The government recommends having enough supplies in the kitchen to last three days, including bottled water and non-perishable foods.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash are also recommended - you can scroll through below to see the full list.

Disaster planning expert Professor Lucy Easthope said the goal of asking household to prepare is to make it easier for emergency service to cope in the event of a national emergency.

For example, the government says people who need medication should have an extra supply just in case. Prof Easthope says: "If people have got their heart pills for an extra 48 hours, it stops [response crews] from having to immediately find an emergency pharmacist."

While the latest government campaign only launched on Thursday, some people are well ahead of the game.

Speaking to Radio 5 Live, Bridgette Clamp, who lives in near Penzance in Cornwall, said she has stocked up on "lots of tinned goods" as well as "flour, yeast and everything to bake bread".

"We're rocking and rolling," she says.

One woman, who spoke to 5 Live anonymously, said she bought "loads and loads" of emergency food - but ended up eating it before it was strictly necessary.

Like others, she wondered if the government was "scaremongering", adding: "I don't know but I've certainly bought into it."

Rob, who lives off-grid in north Wales, told the programme he has stocked up on so many supplies he "wouldn't even notice" if a disaster struck.

But he said he still felt there was "a bit of scaremongering" going on and wondered if he would ever need it all.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the advice - which is similar to guidance issued by the previous government - was not triggered by any "particular piece of intelligence", but rather about improving "national resilience" more generally.

The government's announcement focused on extreme weather events, which are becoming more frequent because of man-made climate change - but Streeting also referred to the threat of "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, and supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".

Prof Easthope said she has been lobbying the government to launch this sort of campaign for "about 16 years".

She said successive governments have been hesitant of "putting out information that might cause tension" - and speculated that this advice may have been "rushed" out ahead of Storm Austen hitting the UK.

While many of us will already have a stash of tinned food in the cupboards, fewer homes are likely to have a store of bottled water.

Paul from Torquay, Devon, said to Radio 5 Live: "Who on earth carries three day supply of water?"

He added: "I think they've made it our responsibility, rather than their responsibility."

Prof Easthope described the UK as "light years" behind neighbouring countries when it comes to preparedness.

"Countries like Scandinavia, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, they've been good at this for years," she said.

France advises people to store 72-hours' worth of food, while the German government says homes should have enough supplies to last for a 10-day period.

"This is one area where I'm very comfortable saying we are playing massive catch-up," added Easthope.

Awareness campaigns such as "think 72 hours" make a big difference in the US, Australia and "all around Europe", she said.

However, in the UK, she said disaster messaging often gets parodied, or governments are accused of "panic-mongering".

"We have seen the pendulum shift" in recent years, she adds, saying that "we are now seeing people recognise this" as an issue that needs tackling.

'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber-security scramble

BBC News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:00:25 GMT

Microsoft boss Satya Nadella says he has not seen anything like the PHP emergency "in a long, long time".

Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix the critical cyber-security flaw in millions of websites, he told a conference "it was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks".

Other IT and cyber experts have told the BBC about their struggles in the last 48 hours, whose stories give us an insight into what it is like at the coalface of a major cyber emergency. But also highlight how misinformation and panic has made things a lot worse.

"It's been relentless," says UK-based system administrator Adam Mudd.

He said he had never had so many messages from people who were worried about their websites.

"The biggest challenge has been juggling clients who want their sites taken offline as a precaution, while trying to coordinate updates and fixes across countless different setups," he said.

"Sometimes it takes me longer to take a website down than to fix the PHP problem."

PHP is a very popular programming language which powers millions of websites.

But two critical flaws were found with the system that led to the emergency response, with national cyber-security authorities urging IT teams to download a security fix urgently or take websites and servers offline.

Mudd says since then he has been under enormous pressure and has lost a huge amount of sleep - working early and not finishing until 22:30 BST to secure his customers' systems.

In Mauritius, IT administrator Loganaden Velvindron said he too was flat out since his team realised just how much software relies on PHP.

"Many versions of php running are completely end-of-life, so we are having to rebuilding web apps and change code in some cases," he said.

He said part of the problem was the announcement about the security vulnerabilities in PHP came as a surprise, without much time to prepare for action.

Jon Jones, Technical director for a digital advertising company, was also spurred into action by the alerts.

"Seeing the warning drop was definitely eye-opening and a new experience we've not dealt with before," he said.

"But, in a way, it was exciting feeling like a bit of a Hollywood action scene."

The PHP Foundation, which manages the programming language, released its software fix and there was a scramble for people to download it.

Jones said it felt like "the race was on" when the patch launched at 15:00 BST on Wednesday.

"It was also a bit nerve-racking as anyone who has applied software updates before would know, there's always a chance than an update can cause other issues," he said.

The rush came as someone had leaked details of the PHP flaw early - and it was heavily rumoured that cyber-criminals were already trying to carry out attacks.

But cyber experts are also now questioning whether or not those rumours were real.

"We were flooded with rubbish intel about hackers being out there actively with working Proof of Concept (PoC) methods," said UK cyber expert Daniel Card.

He said he also been flat out since Tuesday when the rumours of PHP hacks began circulating.

"This isn't the first time we've had a situation like this but it feels like it's been on another dimension," he said.

He agreed that on paper the PHP vulnerabilities were very serious and should be taken seriously, but he and many others are frustrated with the misinformation about hackers being on the loose.

As well as the alerts from government agencies - even the Prime Minister of Japan - cyber-security companies also made errors which didn't help.

One major firm in this space issued warnings saying hackers had a working PoC - only to have to retract it.

In spite of warnings from Cloudflare and AWS that "millions of hacking attempts" had been made every hour, there is also no evidence of large scale data breaches or cyber-attacks.

It is true that hackers have been seen to use AI to attempt to build attack methods, but none of them seem to be working at scale at the moment - something that may well change soon.

AI was also used to find the PHP flaws which had been hidden from human researchers for decades.

The IT workers we spoke to all agreed that these kinds of serious flaws were going to be uncovered more frequently now that AI tools had become so good at hacking.

But some in the industry are concerned about how people were told about the critical vulnerabilities in PHP, as they fear improvements in AI will throw up more incidents like it.

"We're going to find scary vulnerabilities with the amazing capabilities that OpenAI and Anthropic are bringing online, but we need to calibrate the messaging," posted Mark Maunder, founder of Wordfence - a Wordpress security tool.

He said there was a risk of "alert fatigue" which could be a big problem if a fully exploitable and serious vulnerability arose.

A Ballon d'Or campaign as fierce off the pitch as on it

BBC News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 06:06:38 GMT

Ousmane Dembele won the Ballon d"Or in 2025 and is one of 10 PSG players listed for it this year

An emotional Ousmane Dembele had barely settled back into his chair at Paris' historic Theatre du Chatelet last September, gold-dipped orb in hand, when campaigns for this year's men's Ballon d'Or prize began to whirr into action.

Entourages roused their candidates, media revelled in the hype. Who deserved the award in 2026? A World Cup year, no less, in which the narrative occasionally became not just which players could lead their country to glory, but how doing so would help them secure football's biggest individual accolade.

"The Ballon d'Or has been discussed every single day," said European football expert Guillem Balague on BBC Sport's Euro Leagues podcast.

"Quite clearly it follows the pattern of society, where it puts a lot of emphasis on the individual - it's harder to understand why a collective works, it becomes very easy to understand why one dribbles or doesn't dribble."

Clamour for the spotlight only increased as the red-carpet ceremony neared.

"You can't underestimate the PR machine that some clubs and some players are going to use," added French football journalist Julien Laurens.

Managers and sporting directors talked up their charges, and questioned why others on their squad did not make the 30-man shortlist.

Deco branded it a "huge scandal" that Barcelona pair Raphinha and Pedri missed out, but backed Lamine Yamal as overwhelming favourite to win it. Not, he says, because he is also a Barca player, but "because I like football".

Star names have appeared frequently in the media. Lamine Yamal himself insisted he will not "beg for anything" - after last year saying he dreamed of "winning many" - but suggested the prize should not merely go to the top goalscorer.

Paris St-Germain manager Luis Enrique confessed he is "bored of the Ballon d’Or" - although with a record 10 PSG players on the shortlist, perhaps he wishes to keep out of the debate. Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia talked each other up to BBC Sport.

"We can cut it in two," joked Dembele. "Honestly, he deserves it, the season he had was exceptional." Kvaratskhelia responded: "Of course it's him!"

A 'Kvara d'Or' campaign in Georgia celebrated the country's favourite fleet-footed son.

"I think for the big nations it's really difficult to understand what [winning] would mean for the small country," the winger explained.

Kylian Mbappe, who Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho compared to the original Ronaldo, was less subtle than most in his pitch to win the award for the first time.

"I always think I'm the best but everyone has their own opinion," professed the Frenchman, now the all-time World Cup top goalscorer. "Of course, this year could be good for me to win the Ballon d'Or - but journalists vote."

Indeed - since a short spell of national team captains and managers also voting ended in 2015 - the 30-player shortlist drawn up by the publications France Football and L'Equipe has been voted on by one journalist from each of the top 100 Fifa-ranked nations.

The deadline has passed. The winner has already been chosen.

This video can not be played

What does it mean to win the Ballon d'Or?

James Kirkham, a sports brand strategist who has worked with top clubs and players, including Harry Kane, says the build-up has had an election feel.

"You're going out, canvassing, getting your vote and making sure you shore up certain blocks from certain countries, and why wouldn't you?" adds Kirkham.

The lobbying is not for everyone. Max Eberl, Bayern Munich's board member for sport, championed Kane and Michael Olise but said the best players, external "are the ones who don't need to run a campaign".

Mbappe's compatriot, Jean-Pierre Papin, winner of the award in 1991, meanwhile told French TV:, external "I like Kylian a lot, he's a record-breaker. However, there comes a point when it's all about me, me, me and me."

Mbappe did make an interesting observation, alluding to the dominance of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo - the pair won a combined 13 in a 15-year period between 2008 and 2023.

"My idea of the Ballon d'Or comes from the Messi and Ronaldo era - you don't give it to ordinary players, you give it ​to players who are different," explained Mbappe.

AC Milan's Kaka was the last recipient before Messi and Ronaldo's tug-of-war began, the Brazilian pipping the young pair to the prize in 2007.

That was a year after fledgling social media platforms Facebook and Twitter launched to the public. Nokia dominated mobile phone markets, people took digital cameras on nights out.

The world had changed immeasurably by the time Messi won for an eighth time in 2023.

"Today everything moves at the speed of light," explains former AC Milan chief executive and sporting director Ariedo Braida, who witnessed the club land seven awards, from Ruud Gullit to Marco van Basten's treble, George Weah, Andriy Shevchenko and Kaka.

"Fans follow individuals - the players - rather than the club themselves. It's a widespread phenomenon, which we see, for example, in politics too.

"Once upon a time, you'd be a Milan fan and go to watch Milan. Today, everything is live and with the Champions League you always get to see all the great stars straight away.

"I must say this makes me feel a bit nostalgic, because the event is always immediate. Anticipation creates that sense of longing which has now disappeared."

Are fans now more invested in star names than clubs?

Messi and Ronaldo's brilliance, and often tribal online following, has also driven an increased emphasis on individual records - among fans, media and the players who grew up dreaming of emulating them.

"You could argue we are in a more interesting time because for basically 15 years it was Messi v Ronaldo and it certainly feels more open. It is a different play now," adds Kirkham.

"The social noise is deafening, relentless, all-consuming - every fan has an insatiable appetite, every point is riffed on, reacted to, but you also have this domino effect in microcosms of the media on every platform."

Clips go viral - a great goal, magical piece of skill, a dazzling dribble - but so do opinions.

"Now a solitary word on a broadcast can get played out as tweets, reacted to by creators and ex-players in video content that exists on reels and shorts and stories, that gets back-played through radio and on TV screens," adds Kirkham.

"It's the whole ecosystem, the manner in which it amplifies across these different spaces and platforms, then it generates narratives.

"No-one is doing anything wrong, creating something they believe is resonating with their audience. But en masse that is a machine, a fierce output that is generated for a player or against a player or whatever that may be."

Braida, who was at Barcelona when Messi won the 2015 prize, would agree: "These days, media exposure is absolutely crucial. With the advent of social media, the world has changed radically compared to my day.

"There's been a global transformation, and today we live in a small global village, because with the internet you can reach everywhere in real time."

This video can not be played

Harry Kane reflects on potential Ballon d'Or success

Michael Owen tells a story about how when Liverpool boss Gerard Houllier rang to break the news he had won the award in 2001, the 22-year-old did not even know what the Ballon d'Or was.

Owen engaged in a photoshoot at Liverpool's Melwood training ground a fortnight before the images were distributed to the media, with the striker officially presented the trophy on the Anfield pitch before a game against Derby County.

He was the first winner playing for an English club since Manchester United's George Best in 1968, the period in between dominated by Italian, Spanish and German teams.

From its launch in 1956 until 1995, when Weah became the first and so-far only African player to win it, only European players were eligible.

Only in 2007 did the award became truly global, open to players from any club - not just those representing European teams. Not until 2011 was it awarded at a glamorous ceremony. And only in 2018 was the women's prize launched.

"Winning the Ballon d'Or has an extremely positive impact," adds Braida. "We at AC Milan bought Kaka for around 7.5m euros and sold him for 67m euros [to Real Madrid].

"I must tell you, however, that in 2008, following his Ballon d'Or win in 2007, Manchester City made us a written offer of 105m euros. We're talking about a written offer, not a sounding-out or mere words.

"We were probably still in the early stages of certain commercial developments at that time, but now it clearly has a massive impact. Even back then, his value increased fivefold and winning the Ballon d'Or brought him global exposure and fame."

For someone like Three Lions captain Kane, hoping to become the first English winner in 25 years and only the fifth of all time, the prestige is huge - especially with the ceremony held in London to mark the 70th anniversary of Stanley Matthews winning the inaugural prize.

"It would be a massive achievement if it did happen," Kane said on Wednesday, having remained coy on his own chances.

Kane has done his share of recent interviews but others, such as Rio Ferdinand on Bayern's official social accounts, have made his case for him. "Ballon d'Or!"

He is, after all, vying to become Bayern's first winner since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge's second successive triumph in 1981. Not since Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer 30 years ago has it returned to the Bundesliga.

Bayern will also remember the case of Robert Lewandowski, who was widely tipped as favourite in 2020, scoring at an astonishing rate as the Bavarians won all six trophies available, including the Champions League, before the ceremony was cancelled because of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The Poland striker, who finished runner-up to Messi the following season, told BBC Sport last year the prize has become "part football, partly politics" and was "more commercial" than its counterpart, The Best Fifa Men's Player award.

Ballon d'Or snubs can cut deep. Franck Ribery said it felt "like a robbery" when he missed out to Ronaldo in 2013. Real Madrid boycotted the 2024 ceremony when they learned Manchester City midfielder Rodri would scoop the gong instead of Vinicius Junior.

"In Brazil, the hype is also giant," explains Caique Andrade, international football reporter at Globo. "When Vini didn't win the 2024 Ballon d'Or, there was a lot of commotion about it."

It may be an individual award, but winning is huge for clubs, too.

"This means an incredible impact in terms of popularity, visibility and also financial returns for the club," explains Braida. "Today, with the rise of social media and followers - factors that shape commercial aspects - this is even more true."

Kirkham concludes: "It is a global point - that means more audience and more eyeballs, and that means more money around the world."

Tiny ‘solar flares’ recreated in the lab may explain corona mystery

New Scientist October 22, 2026

With powerful lasers and a tiny piece of plastic, researchers have for the first time emulated a violent process that may take place on the sun. The experiment could help shed light on why the outermost layer of the sun’s atmosphere is so mysteriously hot.

For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why the sun’s outer atmospheric layers – a region called the corona – are thousands of times hotter than the sun’s surface, reaching several millions of degrees. “It is as if the air grew hotter as you walked away from a campfire,” says Wei Sun at the China Institute of Atomic Energy.

Now, Sun and his colleagues have emulated some of the conditions on the sun in the lab and, for the first time, observed how tiny bursts of electromagnetic radiation, or solar nanoflares, could power the corona’s puzzling heat.

Advertisement

Sunquakes may be caused by weird beams of electrons from solar flares

Nanoflares are known to occur when magnetic fields within the corona abruptly rearrange themselves and emit energy in the process. But for this rearrangement to happen, the exact conditions, such as the shape of the magnetic fields, must be just right, says Sun. He and his colleagues investigated how these conditions could arise and ultimately lead to nanoflares. They fired four very powerful lasers onto a tiny plastic target, which produced a patch of plasma – a hot mixture of charged particles – about 2 millimetres across. This plasma was not an exact recreation of plasma in the sun’s corona but behaved analogously.

The team created plasmas in two different scenarios, once using a flat target and once using one with a wavy surface. In the second case, the plasma became unstable and the magnetic fields it contained rearranged themselves and ultimately produced a nanoflare.

This nanoflare made a big difference to the temperature of the plasma. It reached temperatures of 799,726°C, which was nearly double the temperature achieved in the flat target version of the experiment where no nanoflares occurred.

A similar process – instability leading to nanoflares leading to plasma heating – could feasibly happen on the sun, says Sun. In fact, the parameters that determined their tiny plasma’s behaviour matched those observed in regions of the sun where blobs of colder plasma “rain” down through the corona. He and his colleagues also completed a computer simulation that corroborated this.

Coronal holes allow more charged particles to escape the sun as solar winds, and on 29 January, NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory spacecraft spotted a vast new one

Rony Keppens at KU Leuven in Belgium says that these simulations support the team’s interpretation of the experiment and make for an interesting entry on to the list of effects that may be contributing to coronal heating. Coronal rain blobs really could lead to the kinds of instabilities that the researchers now spotted in the lab, he says. Yet, in Keppens’s view, the new experiment does not definitively resolve the coronal heating puzzle, as other plasma behaviours, such as certain types of waves in it, could also contribute to it.

Going forward, Sun and his colleagues want to upgrade their experiment to create more three-dimensional plasmas and use more precise techniques for diagnosing its behaviour. And they want to make their laboratory measurements more directly comparable to reality – for example, by using data about the sun collected through telescopes, says Sun. “It is important to check that the laboratory is reproducing what the sun does,” he says.

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/tmll-158c

Earth entered its ‘bad decades’ after dinosaur-ending asteroid strike

New Scientist October 22, 2026

Decades of chaos and destruction, filled with devastating earthquakes and tsunamis, followed the asteroid strike 66 million years ago that wiped out all dinosaurs apart from birds.

The long-term global chaos inflicted by the Chicxulub asteroid, which was up to 15 kilometres in diameter and struck what is now the Gulf of Mexico, has been revealed through analysis of sediments preserved on the New Jersey coast, thousands of kilometres away from the impact crater.

It has become increasingly apparent in recent years that the asteroid’s effects weren’t confined to a single, disastrously bad day, but instead lasted a lot longer. For instance, the deformation of the crust to a depth of 35 kilometres left the impact site hot for millions of years.

Advertisement

We could protect Earth from dangerous asteroids using a huge magnet

It is also now thought that in the shorter term, a catastrophic maelstrom of fire engulfed much of the planet as debris that was hurled into space rained back down on Earth, burning up as it re-entered the atmosphere.

“Earth’s ‘bad day’ is when the Chicxulub impact occurred,” says Kenneth Miller at Rutgers University in New Jersey. “However, that was just the beginning of the story.”

The asteroid strike unleashed an earthquake felt around the world that was between magnitude 10 and 11, creating tsunamis that may have been a kilometre high close to the impact zone.

“Chicxulub rung the bell of the planet, and then it continued to ring for decades,” says Miller.

Free newsletter

“These deposits in New Jersey change our view about how long organisms were exposed to extremely detrimental environmental degradation,” he says. “That’s a fancy professor way of saying shit was really bad for 20 years.”

The researchers took rock cores from multiple sites on the New Jersey coastal plain, more than 2500 kilometres from the impact crater, to study the geology in the area in the years following the disaster.

These cores show that sediment layers deposited after the fallout from the asteroid were mixed and remobilised multiple times.

Such reworking of deposits is only possible through large, ongoing earthquakes and tsunamis, says Miller. Possibly more than a dozen aftershocks, which may have been in the order of magnitude 7 and 8, were felt on the New Jersey coast alone.

Earliest alligator flourished in the wake of the dinosaur extinction

Miller and his colleagues say the cores recovered from New Jersey record the transition from the catastrophic moments following the Chicxulub impact right through to a longer-term disruption, a period they have now named Earth’s “bad decades”.

Another intriguing finding from the New Jersey cores is the presence of large quantities of kaolinite, which normally forms over centuries from weathering in tropical regions, but may have formed in just years at the team’s study sites.

This could have been due to the presence of vast amounts of fungi, which can accelerate the formation of kaolinite, says Miller. The team speculates this is possible evidence that, during the nuclear winter-like conditions thought to have followed the impact, much of the planet’s vegetation died, providing a veritable feast for microorganisms.

Top predators still prowled the seas after the biggest mass extinction

The team has developed a new timeline for the first 20 years post-asteroid, beginning with the extraordinary and dramatic events of the first day.

This was followed by dust settling back to Earth from the atmosphere, leading to near-complete darkness for up to three years, followed by nuclear winter-like conditions for up to 20 years and fungal proliferation. All the while, the planet was beset by aftershocks and tsunamis.

“New Jersey preserves one of the highest-resolution records yet recovered of the first decades after Chicxulub, allowing researchers to resolve environmental and geological processes year-by-year to decade-by-decade, rather than viewing the aftermath as a single catastrophic instant,” says Miller.

Craig O’Neill at Queensland University of Technology, Australia, says the team has presented a record that “lets us really unpick what was going on immediately after the impact”.

“This builds on a long compendium of work globally suggesting that the environmental and biological impacts of ‘mega-events’ like Chicxulub go far beyond the impact blast itself,” he says.

The Chicxulub impact 66 million years ago filled the sky with fine silicate dust, which blocked out sunlight and lingered for 15 years

Chris Kirkland at Curtin University, Australia, says the site records processes that operated over years to decades after the impact, rather than simply its immediate aftermath.

“The really interesting aspect of the study is the potential to resolve not just the immediate consequences of the impact, including ejecta fallout, sediment reworking and tsunami-related processes, but the longer-lasting environmental disturbance,” he says.

Annemarie Pickersgill at the University of Glasgow, UK, says the New Jersey findings provide further evidence for long-term seismicity also recorded in other regions of Earth.

“These [New Jersey] sites preserve a detailed record of the geological and environmental conditions in the decades following the Chicxulub impact, providing new insights into the aftereffects of a very large impact event,” she says.

EarthArXiv DOI: 10.31223/X5Z215

All tropical coral reefs could collapse within 50 years

New Scientist October 22, 2026

Imagine a world without tropical coral reefs, a world nearly devoid of iconic species like elkhorn and pillar corals and sea creatures like the clownfish from Finding Nemo. That world could come to pass within 50 years due to humanity’s continuing fossil fuel emissions.

At least 96 per cent of shallow-water coral reef ecosystems are at extremely high risk of collapsing by 2075, according to an assessment by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the leading authority on endangered species. The remaining ecosystems weren’t evaluated due to lack of data, but are probably just as vulnerable, according to Marcos Valderrábano at the IUCN.

“All coral reef ecosystems that we assess, they are all critically endangered, and that’s really surprising,” he says. “In some regions of the world, there is a lot of bleaching, but some other regions of the world are not doing that bad. But what the projections are telling us is that this is going to be affecting all coral ecosystems in the planet in the next 50 years.”

Advertisement

Fishers detonate a bomb every hour on one Indonesian coral reef

The IUCN assessment was presented at the biannual UN biodiversity summit now taking place in Armenia. It shows countries where they need to protect reefs by reducing fishing quotas and pollution, according to Valderrábano.

Scientists have previously cautioned that warm-water coral reefs are probably crossing a tipping point beyond which they couldn’t recover, but the IUCN warning demonstrates how quickly and massively reef die-offs could unfold.

The shallow reefs in tropical and subtropical waters undergird ecosystems that can include thousands of species of corals, molluscs, fish and larger vertebrates like sea turtles and sharks. They cover only 1 per cent of the ocean, but support 25 per cent of marine species. Up to 1 billion people rely on coral reefs for fishing, as well as for tourism income and for protection from erosion and storms.

Free newsletter

While small pockets of coral could live on after the collapse of larger ecosystems like the Great Barrier Reef, they could become too dispersed for the eggs and sperm they release into the water to cross-fertilise.

“If the population size gets so small that you don’t have another coral to mate with nearby, then reproductive failure will happen,” says James Guest at Newcastle University, UK. “That species is in what’s called an extinction vortex.”

Coral reefs also exist in deeper, colder waters, including around the UK coast, but they are much less biodiverse and corals there don’t form symbiotic relationships with algae.

Coral reefs on a remote archipelago shrugged off a massive heatwave

So far, only one shallow-water coral reef ecosystem has collapsed. The reefs of the western Galapagos Islands lost 95 per cent of their coral – the IUCN’s threshold for ecosystem collapse – after the 1982/83 super El Niño climate phase unleashed a marine heatwave, turning golden brush corals into white skeletons overgrown by string algae.

But since then, four mass bleaching events have devastated many other corals. These animals form a symbiotic relationship with algae, which live inside the coral’s tissue and provide it with sugar from photosynthesis. However, algae stressed by warming or polluted waters can give off damaging reactive compounds like free radicals. It is thought that corals temporarily eject the colourful algae in self-defence, leaving the coral a ghostly white. If the warming lasts long enough, the corals essentially starve to death.

All these mass bleaching events came after strong El Niños, and experts fear the current record El Niño will usher in another one. Regardless, individual reefs are now bleaching nearly every year due to global warming, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Yet another mass-bleaching event could speed up coral collapse, since reef ecosystems don’t have time to recover if they are hit by more than three bleaching events within five years, says Valderrábano. “It would definitely reinforce that perverse loop,” he says.

Bleaching has devastated reefs around the world, raising fears of an irreversible shift. Yet new interventions have revealed that corals can be remarkably resilient if we can give them enough help to recover

The IUCN projection is based on a “middle-of-the-road” scenario with moderate emissions reductions. Advertisement

These studies were often based on a single task, like imagining alternative uses for everyday objects, says Benedek. Taking a broader approach, he and his colleagues recruited 92 children (aged between 4 and 7) and 70 adults (aged 25, on average) to carry out three creative tasks.

First, they had to come up with as many alternative uses for a tin can as possible within 3 minutes. Then, they drew freely for 8 minutes, and in the final task, they had 8 minutes to draw an animal that doesn’t exist.

Five people who weren’t involved in the research were then trained to objectively judge creativity based on originality and whether the final result fulfilled the brief of the task.

In the first task, the adults scored 3.9 points, on average, out of 5, while the children scored 2.9 points. One of the adults imagined a tin can could be used as a “Halloween candy box when on (a) diet”, whereas some children imagined it as a rattle.

In the second and third tasks, the adults scored 0.6 and 1.9 points higher, respectively, than the children.

After completing the tasks, the participants were asked questions like “How well do you think you performed the task?”, “How much were you worried/anxious to not perform well on the task?” and “How much fun was the task?”.

The researchers found that the children were substantially more confident in what they produced, scoring their performances 4.8 and 4.6 points for the free drawing and animal tasks, respectively, compared with the adults’ 2.8 and 3.3 scoring.

Engaging with the arts has been linked to reduced mental health problems and greater social skills. “Creativity, especially when done with other people, is really beneficial to your mental wellbeing – and you don’t have to score 5 out of 5 on a ranking scale,” she says.

The issue actually involves two flaws, both found by cloud security company Wiz. They relate to how PHP handles errors involving memory: in certain circumstances, data can be left behind after an error, which can then be accessed by a malicious actor. That data can include private information, but it can also allow an attacker to run malicious code.

Every PHP version released in the past decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, but the PHP Foundation, which oversees development, has already issued an update to overcome this.

The foundation didn’t respond to a request for interview, but said in a blog post that signs of the vulnerability emerged in 2024. Yet nothing was done. This is because there was no immediately obvious practical way for hackers to exploit it at the time, and because there was debate about which of several fixes was most appropriate.

Free newsletter

“We won’t pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team’s decision process and its lack of resources,” the PHP Foundation said.

In 2024, the flaw was thought to be impractical to take advantage of, but Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey, UK, says AI has moved the goalposts of what is possible since then.

“It’s actually very, very difficult to exploit it. It requires millisecond timing,” says Woodward. “The reason it was thought to be too complicated was it would have taken a team of people yonks to actually work out the right timings. But what AI does, it doesn’t go for tea breaks, it doesn’t go home at 6 o’clock: you can just set loads of them running and eventually they’ll come up with the right answer of how to exploit it.”

Wiz said in a blog post announcing the discovery that there are probably further bugs along similar lines in the PHP code base, which developers will also need to identify and rectify. Wiz didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Independent cybersecurity expert Junade Ali told the Science Media Centre that two thirds of websites use PHP and may be vulnerable to this latest technique.

“The key long-term risk with these new vulnerabilities is that organisations fail to implement protections and update software, particularly in legacy systems,” said Ali. “The security posture of websites using PHP has dramatically improved over the past decade, but this highlights that this is an ever-present problem – particularly when AI agents are capable of remorselessly pursuing the goal of finding new vulnerabilities.”

Woodward thinks that while most large websites will have already patched their systems, smaller sites with less expertise and resources could still be vulnerable months or years from now. “There will be this long tail and you’ll find some surprising sites have not been patched,” he says.

AI has grown extremely capable in the field of cybersecurity over recent months, which includes working out how to hack computers and how to defend them from hackers, creating a destabilising effect that is yet to reach an equilibrium.

A personalised mRNA vaccine for melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, is expected to be approved for use in the US, Europe and the UK next year. The vaccine is designed to stimulate immune responses against genetic mutations that are unique to an individual’s cancer. When used alongside standard treatment in a late-stage trial, it substantially cut the risk of cancer recurrence or death within the next two years.

“I think approval could be quick, and next year sounds reasonable,” says Alan Melcher at the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn’t involved in the trial.

“It is a huge deal,” says Rebecca Lee at the University of Manchester, UK, who also wasn’t involved. Thousands of people in the UK alone could benefit from this, based on the trial’s patient population, she says. “It’s highly likely the US and Europe [including the UK] will approve it next year.” However, producing the vaccine is very expensive, and it may not be deemed cost-effective for use on the UK’s National Health Services (NHS), she says.

Advertisement

In August, drug-maker Moderna announced that the vaccine had positive results in a late-stage trial. More specific findings have now been released.

The trial recruited more than 1100 adults who had surgery to remove high-risk melanomas that were likely to recur or spread to distant sites. In the UK, 19,400 melanoma cases are diagnosed annually, of which about 25 per cent are deemed high risk.

Two-thirds of the participants were randomly assigned to receive a bespoke vaccine on top of standard immunotherapy, called pembrolizumab, which helps the immune system find and destroy cancer. Both were delivered every three weeks for up to a year. The remaining participants received placebo injections plus pembrolizumab.

The vaccine is made by genetically sequencing a small sample of a person’s cancer and comparing that sequence with the DNA in the individual’s healthy blood cells. This enables researchers to pinpoint mutations specific to the cancer.

Free newsletter

Based on the same technology used in covid-19 vaccines, the cancer vaccine contains mRNA molecules that encode for proteins with up to 34 of those mutations. “The jab contains a fingerprint of proteins specifically associated with the cancer,” says Lee. “This helps [immune] T-cells recognise the cancer better, and then pembrolizumab prevents those T-cells from becoming exhausted once they’ve started attacking the cancer cells.”

About two years after the start of treatment, 82 per cent of the participants who received the vaccine plus pembrolizumab were alive without their cancer recurring, on average, compared with 70 per cent among those on pembrolizumab alone. “It’s a really exciting result,” says Lee. Side effects were similar between the two groups.

The results combine cancer recurrence and death rates into one figure, but since a treated cancer has to recur for it to cause death, this combined measure should be interpreted mostly as a sign of the vaccine reducing recurrence, says Melcher. The participants haven’t been tracked for long enough to robustly determine whether the vaccine improves survival rates. These results should be available within a few years, says Lee.

We have long treated cancer based on its location in the body. But a whole new approach that analyses tumours differently is now helping people survive forms of cancer that were once considered a death sentence

But because the vaccine has to be tailored to and manufactured for each individual, it is expected to be very costly, which could affect NHS access. “If it was a cheap drug, I’d definitely say it will get approved [for NHS use], but it’s going to be expensive,” says Lee. In January, a report by Reuters suggested it would cost around $200,000 per treatment. Moderna and Merck (also known as MSD), which was also involved in the vaccine’s development, did not respond to a request about its cost.

Further research is needed to better understand who is mostly likely to benefit from the vaccine, says Melcher. Some people may have mutations included in their vaccine that fail to stimulate anti-cancer immunity as predicted, or pembrolizumab could work so well that the vaccine can’t lead to further improvement. “If we can find immune markers in the blood or tumour that predict patient responses, we could use those to determine who to give the jab to,” says Melcher.

James Larkin, also at the Institute of Cancer Research, says personalised vaccines could also work for other types of cancer, such as those affecting the lungs, bladder and kidneys, which are also routinely treated with immunotherapy. Further research is needed to verify this and explore whether the vaccines could work as standalone treatments.

Body temperature may drive the higher risk of autoimmune conditions in women

New Scientist October 23, 2026

The menstrual cycle and menopause mean that women’s body temperature fluctuates more than men’s, which could help explain why they are much more likely to develop autoimmune conditions. Our body temperature influences our immune response, and frequent fluctuations in women could affect their immune cells’ ability to differentiate between a dangerous invader and healthy tissue.

“If women’s immune cells are experiencing more changes in temperature, they might be getting more overwhelmed and dysfunctional, which could contribute to an increased risk of autoimmunity,” says Elizabeth Maloney at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, who presented the findings at the Immunology of the Exposome conference at the Royal Society in London on 12 October. “It could be one piece of the puzzle in understanding sex differences in immunity.”

We may finally have a cure for many different autoimmune conditions

Women generally mount stronger immune responses than men, making them less prone to infections. But this comes at a cost: women are up to four times more likely to develop autoimmune conditions, such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, which occur when the immune system overreacts to healthy tissue.

Advertisement

Such differences are due to several factors, including the genetics that determine sex. Most women have two copies of the X chromosome, which carries many immune genes, whereas most men have one X and one Y chromosome. This means women have greater genetic variation, strengthening their immune response.

Hormonal differences also play a role. Oestrogen, the main sex hormone in women, generally bolsters immune system activity in those of reproductive age, while declining levels during perimenopause and menopause seem to accelerate inflammation, which plays a big role in autoimmunity. Men’s main sex hormone, testosterone, generally reduces inflammation.

Now, Maloney and her colleagues have looked at the role of body temperature. They measured the core body temperatures of more than 900 adults, aged between 20 and 69, via a thermometer in the inner ear. The group was made up of a roughly equal number of men and women, none of whom had a known autoimmune condition.

Free newsletter

The researchers also collected blood samples, which they exposed to a powerful immune-stimulating protein from Staphylococcus aureus bacteria in a test tube.

The one-off temperature readings were similar between the men and women. But among the women’s blood samples, a higher body temperature was linked to suppression of T-cells in response to the protein. T-cells are part of the adaptive immune system, which responds to threats like viruses or – inappropriately – to molecules in the body. The latter response can bring about autoimmune conditions.

Among the women’s samples, the researchers found that every 1°C (1.8°F) increase in body temperature was linked to a 36 per cent decrease in these cells’ ability to produce interferon-gamma. This is an inflammatory protein that enhances the ability of T-cells to attack target cells, whether they are healthy or infected.

“This may be counterintuitive because we generally think of fever as stimulating inflammation,” says team member Darragh Duffy, also at the Pasteur Institute. But it seems there is also a mechanism by which high temperature can dial down the immune response to stop it getting out of hand, he says.

One interpretation of the sex differences in the results is that the more frequent temperature fluctuations experienced by women caused their T-cells to switch between suppressed and activated states more often, says Maloney.

Antibodies mistakenly attacking the brain are linked with conditions including schizophrenia, dementia and OCD, prompting a revolution in how we think about mental health conditions

The core body temperature of premenopausal women rises by about 0.6°C (around 1°F), on average, after ovulation, then falls a day or two before menstruation. Perimenopause and menopause can also cause sudden increases in body temperature, manifesting as hot flushes. “Maybe the adaptive immune system is having to constantly change its set point, which sort of wears it out, and then that contributes to autoimmune risk,” says Maloney.

“The findings add another dimension to sex differences in immune function,” says Sabra Klein at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. Future studies should examine whether body temperature affects immune responses between men and women independently of their hormonal differences, she says.

They could also track links between the menstrual cycle, body temperature and T-cell response, says Maloney. For now, the team is working with another group of researchers to implement body-temperature measurements in a vaccine trial starting next year, she says.

Why do mathematicians keep proving things they already know?

New Scientist October 23, 2026

Earlier this month, I wrote a story about how OpenAI had inadvertently produced two versions of its proof of the Navier-Stokes problem. You can read the details here, but one thing that has stuck with me is that some non-mathematically minded people I spoke to about the story struggled with the idea that two different proofs of the same problem could both be correct. It got me thinking about how and why mathematicians prove things multiple times – and what happens when it goes wrong.

One thing it’s important to grasp is that proofs are not homework problems. A couple of mathematicians have made this point to me recently: because most people’s experience of maths begins and ends at school, there is a perception that mathematicians are simply working down a big list of problems and writing answers to be ticked off by some sort of cosmic maths teacher. This is not the case – proofs are a way of organising and developing mathematical thinking. You can think of a proof as a journey, from statement to conclusion – and as with many journeys, there are many routes you can take to get from A to B. This is where we get multiple proofs of the same problem.

Terence Tao’s Six Maths Essentials opens his field to all of us

This act of reproving, of taking the mathematical road not yet travelled, dates back to antiquity. One of the earliest examples is the statement that an isosceles triangle always has two equal sides and two equal angles at the base. Writing around 350 BC, Aristotle describes a proof of this that involves drawing lines from the centre of a circle to its circumference – the original author of that proof is lost. Around 50 years later, Euclid described a proof that only requires triangles, not circles. This neatly avoided a mathematical disagreement about how to define angles formed between a straight line and a curved line – a question that wasn’t settled for thousands of years, as it happened.

Advertisement

Euclid also crops up in another example that shows how useful it is to keep attacking “solved” problems. He recorded a proof that there are infinitely many primes, and you may have learnt it at school. Suppose you have a finite list of primes. If you multiply them all together, you get a new number, P. Now, define q = P + 1. If q is prime, it can’t have been on the list, because it is bigger than P. If q isn’t, it must instead be divisible by a prime, as all non-primes are. If that prime we divide by had been on the list, it must also divide P, but that must also mean it divides q – P = 1, which is impossible. Either way, we have identified a prime not on the original list.

According to a 2023 survey, they are now 200 different proofs of Euclid’s theorem, as it is known. One that particularly added to mathematical knowledge at the time was published by Leonhard Euler in 1737, who found a formula that related the sum of all numbers to the product of all primes. He also used this to hint at the structure of the primes – not only that there are infinitely many, but that they become sparser as you go up the number line. Euler’s formula inspired Bernard Riemann over a century later to propose the Riemann hypothesis, a deep question about the structure of prime numbers that is considered one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in maths today – so it was well worth Euler having another crack at Euclid.

Perhaps surprisingly, there are even times when mathematicians have produced multiple proofs of the same theorem before revealing a flaw in the reasoning. In 1933, mathematician Wilhelm Grunwald published a proof showing that a number, a, with a certain property in relation to all prime numbers, must always be able to be written as some other number, x, raised to the nth power, so a = xn. A second mathematician, George Whaples, gave a new proof of this using slightly different maths in 1942. But then in 1948, Shianghao Wang found that actually, this isn’t true for 16, because 16 isn’t equal to x8 for any x. The correct result is now known as the Grunwald-Wang theorem.

Hannah Fry: How OpenAI has caused an existential crisis in mathematics

Pleasingly, researchers have even studied the idea of taking proof journeys mathematically. In a 2022 paper, Scott Viteri at Stanford University and Simon DeDeo at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania point out that if a mathematical proof is a sequence of logical steps, each with a tiny probability of a mistake, the odds are that a long enough proof is more likely to be wrong than not. Roll enough times, and the dice will be extremely likely to land on a 1. How then can mathematicians prove anything?

The pair show that a mathematical proof is structured like a network, with “truth” being transmitted along paths between each step, exactly like a journey. With the potential for error at each step, the strength of this truth diminishes along longer paths. But proofs aren’t random walks around a conceptual arena – they have structure, and claims are often reinforced by multiple routes. This structure allows truth to be transmitted along the strongest paths, even if it fails along other routes. Because of this, the network undergoes what the pair call an “epistemic phase transition”, a scenario under which you can be extremely certain the proof is correct.

This is just a model, and not necessarily something accepted by all mathematicians, but I find it appealing. It also fits with what you would naturally expect: the more proofs mathematicians have of a result, the more paths that are carved from A to B, the more certain you can be that it is true. In an age when AI is beginning to produce maths that humans don’t necessarily understand, we might find that having multiple routes to the truth, whether human or AI derived, can bring confidence where we might otherwise have uncertainty.

Dellow punched one man 12 times to the head and face. Several of his associates then joined the assault, surrounding the man and repeatedly punching and kicking him.

Judge Richard Earwaker said Dellow could have used his seniority in the gang to stop the violence, rather than aggravate it.

“Everyone else climbed in because he was,” Judge Earwaker said.

One of the associates, Christopher Wirihana, who was involved in attacks on three people, later told police: “I saw some people I knew attacking, so I jumped in.”

Dellow admitted 10 charges, including injuring with intent, male assaults female and common assault.

He was sent to prison for two years and seven months. He has already been in custody for more than six months, which will count towards that sentence.

Ratahi Caleb Rawiri Lay admitted two charges against two victims in the Common Room brawl, and his sentence also took into account two assaults he committed in an unrelated incident at Mangakino last year.

He received 12 months of home detention.

Wirihana admitted four charges against his three victims.

Jhon Charles Hanara faced three charges against three victims.

Masyn Ratima pleaded guilty to five charges against five victims.

They all received six months of community detention, involving being on an ankle bracelet with a night-time curfew, and 12 months of intensive supervision by a probation officer.

In addition to Dellow’s assault on the woman he uppercut, the summary of facts described attacks by Dellow on two other women.

He twice punched one of them in the face with such force that she fell backwards to the ground, in separate assaults about five minutes apart.

Contact the Open Justice team

On the second occasion, she got back onto her feet and raised her hands and arms in an attempt to ward off any further blows.

Dellow then punched her in the face again, causing her to fall once more.

He assaulted the third woman while she had her arms around the second woman, trying to protect her.

Dellow punched the third woman in the face also, causing her head to snap backwards.

Ric Stevens spent many years working for the former New Zealand Press Association news agency, including as a political reporter at Parliament, before holding senior positions at various daily newspapers. He joined NZME’s Open Justice team in 2022 and is based in Hawke’s Bay.

India Free Trade Agreement is a chance to build a smarter export economy – Fran O’Sullivan

New Zealand Herald October 23, 2026

The India Free Trade Agreement came into force this week.

With just two weeks to go before the November 7 election, Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins remain at each other’s throats politically.

But their trade champions, Todd McClay and Damien O’Connor, kicked all that infighting to the kerb on Thursday as they came together to celebrate the coming into force of the Indian Free Trade Agreement (FTA).

The stellar crowd down at The Cloud on Auckland’s Queen’s Wharf appreciated this. There was no awkwardness. Both politicians were generous in acknowledging the role each played in getting this historic deal over the line – McClay and top trade negotiator Vangelis Vitalis for getting the deal done against India Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal’s aggressive team; O’Connor for painstakingly getting Labour colleagues to support a bipartisan agreement.

The agreement did not command unanimous parliamentary support, but cross-party engagement on trade provides a foundation for businesses seeking confidence that important economic relationships will endure as governments change.

McClay was buoyed up. He had just been rated by chief executives as the second top-performing, “very impressive” Cabinet minister in the Herald’s Mood of the Boardroom survey.

Chief executives rated trade and cementing the FTA highest among the policies executed by the coalition Government this term.

The Prime Minister deserves praise here. Luxon set an ambitious objective to secure an India FTA in the coalition’s first term in office. There are wrinkles that will have to be addressed. But they succeeded.

The Indian deal also provided a backdrop to Westpac’s Strategic Outlook Forum – Navigating Disruption: What Matters Next in Geopolitics, Technology, Capital and Leadership, which took place earlier in the week.

The cliche goes: New Zealand is the “last bus stop on the planet”. It has been used in countless presentations to underpin that this country suffers from “the tyranny of distance” (another cliche).

International thought-leader and keynote speaker Samir Saran was blunt that the map is out of date. “The old order is dead, the new one is not yet born, and we are living in the interim,” the president of the Observer Research Foundation told business leaders, paraphrasing Italian political theorist Antonio Gramsci.

Saran is also a member of the Global Risks Advisory Board and co-chair of the Global Future Council on Geopolitics at the World Economic Forum.

He sees the global order being reshaped by three forces: more conflict, an information-saturated world in which trust is scarce, and an intensifying contest for technological supremacy.

“Trump will go, but Trumpism may not,” he warned, urging business leaders to prepare for lasting structural change rather than assume that disruption will end after the 2028 US presidential election.

His challenge to New Zealand was to turn its international reputation into practical influence. That means abandoning the reflex to think of itself primarily in terms of its distance from the world’s centres of power – that positioned between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, New Zealand has an opportunity to build relationships across regions whose economic and political weight is growing.

Saran sees scope for New Zealand to become a useful hub, providing services and capabilities that matter to the wider world. Digital infrastructure could be one such opportunity: a stable location offering an alternative for global data services when geopolitical disruption threatens established networks.

But he offered a crucial qualification.

“Don’t become the plan B of everyone. Become the plan B of anyone.”

In his view, New Zealand should identify specific markets, partners and services where it can be a credible, valuable alternative. That proposition depends on reliable energy, predictable investment and data rules, resilient infrastructure and institutions that can withstand scrutiny.

The opportunity to make that shift comes into sharper focus with the Indian FTA. The agreement opens the door wider to one of the world’s major growth markets.

From day one, almost 57% of New Zealand’s exports to India became tariff-free. That proportion is scheduled to rise to 82% over time, with 95% of current exports eventually benefiting from tariff removal or reductions.

The real prize in Saran’s view is the opportunity to build a deeper economic relationship with India at a time when New Zealand needs to diversify its markets and reduce concentrated exposure to geopolitical risk.

His argument is that New Zealand’s agricultural expertise, food-processing capabilities, technology and services could help improve productivity and develop value chains in India. That requires partnerships, investment and a willingness to understand the market over the long term.

Further, New Zealand cannot afford to confine its economic future to a narrow group of partners or allow geopolitical rivalries to dictate every commercial relationship.

It must be capable of working across competing powers while remaining clear-eyed about its own interests and vulnerabilities.

India should not simply become another market in which New Zealand repeats its existing export model. The opportunity is to build a more sophisticated relationship connecting businesses, research institutions, technology companies and skilled people, as well as exporters and importers.

That will demand choices, and Saran was explicit about the need for strategic focus.

“You can’t do everything for everyone. You have to do a few things for everyone,” he said.

For New Zealand, that means identifying the industries and capabilities where it can become exceptional and globally important, rather than spreading scarce resources across an endless list of ambitions.

Digital infrastructure, advanced agricultural technology, food innovation and specialised services may all offer opportunities, but each requires a credible proposition and the investment to deliver it.

Attracting high-calibre talent will also be essential if those industries are to be built at scale. A strategy based on innovation and specialised expertise cannot succeed if New Zealand fails to attract the people who can develop it.

Saran pointed to countries such as Singapore and the United Arab Emirates, which seek to maintain commercial relationships across competing powers.

New Zealand cannot replicate their circumstances, but it can learn from their determination to create strategic relevance rather than rely on geography or goodwill.

Conflict, technological rivalry and economic coercion are likely to remain features of the international environment.

Diversifying markets, strengthening domestic capabilities and embedding geopolitical risk in boardroom decisions are all part of staying competitive.

Saran’s message is that New Zealand cannot control the new global order, but it can decide what it brings to the table: trusted institutions, reliable infrastructure, distinctive expertise and economic relationships built to last.

A strategy for whichever coalition runs New Zealand after November 7 to contemplate?

New Zealand Herald October 23, 2026

The team of Dutch cyclist Marijn Maas has denied that he deliberately spat at Kiwi rider Kiaan Watts before being punched during a race in the Netherlands this year.

During the Salverda Bouw Ster van Zwolle on March 7, cameras captured Watts punching Maas in the head while racing, making global headlines.

Watts was disqualified from the race, and his NSN Development Team suspended him for 25 days.

The Kiwi had remained quiet about his side of the story until this week, when he told Newstalk ZB, he reacted after Maas allegedly spat in his face.

Watts acknowledged there needed to be consequences for his actions but believed some of the criticism he received was unfair, saying he had been sent abusive messages, including some telling him to kill himself.

However, BEAT Cycling performance director Thijs Zonneveld told the Herald that Maas denied spitting at Watts deliberately or knowingly and had been shocked by the punch and the media attention it attracted.

“Marijn denies to have spat at Mr Watts,” Zonneveld said. “He did not know him or had a problem with him in the race before the blow on his head.

“We looked at the footage of the race and couldn’t find anything that suggests otherwise. It would be very, very much out of character from him to do such a thing.”

Zonneveld also defended Maas’ character, describing him as a shy person who would be unlikely to deliberately instigate such an incident.

“He was completely surprised by Mr Watts’ blow on his head - you can see that as well in the way he reacted,” Zonneveld said.

“He has been shocked by what happened; we had several talks with him in the week afterwards because he was flabbergasted by what happened and the attention in the media the incident provoked.”

Watts told Newstalk ZB that Maas had taken issue with the way he was racing before allegedly turning around and spitting at him, with saliva going over his face and into his mouth.

“I just saw red and proceeded to sprint up next to him on the front of the peloton and what happened, happened,” Watts said.

“If I could go back and redo everything again, I definitely would have probably kept my composure, but that’s just how things played out. What I did was definitely the wrong thing to do, but what he did was also the wrong thing.”

The fallout for Watts has extended beyond his suspension and the online abuse, which he said led to him seeing a sports psychologist, and searching for a new team for next year.

Watts said he was disappointed with how contract negotiations unfolded, claiming promises were not kept and communication from management was lacking as he sought clarity over his future.

He said he had been left chasing an answer about whether he would be retained, with confirmation only arriving in mid-September.

NSN have re-signed fellow New Zealanders George Bennett, Corbin Strong and Dion Smith.

Watts said he now had one or two concrete offers on the table while awaiting responses from other teams.

Ben Francis is an Auckland-based reporter for the New Zealand Herald who covers breaking sports news.

Tairāwhiti forestry group gets wider land-use transition role

New Zealand Herald October 23, 2026

Pilots on land-use transition and sustainable forestry on hillsides will inform policy and funding decisions, according to Forestry Minister Todd McClay, pictured with East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick. Photo / Gisborne Herald

A refocused advisory group and redirected funding aim to tackle woody debris, land use and forestry in Tairāwhiti.

While Government-appointed facilitation and a Gisborne District Council-ordered independent review take place, Forestry Minister Todd McClay said the changes will co-ordinate regional work.

The former Tairāwhiti Forestry Action Group has been refocused as the Tairāwhiti Transition Advisory Group (TTAG), with a “wider mandate” to support regional resilience and land-use transition.

“No one organisation can fix the challenges facing Tairāwhiti on its own. The group’s wider role will help join up the work across the region and keep it focused on the long term,” McClay said.

The group had begun operating.

The Government also redirected the remaining $16.4 million from a $27m Ministry for Primary Industries woody debris package towards debris clean-up and pilot projects.

“Clearing it [debris], and catching what does come loose before it gets into the rivers, protects vital infrastructure. It’s also work for local contractors over the coming season,” he said.

The pilots will explore sustainable logging on hillsides, land-use change and slash traps to reduce debris entering waterways.

Initial work will prioritise high-risk areas and work with landowners to address barriers such as harvesting risks, consent requirements and establishment costs.

The results would help inform future policy and funding decisions, he said.

Council chief executive Nedine Thatcher Swann said it represented an important step towards addressing the challenges caused by vulnerable terrain and extreme weather.

“We need a future where forestry can continue on appropriate land, harvesting is undertaken well, and land carrying the greatest risk has a realistic pathway to transition.”

Council had worked closely with central government, mana whenua and regional partners to establish the refocused group.

“It gives us an opportunity to build on the evidence, relationships and practical work already developed, strengthen co-ordination and move towards delivery.

“The next step is testing different land-use options in real situations and identifying approaches that could be applied more widely across Tairāwhiti.”

The council pointed to Te Ārai demonstration catchment as work underway, building off local efforts, and working with landowners to develop property plans and a catchment transition plan.

“This is about finding the right land use for the right place, while supporting viable livelihoods and reducing risks to communities and the environment.”

It said the issue required all parties to work together from the same evidence to find solutions to protect communities and support the economy.

Eastland Wood Council chairman Julian Kohn said the region had been through tough years, and the council wanted a future with resilient communities and continued opportunities for local families in forestry.

Some of the most erosion-prone land would need to transition, and he welcomed Government funding and recognition of a co-ordinated approach for land use changes.

“We’ve already seen the pressure on local contractors, workers, businesses and families who depend on the hundreds of millions of dollars forestry and wood processing contribute to Tairāwhiti’s economy each year.

“We can’t afford to lose more skilled workers and businesses while the region works towards a future that is enduring.”

He said the refocused TTAG would bring all parties together to create a workable plan for community protection and a stronger future for forestry in Tairāwhiti.

Henare Walker, interim chief executive of Ngāti Porou’s governance entity Te Rūnanganui o Ngāti Porou, said broadening focus to long-term land use transition was something Ngāti Porou had called for and it was encouraging for the iwi and the wider region.

“We have been saying that Ngāti Porou cannot keep focusing only on cleaning up after each major event. We have to deal with the bigger question of what land use should look like across the rohe and how we protect our whenua, our people and our economy for the future.

“For Ngāti Porou, the important thing now is making sure we are part of shaping that transition from the outset, so the decisions being made today deliver lasting benefits for our whenua and our people.”

He said the Government needed to consider existing commitments to Ngāti Porou and existing structures to determine the best response to the significant problem.

Working with Ngāti Porou to decide what tests, priorities and success levels were in pilots would be important, he said.

Mana Taiao Tairāwhiti spokesperson Manu Caddie welcomed recognition that land-use transition could reduce ongoing damage to the environment, infrastructure and properties.

However, he said the advisory group needed representation from affected communities, clear links with existing work, including the Land Use Transition Business Case, and transparent measures of progress.

“This could be a constructive first step, just a pity it has taken so long and is still not a comprehensive response from the minister.”

A clear implementation timetable, details on funding distribution and long-term investment were needed, he said.

“Communities deserve to know when the risk will actually start coming down.”

He hoped the Government would build on the rejected Transition Business Case to implement pest control, scientific research and “fit-for-purpose regulation”.

More evidence was needed on slash trap designs and placement, and how to remove mature trees from high-risk sites, he said.

Sustained investment in permanent indigenous cover, pest and weed management, and supported employment was needed to give landowners confidence in the transition, Caddie said.
