Brothers’ near-death ordeal on Lake Rotoiti sparks lifejacket warning

New Zealand Herald October 23, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Two brothers are sharing a warning forged in 90 minutes of fear and a desperate fight for survival: wear your lifejacket.

The warning comes as boaties prepare to hit the water this Labour Weekend.

In March last year, Ian and Allen Hurne went to help people on a sinking boat on Lake Rotoiti.

Within moments, both vessels had gone down, and the lifejackets aboard were out of reach.

“It happened in seconds. You don’t have time to think, you don’t have time to grab anything, the only thing that will save you is wearing a lifejacket.”

For 82-year-old Ian, who lives in Katikati, the experience shattered a belief formed over a lifetime on the water.

“I’ve been boating all my life, from when I was a youngster in Sea Scouts, and I’ve always carried a lifejacket on board,” he said.

“I never thought I needed to put it on because it’s not going to happen that quick, you think, you’ll have plenty of time to slip it on. But when the boat sank, it was seconds, not minutes.”

As Ian entered the lake water, he said he lost sight of his brother.

“I thought he was gone. Then I felt something brush against my leg. I didn’t know what part of him I had, but I grabbed hold and yanked him up; he came up huffing and puffing.”

The people Ian and Allen helped made it safely back to shore to raise the alarm.

The brothers were left in the lake, fighting to stay alive.

“Reflecting on the incident, I do get emotional,” Ian said.

“It really hit me afterwards when I sat down and started thinking about the ‘what ifs’.”

Ian now has a new rule he thinks everyone should adopt.

“No one steps foot on the boat without a lifejacket, not just carrying it but wearing it.

“We’ve learned a lesson, and I have to say it was a lesson we were extremely lucky to survive.”

The brothers’ warning comes as boaties head into the first major holiday weekend under new national lifejacket requirements.

Lifejackets are now required to be worn on all small vessels under a new maritime safety law adopted by Parliament.

The Maritime Transport (Lifejackets on Recreational Craft) Amendment Bill passed its third reading in Parliament in September, and the resulting act came into effect on October 9.

The law requires occupants of recreational boats 6m or less in length to wear a properly fitted lifejacket while the vessel is underway.

Ian’s younger brother Allen had travelled from his Gisborne home to Lake Rotoiti when the brothers’ boating trip turned into a fight for their lives.

His most “vivid memory” was being in the water with his brother clinging tightly to the boat.

“It just slowly dragged down, filled with water, and slid away; we had nothing,” said Ian.

“You always think, oh well, if something comes along, I’ll have time; there was no time, simple as that.”

After an hour and a half of “flopping around” in the water, he was exhausted.

“Suddenly there’s this desperate feeling like, am I going to be alive? Am I going to see my wife and kids again? Am I going to see my grandkids? How long can I keep this going?”

After 90 minutes, the brothers were rescued by a vessel responding to the Coastguard’s all-stations mayday call.

They were brought ashore by Coastguard volunteers, where emergency services were waiting.

Allen said the experience had made him a firm supporter of the new lifejacket legislation.

“It always puzzled me as to why you were required to have them, but not wear them.

“It goes wrong so quickly, you have no reaction time, and if talking about it helps more people to come home from a fishing trip then we’re all for it.”

Surviving the ordeal had brought the brothers even closer, giving them a deeper appreciation for their relationship, Allen said.

“When we sit down with a beer or something, we talk about it, and realise just how lucky we are.”

Coastguard Rotorua Lakes president Jeremy Doorman said the region’s lakes might appear sheltered, but they carried their own unique hazards.

“Freshwater is less buoyant than the ocean, so you don’t float as well, and conditions can also change quite quickly.”

While Coastguard NZ does not enforce lifejacket rules, a responsibility that falls to Maritime New Zealand, Doorman said lifejackets were a critical “line of defence” for keeping people safe on the water.

“In the absolute unfortunate event of a boat going down, which the brothers’ did, rather than having to swim and tread water, you can float.

“There shouldn’t be any panic stations trying to find lifejackets, as they should be on.”

Doorman encouraged boaties to take their time, seek local knowledge, wear lifejackets, carry waterproof communication devices, and let someone know their plans before heading out on the lakes this weekend.

“We’ve got some beautiful lakes around the region, but if you’re not from the area, take your time, and if you see a local at the boat ramp, have a chat to them.”

Kaitlyn Morrell is a journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post. She has lived in the region for several years and studied journalism at Massey University.

A TV joke gone wrong sparked an incredible backlash. Here’s how Reuben Kaye weathered that storm

Sydney Morning Herald October 24, 2026

Bullied as a child, publicly piled-on for a joke – how the cabaret star is having the last laugh.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No gift articles left

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Article gifting is here

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

The joke that nearly broke Reuben Kaye was meant to be the safer, softer, conservative option. The drag artist, comedian and cabaret star waltzed onto the set of Network 10’s The Project more than three years ago, dressed to the nines, wearing his warpaint, armed with his zingers and ready for his close-up. Live television is rarely truly live and unscripted, however, meaning Kaye had been provided with his big set-up question from the panel – How do people react to you? – well in advance.

Kaye is queer, and cutting, and so was his first draft reply: “How do people react to me? People have called me genre-bending, gender-bending, the boy next door – oops, sorry, that’s George Pell’s shopping list.” So far, so provocative. His second option? “Well, I get a bit of flak online. It all tends to come from the religious right, who say, ‘You have to accept Jesus or else you’ll burn in hell.’ And to them I say, ‘That’s ridiculous, I love any man who can get nailed for three days and come back for more.’ ”

Boom-tish. Structurally solid gag. Albeit well-worn territory. Almost a (dirty) dad joke, in the same blasphemous ballpark as some of Jimmy Carr’s stand-up, or a South Park episode. A producer thought it prudent to avoid Pell (who had died just one month prior) – better to do the Jesus one instead.

“So I went on, did it, everyone’s laughing, we shake hands, job done,” says Kaye, snacking on a Malteser. “Then I go back to the Airbnb I’ve got for the night on tour, and I can see this counter of clips on TikTok and Instagram going up and up and up. And up.”

A digital holy army had mobilised, immediately rallying an offensive against Kaye. He was meant to be doing a morning TV spot the next day, for example, but got a call at 4.30am, pulling him from the segment with little explanation. Little was needed either, given the torrent of hate already spewing forth. The next night, The Project waved the white flag, too, apologising to viewers. “If they had said, ‘We understand that this joke offended a bunch of people, but we stand by Reuben’s right to make that joke,’ that would have had more integrity, and been more interesting. And it would have given them more kudos at a time when they could have used it,” says Kaye, eyebrows raised with devilish schadenfreude – a clear nod to the fate of the since-cancelled TV show. Grinning, he adds: “Only one of us is still here.”

Instead, they played it safe, leaving Kaye feeling the opposite and facing a deluge of death threats. “I can’t express what the pile-on was like,” he says now. “It was just constantly ‘Kill yourself. Die, faggot. We’re coming for you. Watch yourself at your next gig. We know where you’re performing. We know where you live. We’re going to set your face on fire.’ ”

His talent agency was bombarded, one man smashing through their front doors, demanding an apology. Others marched in black at his shows, carrying crucifixes and chanting the Lord’s Prayer. Gigs and galas were cancelled. Metal detectors were recommended at venues, and private security was hired. His family was put on a priority response list with police, prompting conversations with relatives, urging them not to open any packages addressed to him. “Their world had suddenly become scary, because of a joke,” Kaye says. “That really broke my heart.”

The die-down was gradual, but for many, many months his phone felt like it was emitting a constant hum of electric malevolence, evidence of what many of his queer performing peers now routinely note – that intolerance is rising, that who tells a joke matters more than the joke itself, and that it is now easier than ever before to whip people into a frenzied fervour.

“That’s the scary thing and the relevant thing today. That’s what my experience has taught me, because if your faith is really solid, a joke isn’t going to shake it. And there’s so many other things to watch, so much content, so much other art. There are so many other avenues for your attention in this world,” says Kaye, 42, shaking his head. “I really shouldn’t be your problem.”

Tonight, he’s no problem at all. Tonight, Kaye is marvellous company. We’re in a basement space in London, far below the West End, waiting to take in a show together. It’s a special hospitality suite but, as Kaye points out, when you’re in the UK it doesn’t matter how fancy the setting, there’s always that faint smell of damp when you enter a room. “We’re still very much in a Dickensian framework,” he says, smiling, “with set dressing.”

We’re here to see Moulin Rouge! The Musical, not just because the Baz Luhrmann film was one of his core cinematic obsessions, but because Kaye – who cut his performing teeth here – has just been cast as one of the leads in a new production of the show coming to the Sydney Lyric Theatre in March. He’s on a high right now, and could not seem further away from his post-joke nadir.

Next year, on the big stage back home, the Melbourne performer will be playing Harold Zidler, the owner of the titular Belle Époche Parisian club – a role that fills him with enthusiasm “but also panic, because it’s so big. It’s momentous. The sheer scale of the show is outrageous,” Kaye says. “But Zidler gets some amazing things to do. He’s got so much light and shade. He’s compromised, right? He hasn’t got time for innocent love. There’s a cynic in him, and that suits me 100 per cent. He gets comedy. He gets sex. He gets menace. It makes me think, ‘I’m glad I’ve got six months to rehearse,’ because there’s a lot of detail in that.”

The theatre chimes ring. Good evening and welcome to the Piccadilly Theatre. Would you kindly take your seats as this evening’s performance of Moulin Rouge will commence in three minutes.

And with that, Kaye takes his mint ice cream, his gin and soda, and that box of Maltesers, and we wander into the world he’s about to inhabit. He’s engrossed from the start, too, tenting his fingers and nodding, or murmuring an emphatic “Yes” under his breath. He looks up from our seats at the gargantuan set – glittering, gritty and ever so glamorous – and whispers, “Doesn’t it just make you wish you were alive during the time of syphilis?”

The time of COVID was the last time Moulin Rouge! The Musical opened in Australia. That 2021 run ended in 2024, when theatre availability became scarce, but Carmen Pavlovic, the CEO of production company Global Creatures, always felt they left demand on the table. Zidler is pivotal to the show, she adds, embodying the entire story: art and love versus commerce and survival. British actor Jim Broadbent played Zidler in the movie, of course, but it’s a role somewhat open to interpretation, played on stage by everyone from Boy George to Megan Thee Stallion. “The book remains the book,” says Pavlovic, “so it’s really about how Reuben engages the audience – how he connects. Zidler makes morally questionable choices, and the audience needs to stay on his side as he does so.”

They cast the net wide before settling on Kaye, aware of his showmanship, vibrancy and danger; his singing range and fondness for direct address. The only thing casting director Lisa Campbell didn’t know was whether he was dexterous enough to show heart. Basically, until his audition, she didn’t know if he could act. “But that’s what surprised me most: the delicacy and the vulnerability he was able to access,” she says. “Afterwards, we all sat back shell-shocked by what we had seen.”

They might not have been shocked, of course, had they known Kaye’s history. Yes, this is that part of the longform profile piece where we get to the obligatory origin story, but I promise you, it’s unlike any personal creation myth you’ve heard.

There’s the tale of his paternal grandmother Roza, for example – a huge, ebullient woman who described herself as a “witch” in Stalinist Russia and married her husband in a labour camp, then gave birth to Reuben’s dad Lazar (a painter and sculptor who passed away in 2016), before living out a migrant nanna’s dream life in leafy Kew, spoiling her grandson with Choc Wedges and Yogo.

No, that’s insufficiently wild. Let’s unspool the thread of his maternal heritage instead, through Kaye’s grandmother Elfriede and grandfather Heinrich.

Elfriede and Heinrich came to Australia separately, as Jewish German refugees, and met in Tatura, in Victoria’s Goulburn Valley. Then, due to their staunch communist beliefs, they defected back into East Berlin. Reuben’s mum Karin was born en route – in London in 1946 – then grew up in East Germany singing The Internationale alongside her brother Helmut.

Five years later, Elfriede decided to escape the domineering Heinrich, who had ascended the ranks within the Stasi – but fleeing was dangerous, and meant she could take only one child. Elfriede made her own “Sophie’s Choice” and took Karin, Reuben’s mum, leaving behind poor Helmut, his uncle, who the embittered Heinrich promptly threw into an orphanage. Helmut ultimately became a banjo player and a clown, but a tragically sad figure, too, who died during a bank robbery. “He was the getaway driver,” says Kaye, eating a custard pastry days later, in Soho. “He pulled into a dead-end street and realised there was no way out. And he shot himself.”

Still with me? Next, the independent Elfriede set up shop in Melbourne, running an atelier in Collins Street, but she was a deeply traumatised woman, suffering volatile periods of mania and depression. Elfriede died by suicide when Karin was 18, after which Reuben’s mum spent time in foster care. As a young woman she gave acting a go – even appearing in the 1970 Ned Kelly movie starring Mick Jagger – but ultimately became a documentary filmmaker. When pregnant with Reuben in 1984, her water broke in the back seat of a taxi, then in the hospital she gave birth to Reuben Raoul Krum in the shortest labour possible. “He came out punching,” says Karin. “Damn near hit the wall on the other side of the room.”

Like I said, not your average family tree.

This bouncing baby boy in a hurry was named “Reuben” after both the doctor who delivered him and his godfather, Ben. “Raoul”, his middle name, was for Raoul Wallenberg, a Swedish diplomat who saved thousands of Jews in the Holocaust, while “Krum” comes from the German word for bent. “You can’t make this shit up,” says Kaye (his stage name, after childhood favourite performer Danny Kaye). “Also, ‘Reuben’ is old Hebrew for ‘Behold, my son,’ which kind of translates to ‘Look at my son, the poof,’ which I think is charming.”

Karin’s rules for parenting Reuben and his older brother Samuel were simple: “I had no appropriate role models for parenting in my life,” she says, “so I thought, ‘I will teach my sons three things: how to cook, how to dance and how to tell jokes, and with those three skills they should be able to make their way in the world.’ ”

She probably enacted that final rule too soon. Reuben was raised on a diet of The Goon Show and Jackie Mason but got his first big laugh much earlier, when he was just four. His mum stood him on a tabletop at a cocktail party, then whispered the following joke for him to recite: Why do they call it a pap smear? Because if they called it a c--- scrape, no one would go.

“The joke killed,” he says. “It did not do so well at show-and-tell the next day.”

He had a happy childhood at home, but a deeply unhappy one at school. Performing Groucho Marx routines and West Side Story numbers on the playground didn’t exactly endear him to classmates. “I was being called a faggot before I knew what a faggot was,” he says. “From the minute I landed in school.”

One time, he returned from recess, opened his pencil case and found it filled with saliva. The class had passed it around, giving everyone a chance to spit inside.

Kaye points to a scar above his left eye, from when he ended up in hospital after being chased through the yard, kids throwing stones at him. “I fell and split my head open, and I stood up and this fountain of blood just poured out.”

He’s 6 foot 2 (188 centimetres) and 83 kilograms now, but back then, he was short and slender, and one kid used to grab him by the backpack at the bus stop, then hoist him out into open traffic, before pulling him back. “Into the way of cars, out of the way of cars,” he says, “again and again.”

His bestie in high school, Bron Ryrie Jones, remembers meeting Reuben when he was 12. “He was already absolutely himself,” says Jones. “He either didn’t know or didn’t care that 95 per cent of the references he was using – Cher, Liza Minnelli, Bette Midler – were not on the same planet, culturally, as anyone else.”

The bullying she saw was unrelenting but also an opportunity for him to flex a formidable intellect and comic chops – the same weapons he now wields professionally. “His words were his shield, his armour and his defence, and so it was years of honing his craft and disallowing people to use words to steer him off course,” Jones says. “I met him the day after The Project, and it wasn’t dissimilar to meeting him at the locker bay after copping it again from these horrendous schoolboys: yes it was awful, but you also just felt like if it’s words we’re battling with, Reuben would come out on top.”

His mum spots a parallel between those episodes, too, yet perhaps in the trauma more than triumph. Watching her son suffer on both occasions was, she says, agony. “Absolute agony. There is a wonderful phrase by which I live: no parent can be happier than their unhappiest child,” she says. “It was the same after The Project – they chucked him to the wolves and the wolves went for him. I was utterly terrified, and astonished by the courage with which he faced it. I thought they were going to kill him.”

Kaye sees it all, too. Someone hurls a rock at him, he hurls one back. Someone lights a match, he pours the petrol. “All I ever got told was, ‘You just like the attention, whether it’s good or bad – can’t you just tone your behaviour down?’ ” he recalls. “And that sets up two voices in your head – one saying, ‘You’re not worth anything being you,’ and the other one saying, ’F--- ’em.’ Those are the two devils on my shoulder my entire life.”

The shining light in this dark chapter, of course, was music. Kaye was first captivated by the stage in primary school, on a class excursion to see The Phantom of the Opera. “I was like, that’s magic,” he says. “That’s a show.” From there he saw Chicago and visited spiegeltents and experimental theatre, but his love for live performance all dates back to that crucible excursion, which is why he sees something like Moulin Rouge! The Musical less as a huge commercial enterprise than as an access point for laypeople.

He gives his best performances, he adds, whenever students are in the house. “School groups can be badly behaved, or a struggle, but it’s mostly the first time they’ve been in a theatre, and of course there’s going to be one kid there like me, who doesn’t fit in with anyone else, and I want them to know that there’s a world out there for them: ‘Hey, this is where you belong. Come here.’ ”

Bullied teenagers often have validating happy-ending tales about how the world opened up once they left school. How none of those years mattered in the end. How they found their people. But others can’t escape their past.

Kaye went to Swinburne University, and then the Victorian College of the Arts, creative hotbeds where you might assume he would fit in, but he just didn’t function in groups or the school environment, scarred as he was by both. “I was in my head for a lot of it, in the classroom wondering: ‘Does anyone here like you?’ I carried that me-against-the-world mentality.”

After doing weird little shows and countless auditions without success, he saved for a year and flew – maybe fled – to London in 2010, where he did musicals, panto and cabaret. The fit was tongue-in-groove. His first night performing there was at a place called Cellar Door, which was an old pissoir – a public bathroom Oscar Wilde was said to frequent, which is now a performance lounge underneath The Lyceum, where The Lion King is staged. “Which is so funny,” he says. “All these families and kids are on queer hallowed ground, where acts of gross indecency were committed, and they’re singing Hakuna Matata.”

He found himself living in an old bus in Whitechapel and paying the bills with shifts at the exclusive Travellers Club in Pall Mall. On a walk through the city, he points out the big, grey building where he was a butler in a morning suit. Grey tails. White gloves. “Slicked hair and silver service for these Hogarthian figures who were richer than Croesus. It gave me this insight into the extreme wealth here in the UK – ‘You! Boy! Port! Here!’ – and very much where I sat, as both a person who did not have access to that world, and as an Australian, and as an outsider. I was also eating nothing but pâté and pheasant from the kitchen.”

He started working as an MC at night, and began to realise his greatest joy was in building crowd energy and throwing it to the next act. “I love that moment of staring out at the audience and going, ‘Right, we’re here in this room together, it’s immediate, it’s just tonight,’ ” he says. “You’re part of them, but you’re in charge.”

Just under two decades ago, for about three minutes, I performed as a drag queen. It was for a story but I took it seriously, practising diligently under the guidance of a local “drag mother” in Indianapolis, putting care into forging my own identity – “Miss Indy Starlet” – before hitting the stage at a local gay club there, dancing and lip-synching to Finally by CeCe Peniston. With my bouffant wig and high heels, I stood approximately seven feet tall and looked like a glamazon warrior, or possibly a very lost giraffe. But I felt amazing. Free to access another side of myself – the somewhat transgressive side that drives alone with the stereo up, windows down, gamely straining to hit the pained high notes on Careless Whisper. To a straight white guy like me, drag is subversive.

I can’t help but wonder what drag feels like to someone as utterly gay as Reuben Kaye. He’s sitting opposite me in a pub by London Bridge, sipping a gin and tonic, thick, longish blond hair pulled back, wearing a translucent white singlet top and black capri pants.

“I always used to say, ‘It’s not a character, it’s an amplifier.’ It just turns the volume up a little bit,” he explains. “My body feels like it makes sense in heels. I can be all the things I want to be. I can be incredibly sexy. I can be incredibly powerful. I can be aggressive and flirtatious and coquettish and strident, and I’m able to embody all those contradictions. And I look at myself in the make-up and go, ‘Oh yeah, this is a face people will listen to, because that’s who I am inside.’ ”

What was it like, then, when drag itself was dragged into the crosshairs of the culture wars? When Drag Queen Story Hour – events held in libraries around the world, with drag queens reading children’s stories to kids – was attacked for sexualising, corrupting or grooming minors? Kaye says it felt tired and predictable – yet another wedge seized by conservatives to hound the LGBTQI+ community. “It always just feels like, ‘Oh, this is the tactic they’re trying now.’ That particular brand of homophobia, queer-phobia, transphobia, they’re like the anti-abortion bracket – they just try everything until one thing gains traction. But it’s sad to think that they’ll use something as innocent as children as a manipulative fulcrum.”

Kaye hadn’t taken part in the library program, but he has spent time around kids in full stage regalia, including visiting a class on a UK television special, Kids React to Drag!, where he watched their non-judgmental inquisitiveness bloom. “Kids are more adult and capable of extensive rationality than we give them credit for,” he says. “They’re willing to receive information but they’re also willing to challenge you on stuff and talk about what they think is right. They want to have the conversation.”

I’m always curious about the experience of people who are high-profile members of some societal out-group or another, and whether they get tired of having to be a spokesperson for their kin. Kaye was often called on by the BBC as a talking head, and back home he’s been a panellist on Q&A. “I got asked to be on Piers Morgan once, and I didn’t really want to, but I wanted to at least find out what they wanted to ask me, and the questions were on every single hot-button issue for queer people everywhere, ranging from book bans to trans women in sport,” he says. “That’s not fair to one member of any minority.”

Questions, of course, should be expected when your act is as political as his. He’s comfortable going to more uncomfortable places, too; the Israel-Palestine conflict, for example. Not easy territory, given Kaye was raised culturally Jewish, going to synagogue until his bar mitzvah. “It was a reformed ‘Judaism lite’,” he explains. “It was a lot of call and response, and sitting and reading and reciting, which I feel milks all of the beauty that faith can have, turning it into this gruel of service and prayer.” He also remembers the calls within the temple – repeated and resounding – to preserve Israel. “I was like, ‘I’m trying to make it through school, I’m getting the shit kicked out of me, what the f--- do I care about this?’ ” One of his recent solo cabaret shows, Hard to Swallow, is largely inspired by the division that’s emerged since the October 7 attacks, and the further atrocities it wrought, now broadcast and fed to the world. “But I don’t agree with organised religion at all,” he says. “I think it’s a way of combining nationalism with lovely calligraphy.”

He works with a bunch of people to interrogate his arguments, making sure they’re bulletproof before sharing them on stage. Pianist and composer Shanon Whitelock is one such collaborator. “I’ve worked with a few people who worked with Reuben prior to me, and they all ask the same thing: ‘Is he still really angry?’ ” says Whitelock. “He is. And that manifests in his shows as satire, and that makes it fun, but underneath it is real anger. He wants to make a point.” They met more than a decade ago, Whitelock answering a Facebook post from Kaye seeking a music director for a gig at the Perth Fringe Festival, where they spent two days rehearsing together. “Reuben had that ADHD energy, always jumping around,” says Whitelock. “At the end of that I pretty much went, ‘This guy is nuts – this isn’t going to last.’ ”

It does make me wonder how a performer who is so used to producing his own solo shows – writing and directing, lights and costumes, press and sales – will go when rowing a long boat with a big crew, as he’ll have to on Moulin Rouge! The Musical. Will Reuben Kaye play well with others? “I don’t know the answer. I hope I do!” he says. “I do wonder what will happen – whether my inherent mistrust of conformity or my desire to be liked will win.”

There exists at least some proof of his ability to assimilate and uplift – Kaye is in his second year as director of the Adelaide Cabaret Festival – but it’s hard to imagine him suited to a world of emails and video chats and … groan … stakeholders. “What are you saying about me?” he asks, laughing. “Look, you’re not wrong, but you have a chance to lift up a whole bunch of people you love. In the arts, you can’t just pull that ladder up behind you.”

The dream for his career is consequently pragmatic and modest, and probably realistic. He wants to make people laugh. Anyone can get applause, he points out, because it comes at the end of every song, the fall of every curtain. A laugh is involuntary, spontaneous and contagious. And when an audience of different people with different beliefs share the same laugh in the same moment, it becomes a seed of revolution. Laughter is the sound of collective honesty.

Beyond that, he wants to be the poster child for jobbing generalist performers everywhere, storming the stage, finding his audience and cashing his cheques. He wants to prove that you don’t have to do one thing as an artist, and can make a living just being you – with room to poke the bear when the bear needs poking. “I want to make people think and wince and laugh at the same time,” he says, grinning. “It’s not enough just to thrust – you’ve got to be able to twist the knife as well.”

Good Weekend travelled to London courtesy of Global Creatures. Moulin Rouge! The Musical opens in March 2027 at Sydney Lyric.

Follow the money: Musk, mega-donors and the most expensive election ever

Sydney Morning Herald October 24, 2026

The Republicans have built up a huge cash reserve that they hope will rescue them in the final days of the midterm election campaign. But Democrats have their own financial advantages.

Des Moines, Iowa: Although he has been dead for seven years, Jeffrey Epstein has become a central figure in the US midterm elections.

In the Midwestern state of Iowa, Democratic attack ads accuse Republican members of Congress Zach Nunn and Ashley Hinson of protecting paedophiles by blocking the release of the so-called Epstein files.

Both eventually voted to release the files after US President Donald Trump gave the OK. Hinson, who is in a tough race for the US Senate, hits back at Democrat Josh Turek in her own ad.

“Men like Epstein who hurt children – they’ll have to answer to God,” she says. “But men who lie about it to win an election? They’ll have to answer to you.”

Epstein fuels dozens of TV ads across the country. But it’s not just him. On Wednesday night in Des Moines, during a Dolly Parton tribute show, the late news and Jimmy Kimmel Live!, most of the commercials on the ABC are election ads. Ads for the Senate, governor, House of Representatives, state attorney-general, and state Senate races. There is little respite.

It is easy to see how this midterm election is on track to be the most expensive in US history. AdImpact, which tracks advertising spending, forecasts that $US11.6 billion ($16.4 billion) will be spent on ads alone in the 2025-26 election cycle – surpassing the $US11.2 billion spent in the 2024 presidential election. Spending on aired and future reservations crossed the $US10 billion mark last week.

With Democrats striving to take control of the US Senate and Republicans desperate to cling on, races for that chamber have accounted for more than 60 per cent of ad spending aired so far. As well as aligning with the biggest population centres, the expenditure shows which contests the parties believe are tightest.

As of October 16, AdImpact said more than $US452 million had been spent on ads for the Senate race in Ohio, where Jon Husted (who replaced JD Vance in the seat) is in a tough battle against Democrat Sherrod Brown.

Meanwhile, $US342 million was spent in Texas, where James Talarico has a real chance of becoming the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from that state since 1988, $US205.8 million was outlaid in Michigan, and $US204.2 million in Maine.

Those figures don’t include primaries and run-offs. Across the entire 2025-26 election cycle, more than $US500 million has been spent on the Texas Senate race, and it is set to pass the 2024 Ohio Senate race as the most expensive non-presidential election ever.

Keeping track of fundraising and spending is a complex business, as candidates’ campaigns operate alongside political action committees (PACs) run by party headquarters or outside groups and individuals.

The Republican Party enjoyed a massive cash advantage coming into the midterms. Its central PAC for Senate races had roughly $US100 million more in the kitty than the Democrats’ equivalent at the end of June, and the House fund about $US50 million more.

The Republican National Committee had a healthy $US130 million in the bank. Meanwhile, the Democratic National Committee was broke. Last year, it used its Washington headquarters to secure a $US15 million loan. It was only this month that it again had more cash on hand than debt.

“It’s hard to imagine how an organisation like the DNC could not raise money when you have President Trump in office, but that is what it is,” said Morgan Jackson, a Democratic strategist based in North Carolina.

The Republicans have another advantage: the fundraising juggernaut of Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc, which had $US415 million cash on hand at the outset. It was slow to begin spending money, but by mid-October, it had disgorged about $US300 million. There is no real Democratic equivalent.

And then there is Elon Musk. The world’s richest man has ploughed at least $US366 million into Republican campaigns this election cycle, including more than $US276 million since July 1, filings to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) show.

That included two payments to the Senate Leadership Fund PAC, the Republicans’ main vehicle for Senate campaigns: $US75 million on September 9 and $US83 million on September 23. The payments, $US158 million in total, were transferred the next day to the campaign to elect Ken Paxton over Talarico in Texas.

“Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat,” Talarico said this week. “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US senator.”

It’s not just money. Musk has used his massive following on the social media platform he owns, X (formerly Twitter), to denigrate Talarico as a “creep” and promote a conspiracy theory that Talarico spent 10 days in a mental health facility during the campaign.

Musk is the largest known donor to this midterm campaign by a wide margin. But there are others. MAGA Inc received $US8 million from property developer Steve Wynn in September, $US5 million from both Blackstone chief executive Stephen Schwarzman and businesswoman Diane Hendricks, and $US1 million from US-born crypto entrepreneur Bijan Tehrani, who lives in Melbourne.

On the Democrat side, businessman and former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg chipped in a handy $US80 million in September and October, The New York Times first reported. Bloomberg famously spent $US1 billion on a failed 2020 presidential bid.

But while Democrats do use PACs, they typically raise their money through direct contributions to individual candidates’ campaigns. That is why almost all the top-raising candidates on the FEC database are Democrats, led by Jon Ossoff in Georgia and closely followed by Talarico. The only Republican to scrape into the top 10 was incumbent senator Susan Collins in Maine.

It has been this way for years, but in this election, it is pronounced. Talarico’s campaign raised far more than Paxton’s in the September quarter – $US60.2 million to $US10.2 million, FEC records show. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown raised $US23.1 million while Republican senator Jon Husted raised $US4.8 million.

Even in the red state of Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised $US9.4 million from July to September, much more than Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, who raised only $US800,000. Across all the tightest Senate races, Democrats out-raised Republicans multiple times over.

This carries another advantage for Democrats because, under US regulations, candidates typically enjoy much lower prices on the ads they buy than the PACs and super PACs. They must be offered the “lowest unit cost”, sometimes referred to as the “candidate rate”.

“It is much lower than the market rate. It is essentially closer to at-cost,” says Sean Cooksey, a Republican strategist and former chair of the FEC appointed by Trump. In highly contested elections in a big market, the cost differential can be “quite large”, he says – upwards of 10 times.

“You can imagine the most important football game in one of the closest, most contentious jurisdictions or races – there’s going to be very significant demand for that ad space, obviously very limited supply,” Cooksey says.

“You end up in a situation where advertising dollars used by the candidates themselves go a lot further and can purchase more ad space dollar for dollar compared to any other independent group.”

Earlier this year, the Federal Communications Commission, headed by Trump ally Brendan Carr, changed the rules to allow party organisations and joint fundraising committees to access the lowest unit cost.

The change was challenged by the Democrats in court, but has so far survived and is in place for this election. The Supreme Court also removed caps on co-ordinated spending between candidates and party HQ.

For example, the Republican National Committee last week bought $US3.8 million worth of ads for Hinson’s campaign in Iowa. “This marks the first time on record that the RNC is running a co-ordinated ad buy with a non-presidential candidate,” AdImpact said in a recent memo.

The question, then, is whether fundraising by Democratic candidates – and the better bang they can get for their buck on TV and radio – can make up for the enormous cash advantage enjoyed by Republicans at party HQ and through their super PACs and mega donors.

To date, Republicans have vastly outspent Democrats in the eight most competitive Senate contests – by about $US300 million, according to AdImpact.

“Republicans have aired more broadcast TV ads than Democrats in every battleground Senate general election except Ohio,” the group’s latest report said. In Ohio, although Republicans spent tens of millions of dollars more than Democrats, Democrats aired 200 more ads.

Cooksey, the Republican strategist, says both parties are now facing diminishing returns because of the huge amounts of money being spent and the onslaught of advertising hitting voters. “Once you have four commercials during a single football game, there is very limited utility to buying a fifth.”

But Cooksey defends the behaviour of mega donors such as Musk. He says there’s no evidence that any amount of money will change the will of voters, “other than at the margins”.

The US midterm attack ad that crossed the line

The race to become the next governor of Ohio has turned ugly, even by US standards.

Why do both parties raise and spend so much money, then? “It’s a bit of an arms race,” he says. “Part of it is to create equal and opposite opportunities to counter-message the other party.

“People are very motivated, and there’s a lot at stake in American elections. And it matters at the margin. No one would dispute that a campaign with $US100 million will have some marginal advantage over a campaign with $US1 million.”

Cooksey knows the sums seem gigantic, but he says they have to be put in context. If Republican tax cuts were worth $US1 trillion, for example, one would expect people to spend nearly that amount to make them happen.

“Given the size of the American economy, given what’s at stake legislatively in America, given the value of different policy outcomes in the real economy, it’s sort of surprising to me that people don’t spend more,” he says.

Nonetheless, Morgan Jackson, the Democratic strategist, notes the Republicans’ cash advantage is not moving the needle in key Senate races, including in his state of North Carolina, where the GOP has moved funds away from its candidate, Michael Whatley, to spend in Kansas instead.

“Money is not making the difference,” Jackson says. “I’ve seen Republican consultants who have said the more money they spend … the Democratic candidate continues to grow in the polls.

“The fact that we’re talking about Kansas today, Alaska, Iowa and Texas – states that were firmly in [the] Republican column for years and are now tilting blue this cycle – I think goes to show you that voters are desperate for change.”

Sydney Morning Herald October 24, 2026

Mark Seymour has lived quite a life in music – starting with his family singing group as a child – and he is still at it at age 70. The performer, songwriter and co-founder of seminal Australian band Hunters & Collectors has had a long and winding career arc, from angry rock ‘n’ roller to acoustic solo artist.

Along the way, he has penned many hits still popular today, including Throw Your Arms Around Me, When the River Runs Dry, True Tears of Joy and Holy Grail, which became an unlikely sporting anthem sung in arenas around the country.

Seymour joined the Good Weekend Talks podcast to reminisce about his life in music but also his new project, which reflects on 40 years of music since the release of the album Human Frailty with a concert showcasing both his Hunters & Collectors hits and solo projects, backed by an orchestra.

In this edited version of the conversation, he talks to The Age special correspondent Stephen Brook about disappointing his parents, why he keeps performing and whether he is still in touch with his old bandmates.

There’s no way that teenage me back in the ’80s, watching Countdown would ever have conceived that come 2026, I’d be interviewing Mark Seymour. What keeps propelling you forward? I really like writing songs. I haven’t lost the fascination with that process of song construction. That’s what keeps me interested. I discovered music through singing before anything else had happened when I was very little. But once I cottoned on to the idea of writing songs, it’s one of those strange, dark arts that just never seems to go away. It’s a constant mystery as to how you end up arriving at a point where something really works well.

Thinking about songs and thinking about the next song – is that all day, every day? I’m never far from it, you know.

Throw Your Arms Around Me – you released it in 1984 to no chart action. It wasn’t until a couple of years later that it really took off. What was going on there? How do you know that? Not many people know that. The original recording was ’84. You can’t find it. There was this recording done in a warehouse in Hardware Lane. The brief was to try and do a commercial recording. And someone in the group came up with the idea that if we make it really raw, then we’ll get away with writing something really commercial, which was my department, because I came up with a ballad. I can’t find it, I don’t know where it is. It reemerged two years later on an album that became quite famous.

I don’t think I’d be able to handle the disappointment of being a songwriter and writing this masterpiece, as we think of it now, for it to bomb on arrival. Oh, there’s been a lot of disappointments. (Laughs) The whole question of commerciality is such a very strange beast because when you listen to what one generation hears as sonically acceptable, compared with the next generation, there’s no fluency to any of it. Songs become hits for all sorts of strange reasons. If a song doesn’t really get traction on radio it is mildly disappointing, because I’m ambitious. But the songs that I’ve written that have actually translated really well commercially are the ones I least expected.

You’ve got a new project that’s coming to Melbourne in November. Hunters & Collectors was characterised by many as a pub rock band. So for you to be fronting an orchestra sounds like a new musical dimension. Hunters & Collectors was on another planet. It was really, really loud and robust and just big. Symphony, when you’re amongst it, is incredibly moving.

You are living in the shadow of a legacy created by you back in the 1980s and ’90s, with this incredible run of hits and standards and anthems. Is that daunting? There’s a very strong love of Hunters & Collectors in a certain cohort. When I went solo, it was a lesson I had to learn that a lot of people didn’t accept me doing that. People just didn’t turn up. I remember early on, my manager Michael would book me alone into leagues clubs in South Brisbane, and you’d walk into a space on your own with a guitar, and emblazoned on the banner outside is “Mark Seymour ex-Hunters and Collectors solo acoustic”. And the room would be packed. Then people gradually realised it’s got the name on the banner, but it’s not Hunters & Collectors. Then they just stopped turning up, and I was playing to like 50 to 60 people. And that went on for a long time.

Was that galling for you? I struggled, really struggled. My ego was really ... (Laughs). But I was a grown man. I had children, I had to work.

My friend Anna is 24 years old and on her daily walk, she listens to Hunters & Collectors. I find that sort of amazing and wonderful in a way that you’re still finding a youthful audience after all these years. Again, getting back to the mystery of songwriting. Holy Grail was a really difficult birth. The thing about Hunters & Collectors, too, I used to refer to as threading the needle to get a song away with those guys. There was always this feeling that if we get this right, it’s going to be incredible. But how do you do that? There’s so much psychology in that band. It was a big band, big sounds. I was so accustomed to abandoning ideas quickly. But Holy Grail was just weird. The band recorded it really quickly and the band actually hadn’t physically played it together.

I did read somewhere that Holy Grail, and I’m quoting, “is undoubtedly the only Australian sporting event anthem conceived as its lyricist laboured through a Jeanette Winterson novel”. I’m in the middle of this recording program session with the band, and there’s so much angst and anxiety and stress and disputation about where the record was going and the style of the record. And, you know, you could just feel it, and it was like, “Oh, this is going so badly.” And it wasn’t in the end. The record was really successful. But there was so much angst.

The band process sounds quite angsty at times. Looking back on that now, are you still maintaining relations or has everyone gone their separate ways? We’re OK. I think there’s an image bands have of brotherly ... or … just that you create this bond and you share it with an audience. And people think that that’s a beautiful thing and they love it. And it’ll last forever. I mean it’s also a professional organisation. I still communicate with the guys, but we’re not …

Have you got a WhatsApp group? I believe there is one. I’m not in it (Laughs).

Oh, because? I communicate with them. I was talking to a couple of them this morning, actually, in the dog park, on the phone.

Holy Grail is a sporting anthem performed at numerous events. And that’s why I embrace it, because when you just sing it on acoustic guitar, that’s an interesting song. But at the time, people were pulling their hair out. That’s the thing about songs … What’s that famous line of Dylan’s?

This is not an episode of Hard Quiz, Mark. (Laughs) I’ll tell you anyway, a song should be able to walk around. It should have legs and walk around on its own. The idea that the song just has its own capacity, you know, you can play it anywhere, [and] it’ll work. I think that’s what that song’s got.

Born in 1956, in Benalla, regional Victoria, when did the music bug bite for you growing up? Singing was early on at home in front of Mum and Dad and their relatives. I think I knew I was good at it.

The Seymour Family Singers. Was that a real thing? It sounds very von Trapp. Yeah. It was. My mother was very much into that concept. She might have been inspired by Julie Andrews, but I was in love with Julie Andrews – I was seven or something. We performed in country talent quests. It was very, very straight. But it was good, though. The harmonies were on. Country Victoria 1964. I remember the Beaufort talent quest. We came second and we got pipped at the post by a local girl who sang the Dolly Parton song, Jolene.

Your brother went on to great success with Crowded House. What was that like? Nick and I started getting really interested in going out and seeing bands in pubs in Melbourne around 1978. I don’t know why that happened, really, because our family was quite conservative. My father really didn’t like it. We were very Catholic. I wanted my father to like what I did, but I knew he wouldn’t.

How long did that disapproval last? Years and years and years. I had very little to do with my parents on a personal level in my early career. I basically kept away from them because I knew I would end up confronting them. So there were lines we just didn’t cross. They let us go, but they didn’t really support it. And then I discovered my mother had kept a scrapbook. I was very emotional about it. I think Nick did better in that area. Apart from commercial success, Crowded House are incredible, he was the sweet little boy who played the baby Jesus in the Christmas school pageants. Everyone loved Nick. Especially Mum. She just thought Nick was adorable.

Whereas your persona was this angry, muscly, shouty, aggro guy. I think I was angry, I didn’t realise I was. Years later, I’ve been told I was. You are about to tell me.

You did write that Throw Your Arms Around Me was the first song you wrote that wasn’t angry. I think that’s probably right. (It) was really transformative. I remember going into the room with it thinking, they’re not going to like this. And it was so strange. I don’t think anyone really knew what to say because it was so different. There was a kind of stillness in the room when they were watching me do it.

It’s 2026. Could you have done what you did with Hunters & Collectors if you were starting out now? Hunters & Collectors was so different in its original incarnation that it just got immediate traction in pubs. I don’t think there’s a lack of venues to play live music in. People say there is, but there’s a lot of action around where I’m living. I would just make different musical choices. What’s ended up happening for me is that I play a much leaner operation. There’s only four of us.

Well, that’s fewer people to argue with, then. It still happens.

Mark Seymour Orchestrated: Hunters & Collectors The Hits and 40 Years of Songs and Stories, plays at the Palais Theatre, Melbourne on November 26.

The things you only understand when you turn 60

Sydney Morning Herald October 24, 2026

At my age, I’d make a far better criminal than today’s youth – and I’d catch the bus.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No gift articles left

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Article gifting is here

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

Truth be told, I probably understand a little less now than when I turned 50. When I was 20 I knew practically everything. Now I know that many of my abilities are not quite what they were: my backhand overhead volley, unreliable at the best of times, will never win a point again, even as a fluke. No longer can I convincingly pull off interpretative jazz ballet; it’s character roles at best from now on. Doddery colonel, ageing archduke, that kind of thing.

My memory for names is worsening by the minute. Concerned, I sought advice from a medical acquaintance – I can see his face – and he told me I had Nominal Aphasia, a common condition which makes remembering names more difficult. Nothing to worry about, it comes with age. It’s only when you develop Everything Aphasia that things become problematic.

I do understand that the internet has failed on every moral and ethical level, delivering on none of its major promises except providing some slight convenience in the retail experience. Apart from that, it’s ruined everything. There, I’ve said it. Having lived through that quaint time before the digital overlords ran the show, I am immediately suspicious when any tech advance is justified as having the potential to find the cure for cancer. The interactive CD-Rom was going to help find the cure for cancer. I suspect AI will create more cancer than it cures; perhaps we can avert disaster by convincing the bots that they might be coming down with something, and they’d best take it easy, give the world domination a rest for a bit.

Seriously, tell a robot they get paid sick leave and of course they’ll take it, they’re not stupid. And if Elon Musk and his fellow tech-bros want to live on Mars, the sooner they head off the better.

I also understand that there is nothing really new under the sun, except the sun is now cooking the planet to a point where we’ll all be living in Mordor with air-conditioning. Honestly, with the existential threats of AI, climate change, nuclear annihilation and the failed promise of the interactive CD-Rom, it’s hard, as the proverbial frog, to know in which particular pot of water you’re being brought to the boil. Every burner on the stove is being used. Part of the problem is that we’re being told what the problem is every second of every day. When you just had half an hour of James Dibble at seven o’clock, things didn’t seem quite so bad.

Having suspected it for some time, I’m now convinced that art is the only thing that endures. Technology will never make art – it will forge it beautifully – but it is only the human mind with an act of free will that can genuinely create a work of art. Asking a machine to do it for you delivers a pyrrhic victory at best, an illusion as flawed as the idea that technology democratises the creative process. If everyone’s a superhero, no one is.

Which is another thing I now understand: there is no point in giving everyone a certificate just for turning up. There is nothing to be gained by having children play soccer on a round field with no goals. Life is intrinsically unfair; there will always be winners and losers. Better if we strive for a world where everyone gets a turn at being either.

What else? When medical science gave us another 10 years of life, it gave it to us at the wrong end. It would be far better if we got another decade between 30 and 40. What is the point of hanging about at an age when you can barely move, smell a bit odd and – on a good day – the Nominal Aphasia is a fond and distant memory?

Having said that, I now appreciate that an active senior is capable of many things. For one, they’d be a far better hit-person than the youngsters making such a mess of targeted assassinations these days. They’d do a practice run the day before to make sure they got the right bloke, there’d be no need to torch a stolen car because they’d catch the bus – you’d be mad not to with a Seniors Card – and they’d charge very little for the job because they wouldn’t want their pension compromised.

Which is why I chose a bunch of self-funded retirees to go on an art heist caper through the galleries of Europe in my new book, Near Death in Venice, an ideal Christmas gift and readily available. Oh, I also understand that in an age of increasing competition for the discretionary spend, you should never let an opportunity for self-promotion pass you by.

Near Death in Venice (Simon & Schuster) is out October 27.

Cheltenham’s racing return provides romance over jumps and 20-1 shock

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 19:32:55 GMT

Outsider Kingofthefrontier wins Sharp Novices’ Hurdle

Trainer John Dawson gets better of Dan Skelton

The jumping game increasingly resembles the Flat when it comes to the concentration of racing power in ever fewer trainers’ hands, but the opening day of Cheltenham’s new season – the first, in fact, since Gold Cup day in March – brought a reminder that romance has not been drained entirely from the winter code.

Dan Skelton, who dethroned Willie Mullins to become the new champion over jumps last season, had already trained 115 winners in the current campaign before racing on Friday, nearly halfway towards Martin Pipe’s all-time record of 243. John Dawson, by contrast, had sent out a total of six winners from his yard in North Yorkshire since May 2023.

However, it was Dawson’s Kingofthefrontier, a 20-1 outsider and only the trainer’s third runner at the home of jumping, who led the field home in the Grade Two Sharp Novices’ Hurdle, with Skelton’s Cooltobecareless, the 13-8 favourite, only third. The winner was nearer last than first turning in but showed an impressive turn of foot to run out a two-and-a-quarter length winner from Nicky Henderson’s Planters Punch.

Dawson rode into the famous winner’s enclosure aboard Sine Nomine after the Hunters’ Chase at the festival meeting here in March 2024, but his first Cheltenham winner as a trainer was an even better moment in what is still a young racing career.

“We’ve always loved him since the word go,” Dawson said. “I just felt we had a horse to come and have a go with.

He’s still got a lot to learn and the way he went through the race, Conor [O’Farrell, his jockey] said he was a bit stumbly and he had to balance him a couple of times. But speed wasn’t a problem for me, he was always going to have enough boot to get there, and he picked up really well.

“He’s actually a little bit horse-shy and when that big horse of Dan Skelton’s came running towards him, I think he was edging away from him, but he’ll learn a lot from that and he could still be anything.”

Dawson and Kingofthefrontier’s owner, George Critchley, opted to run in Friday’s Grade Two feature event in preference to a novice handicap hurdle at Carlisle.

“He’d never disappointed us,” Dawson said. “George puts a lot into the game, I wanted to bring him here and I thought he had a horse good enough to do it. I just can’t believe it came off.

We’re ambitious [but] we only want the horses to have a go with and hopefully we’ve showcased ourselves [today] to do that. I don’t want to be a massive Dan Skelton in numbers, but I just want real quality.”

Irish stables have been dominant at the festival meeting in March in recent seasons and Gordon Elliott is already looking ahead to a possible run in the Grand Annual Handicap Chase for Bowensonfire after the six-year-old’s win in the card’s two-mile novice chase.

Bowensonfire was the first leg of a double for Elliott, completed when Cosmos D’Ainay took a novice hurdle later on the card, while Cian Collins sent out a third winner for Ireland on the day when Brandt, at 10-1, took the final race on the card.

Doncaster 12.55 Ancient State 1.30 Breacher (nap) 2.05 Bengal Tiger 2.40 National Honour 3.19 On The River 3.55 Pearl Eye 4.30 Zarvali 5.05 King’s School

Cheltenham 1.10 As Legends Have It (nb) 1.45 Road To Wembley 2.20 Idaho Fire 2.55 Katate Dori 3.30 Indian River 4.05 Butch Cassidy 4.40 Cask Of Pimlico

Southwell 4.24 Blake’s Monarch 5.00 Almaty Star 5.30 Raysham 6.00 Ring Of Music 6.30 Geometry 7.00 Lili Marleen 7.30 Gladiadora 8.00 Crystal Dark 8.30 He’s An Angel

Aidan O’Brien and Andrew Balding field four of the seven runners in Saturday’s Futurity Trophy at Doncaster, the final Group One of the British season, but the focus on their neck-and-neck tussle for the trainers’ title could mean that the improving Breacher (1.30) sets off at a value price on ground that promises to suit.

William Muir and Chris Grassick’s colt has progressed by the run in three starts to date over seven furlongs, while also looking sure to thrive at middle-distances next season.

Cracksman, his sire, was at his best with some cut in the ground and a demanding mile on heavy going could well see Breacher outrun his early odds of around 10-1.

Doncaster 12.55: Ancient State seems to save his best form for this track and trip and has been dropped 1lb since finishing around one-and-a-half lengths behind the winner at Ascot last time.

Cheltenham 1.10: Ben Pauling has his string in excellent form and the returning As Legends Have It is an interesting contender at around 8-1. He has gone well fresh in the past, remains fairly weighted on his winning form at the end of last season and his prominent run-style is ideal for this track and trip.

Cheltenham 1.45: Olly Murphy’s Road To Wembley – part-owned by Sir Alex Ferguson – was better than the bare result when fourth on his handicap debut at Worcester in September and should appreciate this move up to three miles.

Doncaster 2.05: Bengal Tiger’s 12-length win in a maiden at Naas last time was backed up by an excellent time and he should handle this step up to Listed company without too much fuss.

Cheltenham 2.20: James Owen’s string remains in strong form whatever the season or code and Idaho Fire posted a new career best at Uttoxeter last time out – a performance that suggests he could cope with a subsequent 10lb hike in the weights.

Cheltenham 2.55: With further rain expected before Saturday’s card, Katate Dori’s form when second over track and trip off a 3lb higher mark in January looks as strong as anything on offer.

Cheltenham 3.30: Four of the seven runners in this four-year-old event were in the field for the Triumph Hurdle at the festival and while Indian River was only 10th, he finished third in the equivalent event at Aintree. A recent run in a handicap at Market Rasen should have him spot on for this.

Macron condemns racism after one killed in ‘terrorist’ shooting near Paris

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 19:23:14 GMT

Gunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl

Emmanuel Macron has condemned racism in French society after a gunman opened fire from a car west of Paris on Friday, killing one person, wounding a 12-year-old girl and injuring four others in what the president called a “racist terrorist attack”.

Macron arrived at the scene of the drive-by shooting in Trappes, a town west of Paris, on Friday night, saying he was deeply saddened by what he called the “premeditated” attack. The 12-year-old girl, who was shot eight times, is being treated in hospital.

“What happened today ​marks a turning point for our ⁠country; what happened today ​was ​a terrorist ​and racist attack,” ​Macron said.

He said the gunman had targeted people because of the colour of their skin. The president said racism had often become part of the “ambient discourse in France” and created “an atmosphere”. He said: “Don’t let this terrorist attack divide us.” He called for “respect and unity”, saying many French people would be scared and thinking “this could happen to me”.

Ali Rabeh, the leftwing mayor of Trappes, said that the gunman had set out by car on Friday morning “firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath” as he drove through the town and neighbouring La Verrière. The mayor called it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.

Rabeh, whose family has Moroccan roots, said: “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.

“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country. Her crime was probably being of colour,” he added. “It’s probably one of the first attempts at a mass crime of Islamophobia and racism.”

Rabeh said everyone in France had a responsibility to bring “calm and harmony”. He called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.

Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether the gunman targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.

The 39-year-old suspect, who was stopped by police in his car, was named by France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor as Kevin T. He had driven through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière in Yvelines at about 10.30am on Friday. Over the course of 15 minutes, he repeatedly fired an automatic weapon, first at a petrol station, then a medical centre and a children’s playground.

The French public broadcaster reported that he shot dead a young black man, then targeted a woman wearing a headscarf, before shooting the 12-year-old girl, who was being treated for her eight gunshot wounds at a children’s hospital on Friday night. The prosecutor said in a statement on Friday night that the medical status of the five wounded victims was not stable. Rabeh said the man killed was “of African origin” and that another of the wounded was “of north African origin”.

Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of La Verrière, told Agence France-Presse that two of the wounded people in his town were cleaners of African origin attending to a school Friday on morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire.

The prosecutor said that when the suspect was stopped by police in his car he was found with a sten gun – a British submachine gun used in the second world war – as well as teargas grenades. The man had also booby-trapped his home with gas canisters and electric wires connected to a timer, authorities said, adding that a member of his family was arrested and taken into custody for questioning.

“The investigations are ongoing, but it is clearly a terrorist crime. It is an extremely serious act,” the interior minister, Laurent Nunez, told reporters from ⁠Yvelines.

The ‌shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France. Last Saturday saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, which left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted, and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country. Renewed protests, over teacher shortages and crumbling buildings in high schools as well as the high cost of living, are expected on Saturday.

Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party, is polling highly ahead of next spring’s presidential election when Macron steps down.

After the Trappes attack, Fabien Roussel, a Communist candidate, wrote on social media that the far right was responsible for “racist hatred” in France.

Le Pen condemned what she called the “abject motive of racism” of the “barbaric act”.

‘A different kid’: from karting to F1 champion-elect, Antonelli’s ability has always stood out

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 19:00:12 GMT

With first drivers’ title all but secure, a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focus

Even as Kimi Antonelli may be world champion-elect, it is sometimes hard to equate the young man who has driven with such exceptional skill and no little verve to touching distance of an historic first Formula One title with the smiling, wide-eyed kid with tousled hair who still almost looks out of place in the F1 paddock. Yet what has become clear in this extraordinary season is that Antonelli’s talent and his personable, endearing character are inextricably entwined.

Whether the Italian seals his place as F1’s youngest world champion, at 20 years old, at this Sunday’s US Grand Prix in Austin or the next round in Mexico or even beyond that is moot – that he will do so is all but assured and for all that he is still in only his second season in the sport, a more rounded, well-liked champion than the Mercedes driver would be hard to find.

Engage with Antonelli and it is almost impossible not to still see the three-year-old child who insisted on taking to his father Marco’s knee to try out the racing simulator the former driver had brought home. Marco would control the pedals and his son the wheel with an irrepressible enthusiasm that could barely be contained and is still there in every dart, feint and incisive pass he makes today.

Pictures from his childhood in Bologna, a couple of hours’ drive from where his father runs a racing team in San Marino, show whenever Antonelli has a wheel in his hands there is a smile on his face and his eyes alight. His joy is clear and it is a passion that has run clearly through his career. From going karting at the age of five, a meteoric rise through the ranks, being taken on as a Mercedes junior driver aged 12, then making his debut for the team in 2025 after a whirlwind of three years moving from F4, to Formula Regional and then F2.

The faith Mercedes placed in him, not least in that he was stepping into the shoes of the departing seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, was huge, yet the team principal Toto Wolff had no doubts as to his talent and his character.

“In the past, there was the opinion in F1 that in order to be winning, you need to be an asshole, you need to be ruthless and opportunistic,” he observed this season as Antonelli made a stunning start with five wins on the trot and the entire world was paying attention to the kid who, for many, had come from nowhere. “I don’t think that Kimi is that. It’s just down to driving faster than the others, and being a nice person also.” It is an opinion often echoed by those close to the young Italian. Gwen Lagrue, the talent scout who led Mercedes’ junior driver programme, remembers more than just his remarkable talent from their early encounters.

“With Kimi, I saw almost from day one that I was dealing with a different kid,” Lagrue said. “First, what impressed me, well, amazed me, was his natural presence. He was already having such an impact on everyone in the paddock, you noticed this kid has something different than the others. Everyone liked Kimi, everyone was hugging him. He was like the Kimi you see today when he was 11. He was so passionate about what he was doing, about racing, about F1, everything.”

At the heart of this engaging character it seems is a grounded and emotionally rich relationship with his family. While he was supported in following his racing dreams, he was told unequivocally that if he was to kart on a weekend, school must follow on a Monday until he graduated. He duly did so, completing his maturità school exams just after coming third – his first podium – at the Canadian GP last year.

“Which driver has done the A-levels or the baccalaureate? Name me one that has finished school. No one,” Wolff observed pointedly of his prodigy. The role of his family has clearly been crucial. His father as guide, mentor and, both have admitted, stern taskmaster at times, whom Antonelli has described as his “rock”. But there is also clearly a hugely important relationship with his mother, Veronica, and younger sister Maggie.

“My dad is always going to give me his point of view, he’s going to give me advice and then if I decide to listen, good, but if I don’t decide to listen, it’s OK as well,” he said. “We always have a strong relationship but this is the same with my mum and my sister. The way I am I don’t think I could cope with having a bad relationship with my family member, it’s something that I would really struggle to cope with, that’s why I couldn’t see myself, you know, just taking distance from them.”

Intriguingly, racing was not a direction his father had initially wanted him to go in. Marco had been a quick sportscar driver and almost signed as works driver for two German touring car teams but was unlucky in not getting a shot. “I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation,” he said. “At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport.”

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

after newsletter promotion

However, having decided to let him pursue the dream, Marco has been there ever since. He is at the track on many weekends and clearly the pair share an easy, close bond with echoes of the one Hamilton shared with his father, Anthony, in his early years. In Hungary, the race after he had risked receiving a penalty for exceeding track limits on his way to a brilliant win in Belgium, Antonelli laughingly recalled his father’s reaction: “He said: ‘Congrats, but …’ Always a but … ‘If I see you doing another track limit for nothing, I’m gonna stretch your neck like a chicken.’”

Antonelli’s boyish honesty has been as engaging as his talent. Wolff has noted his ability to switch into a “race mode”, a zone where he is wholly focused on the task, where he has a daring, aggressive driving style, pushing to the limit and past it, on occasion, but which he always learns from. “We had to teach him instead of always being at 110%, just be at 100%,” Lagrue said which, as Wolff has remarked, is a trait he would rather indulge than having to “take a stick to a donkey”.

Yet alongside that verve Antonelli has shown a maturity beyond his years belied by his character when out of the “zone”. He has displayed the judgment of a veteran while being able to manage the endless adjustments of touch and feel of the car and its balance – especially of these fiendishly complex modern rides – such that he, like many of the greats, has made it look easy.

Watching him do so this season has been a pleasure not least because he is a driver who has taken such untrammelled and infectious joy in doing so. A feeling perhaps summed up by his father, who told La Gazzetta dello Sport just after his son turned 20: “I hope he remains who he is, sweet and generous, and continues to do what he loves for as long as possible.”

Before his extraordinary victory from 19th on the grid at the Italian GP, Antonelli said he wanted to win the championship but that it was important for him to do so by being himself. The latter he can consider a job most admirably well done. The former is only a matter of time.

Swoon! London City Ballet are positively glowing in a night of dreams – and ghosts from dance history

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 19:00:11 GMT

Sadler’s Wells, LondonAlina Cojocaru astonishes in John Neumeier’s Ghost Light, an ethereal meditation on time, while Glen Tetley’s Firebird has much to cherish

A ghost light is the name for a single lamp left on stage when a theatre is dark, and one glows throughout John Neumeier’s ballet Ghost Light. Also never not glowing is Alina Cojocaru, superlative ballerina and guest dancer with London City Ballet, who has a longtime working relationship with Neumeier and his Hamburg Ballet – with whom this work was originally created in 2020.

When Cojocaru materialises onstage in silence, so ethereal it’s almost mystical, she is like a ghost of Swan Lake’s Odette, wings fluttering, eyes half closed, lost in a memory. Cojocaru’s divine delicacy embodies all of the romance of ballet, until suddenly her steps glitch, she stumbles over a chair and comes to. The stage is a place of dreams, for all the dancers who have crossed its boards and will continue to do so (superstition says that ghost lamps also allow spirits of former dancers to return to the stage). Neumeier evokes some of these dances in this piece, from a stray sylph upstage, to earnest solos, sparky allegro and two young men in a tender duet, passing each other sometimes in parallel worlds, sometimes in moments of connection.

The parts of this ballet were created separately during Covid with bubbles of dancers, a practical measure. But the result is actually a beautiful rendering of the passage of time and its circularity – of dance’s, and dancers’, evolution. Neumeier, at 87, has seen his fair share of stages – likewise Cojocaru, now 45, who always brings real poignancy.

It’s only three years since this new version of London City Ballet formed and the company is looking very fine. A major strand of its USP is piecing back together forgotten ballets and tonight that’s the late Glen Tetley’s Firebird (1981), celebrating Tetley’s centenary. An impressive Ellie Young dances the Firebird character, in this case a young woman ostracised from her austere family, who finds a partner in Joseph Taylor – and what a great partner he is: strong, lyrical and so attentive.

Tetley was a bridge between ballet and modern dance and the company pays exacting attention to form, in swift, clean steps and emotive expression. The narrative may be fuzzy, and the final scene – with its glorious Stravinsky score – nowhere near as majestic as in Michel Fokine’s (and designer Natalia Goncharova’s) version, but there is much to cherish here.

At Sadler’s Wells, London, until 24 October. Touring until 6 December
