‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 18:48:48 GMT

After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’

Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.

“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.

The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.

AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.

“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.

While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.

Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.

However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.

Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun.

After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.

“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.

Severe flooding in the Four Corners region on Friday led to water rescues – some from rooftops – and impassable roads, with some residents being told to evacuate low-lying areas of Colorado and New Mexico and others advised to shelter in place until water levels go down.

It followed several busy days of flooding in the region that swamped dozens of homes in Utah. Earlier in the week, tornadoes blew off roofs, knocked trees on to houses and downed power lines in Arizona. At least one person was injured.

An unknown number of people were rescued overnight and continued to be rescued on Friday by New Mexico guard boats, helicopters and amphibious vehicles, Devin Neeley, a San Juan county spokesperson, said.

“We’re picking people off of roofs and pulling people out of houses that have 3 or 4ft (1-1.5 metres) of water in them, and there’s more water coming,” Neeley said.

Skies were clearing but the rivers continued to rise, with forecast crests surpassed, he added.

“This is serious. We’re still sending deputies as I speak to get people out of their homes right now. In fact, our sheriff is damn near going to lose his home today,” Neeley said.

About 600 households were told to evacuate in Farmington, where areas along the San Juan River were closed off, city spokesperson Gina Intoppa said.

Farmington is the biggest city in the Four Corners, the only place in the US where four states – Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah – come together.

National guard members also were deployed to assist with flooding in south-west Colorado. Rising waters prompted mandatory evacuations along four rivers, including the San Juan River through Pagosa Springs. The resort town famous for its riverside hot springs suffered flooding from a similar weather pattern a year ago.

“Please shelter in place, water levels are beginning to recede, but many roads are impassable and unsafe for travel,” the Archuleta county sheriff’s office posted online on Friday.

In nearby Rio Grande county, trailers at a campground were surrounded by high water and trucks were partially submerged in other areas.

Jared Polis, Colorado’s governor, had declared a disaster emergency in 11 counties in response to heavy rain and flooding in the south-west part of the state.

Surreal scenes included a shipping container drifting slowly down a street.

The flooding was not unexpected, just the latest from two months of heavy rain that ended a summer of drought. While parts of the south-west are rocky with little vegetation and are naturally prone to flash flooding, the recent rains have made flooding everywhere more likely, said Kate Abbott, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Grand Junction, Colorado.

“At this point we’re saturated and can’t take too much more without flooding,” Abbott said. “This is the third or fourth round of this kind of moisture we’ve seen in as many weeks.”

Criminals are recruiting vulnerable people, including children, to damage houses suspected of being HMOs, police in Manchester believe.

The houses that have been attacked are either HMOs (houses in multiple occupation), or properties that have been mistaken for HMOs. Police have received at least 46 separate reports of criminal damage, with cars also targeted alongside houses.

“This recent spate of damage is not being tolerated,” he added. “A 42-year-old man has today been arrested on suspicion of causing criminal damage at an address in Salford overnight. He remains in our custody for questioning.”

Salford council has also taken down roadside banners that had been put up, which read: “IRLAM AND CADISHEAD SAY NO TO MIGRANT HMOs.”

‘Realistic and reassuring’: UK public ‘responding calmly’ to Be Ready campaign

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 17:22:18 GMT

Government’s emergency planning advice has sparked sales of essentials but no panic stockpiling, say prepping shop owners

When the UK government launched its “Protect and Survive” public information campaign in 1980 on how to stay alive after a nuclear attack, it was met with a combination of scepticism, disbelief and derision.

The advice included how to build a “fallout room” at home, how to whitewash windows to protect from a blast, and how to store a dead body for up to five days.

You might expect this would have prompted widespread panic, but in fact it led to a political backlash, and was later lampooned on TV and in music.

It shows the risks governments take when launching such campaigns, and the fine balance that must be struck between hammering home a practical message without causing panic – or other unintended reactions.

The government’s new Be Ready campaign is advising the public to stock up on three day’s worth of supplies for use during severe weather or cyber-attacks, so help can be directed to the most vulnerable first.

In a concise, two-page document, it suggests people stock bottled water and non-perishable food for three days, a torch with spare batteries, a wind-up FM radio, a first aid kit and a copy of their passport. To stave off panic buying, it advises people to check their cupboards first and build up items gradually on regular shopping trips.

While there is no evidence the advice has triggered mass panic, the public is clearly responding. Jack Brown, who co-owns Sgt Prepper Shop, which stocks emergency food and survival tools, said he received a month’s worth of orders in the first 24 hours of the Be Ready campaign.

“I thought my phone was glitching or being hacked with the number of orders coming in,” he said.

Brown said the advice seemed sensible and proportionate. Three days was the “sweet spot”, he said, with most everyday emergencies like power cuts, a burst water main or flooding sorted within that timeframe.

It is also “realistic, affordable and fits in a cupboard”, he said, adding that asking people to stock up on a month’s worth of supplies would feel overwhelming and most people would do nothing at all.

A wind-up radio was also a sensible suggestion, and ones with a built-in torch and phone-charging USB port make them “one of the most useful bits of kit you can own”, he said.

Dr Sarita Robinson, associate dean for the school of psychology and humanities at the University of Lancashire, said there was little evidence to suggest these kinds of messaging campaigns cause panic.

“There’s this perception that if we tell people the truth we’re somehow going to panic them and it isn’t the case,” she said.

“When we use accurate messaging about emergency situations, the public will engage with that proactively. It’s when we start to hide information and there’s a void of information, that’s when things can go wrong for government.”

She said Be Ready was “realistic, quite low level, and should be reassuring because it’s basically treating the public like the grownups they are”.

Dan Goss, who runs Start Prepping UK, said traffic to his website was up 700% since news of the campaign emerged in August. He said he was glad to see the subject finally being taken seriously and spoken about in “plain language” by the government, and felt the risk of panic was low.

“The level of uptake required for that would be huge – you would need to have an enormous number of people all take the government’s advice very seriously and all jump on it as a priority,” he said.

“We’re definitely in a phase now where we’re seeing lots of more disruption to people’s lives – not necessarily apocalyptic disasters, but things that have a big impact on small areas, so this advice is very much needed.”

Robinson said the campaign showed how the perception of “prepping” has shifted, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic when most people will remember seeing empty supermarket shelves.

“We did a study during Covid that showed people who did mild levels of prepping, such as having food, masks and hand gel in the house a few weeks before the pandemic, had lower anxiety and depression, and less stress,” she said.

“The government really needs to portray that this is just normal, everyday, very common in other countries, and isn’t wearing a tinfoil hat and building a nuclear bunker in your back garden.”

The Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 17:07:23 GMT

An electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, too

France sneezed, and Europe has again caught the cold. The wave of unrest which began with teenagers at a high school soon drew in hundreds of thousands of people nationwide and then spread across the continent. Protests have filled the streets in Lisbon and Madrid, and have ignited into violence in Milan, Brussels and Tirana as well as in French cities.

French authorities say they are deploying 70,000 officers on Saturday and are allowing only marches organised by unions. They blame hard-left militants as well as opportunistic young perpetrators for last weekend’s destruction and looting, when a minority hijacked largely peaceful protests. But with fuel prices set to rise further over the winter, the demands and participants broadening, and President Macron utterly failing to meet the moment, there is no sign of an end to the wider discontent and no speedy resolution in sight.

Europe is experiencing distinct movements, with distinct causes, demands and actors, which should not be elided. In France, crumbling and overcrowded schools were the touchpaper, with Greek protesters echoing their complaints about educational underfunding this week. In Spain and Portugal, housing is the central issue. German students are angered by the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service. But those involved see the commonalities, with some Italian demonstrators chanting in French.

Underlying all these is the breakdown of the social contract. A generation expect, with reason, to be worse off than their parents. They are understandably angry at inadequate education and job precarity, are struggling to rent places of their own well into their 20s, and are paying for pensions which they don’t believe that they will ever receive themselves, while the climate crisis haunts their futures. They see that governments worried about debt and fearful of the bond markets either cannot or will not offer them solutions. It might be more remarkable if they were happy with their lot, or confident that casting a vote at their next opportunity would fix it.

Meanwhile, increasing inequality means that they watch others grow wealthy, sometimes profiting directly from their misfortune, with flats and houses treated as financial instruments rather than homes.

This unrest also echoes the wave of gen Z protests seen around the world last year – with some of those on the streets in France, Italy and Germany even borrowing emblems used earlier from Morocco to Madagascar. The affordability crisis, heavy-handed security forces and the sense that ordinary people are being left behind while governments have no convincing answers for them were at work in those cases too.

In Europe, far-right parties, egged on by the Trump administration, are seeking to capitalise on the unrest through lies that immigrants and open borders are to blame, and that a strong hand is needed to restore order. Within the next year, four of the biggest states – Spain, France, Poland and Italy – will hold elections, threatening a radical rightwards shift that could fundamentally change the EU. Yet these parties do not have real answers to the questions raised by protesters, and a financial crisis in France might yet highlight Marine Le Pen’s economic weak spot and National Rally’s internal divisions. The future course of the continent is being shaped, for better or worse, on the streets as well as at the ballot box.

The Guardian view on Caryl Churchill’s Triumph: a play for today

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 17:06:30 GMT

At barely 20 minutes, this satire on strongman politics serves to jolt audiences out of their complacency

“Is this theatre for the TikTok generation?” one critic asked of the latest play by 88-year-old Caryl Churchill, lauded as Britain’s greatest living playwright. Triumph, her blistering satire on contemporary strongman politics, is barely 20 minutes long.

Cleverly spliced with Suetonius’s The Twelve Caesars, the play takes the form of a press conference given by a blond-wigged apparatchik, who smilingly extols the barbarities of an unnamed narcissistic emperor. If “Triumph” were a crossword answer, the clue might be “To greet a populist US leader in confusion – a win (7)”. Even given Churchill’s reputation for prescience, the play was uncannily timely. It premiered in London and New York on the same day that President Trump’s short-lived press officer Katie Zacharia was forced to resign. As the American comedian Robin Williams quipped of an earlier administration, “People say satire is dead. It’s not dead; it’s alive and living in the White House.”

Churchill is a playwright of ideas who, throughout her long career, has played with structure. Her 2012 play Love and Information depicted the fragmentation of modern life through 57 scenes and more than 100 characters. With just three actors, this new play is a triumph of form and content: as short and direct as a press conference, its purpose is to alert us to a global crisis. This is the theatrical equivalent of a political sketch.

A story arc in one act, it is not a highbrow version of the 60- to 90-second schlocky microdrama episodes for mobile phones, which have become so popular that Channel 4 is launching its own series. Short plays go back to Suetonius’s time. Chekhov, Beckett and Albee were all masters of the dramatic sprint. Churchill started out writing short radio plays, and in later years her work has become an increasing feat of compression.

But this brevity goes against a trend for theatrical maximalism. To persuade audiences back to theatres and cinemas after the pandemic, plays and films have been getting longer, perhaps to justify the price of a ticket. The Oscar-winning movie The Brutalist required a 15-minute interval in 2024. A two-part RSC dramatisation of Middlemarch has just opened at Stratford, where an epic Game of Thrones ended last month. However, a reducio spell has been cast on the six-hour, two-part Harry Potter and the Cursed Child juggernaut, which has reopened at half its original length.

A play in your lunch break or after a night out is not practical for many. And while mini dramas make use of empty theatre hours and fit around evening performances, only a playwright of Churchill’s stature could guarantee a sellout, weeklong run for a show briefer than an interval without audiences feeling short-changed. Triumph could be seen as a curtain raiser for a revival of her 1979 classic Cloud 9 at the National Theatre next month, and Three and a Bit, a new collection of “biting short plays” at the Almeida in January.

The Guardian’s Michael Billington called Churchill “theatre’s great disruptor”. With Triumph she is disrupting the conventions of theatregoing itself: a play isn’t always something to be enjoyed between an early supper, interval drinks and the last train home. She has turned the attention economy on its head. Like a Covid-era emergency press conference, Triumph interrupts its audience’s day to make them listen. It jolts us out of our complacency.

UK children just as likely to have suffered harm on social media despite crackdown

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 17:06:04 GMT

Campaigners call lack of progress ‘staggering’, as Ofcom also admits little change in severity of harm to children encountering unsafe content

Landmark online safety measures have failed to limit the proportion of children suffering harm from social media, the UK’s online regulator has admitted, in an assessment branded “staggering” by campaigners.

The proportion of children being fed unsafe content that often left them frightened, confused and upset, was almost unchanged, according to an Ofcom review of the first nine months of supposedly strict requirements on social media platforms such as TikTok and Instagram.

Under the Online Safety Act, the tech giants had to protect children from harmful content including pornography, serious violence, suicide material, racism, misogyny and bullying, with a series of specific duties introduced in summer 2025.

But Ofcom found that “at a total level there was no significant change in the proportion of children encountering harmful content over the first nine months after the children’s safety duties came into force in July 2025”.

It called the finding “concerning” and said there was no evidence indicating a change in the severity of harm since the flagship regulations, under the Online Safety Act, took effect.

Examples of harms included children being shown the murder of Charlie Kirk, graphic pornography and weapon-related content making them feel unsafe in their schools and neighbourhoods. Personalised recommendation feeds powered by “for you” algorithms were repeatedly found by Ofcom to be at the root of the continuing tide of harmful material.

The findings come a week after a coroner concluded that access to the suicide-related material on TikTok may have played a significant part in the decision of Adriana Retyte, a 14-year-old pupil at Langley school in Norfolk, to take her own life in May.

They come a day after Clavicular, 20, a popular social media influencer who promotes surgery and drugs as part of extreme male beauty regimes and has appeared with Andrew Tate, pleaded not guilty to rape in a US court, raising fresh concerns about the influence of “manosphere” content creators.

Ofcom’s research included tracking the exposure of UK children aged eight to 17 to harmful content on user-to-user services, its impact and their use of safety tools and an analysis of children’s wellbeing after exposure to harmful content. The assessment has been shared with Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport.

NSPCC, a child protection charity, said the findings showed that children were being exposed to harmful content at an “alarming rate”, which it said was echoed in the flow of calls for help to Childline, its online and telephone support service. Rani Govender, the head of child safety online, said “progress is not happening nearly fast enough”.

“Tech companies have had months to act, yet too many platforms are still built to keep children hooked with their algorithms continuing to push harmful content to their young users,” she said. “We urgently need stronger action from tech companies to rein in features that drive harm to children and stop putting business interests over their safety obligations.”

Dame Melanie Dawes, the watchdog’s chief executive, this week told MPs: “We do not see a safety culture from these large social media companies.” The regulator is already facing a wave of legal actions from tech companies challenging its powers including the Instagram operator Meta, as well as TikTok and X, owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX group. It has warned it risks being “absolutely clobbered legally by deep-pocketed individuals and firms”.

Children most commonly reported encountering pornographic content via personalised feeds, and girls, in particular, reported feeling confused or upset after seeing such content, Ofcom found. Suicide and eating disorder content was also driven mostly through personal feeds, with girls most likely to encounter both types of harmful material. The Ofcom review also found that “young men and boys consuming motivational and self-improvement content can rapidly become exposed to more extreme content which includes the promotion of misogyny and racism”. Misspelled hashtags and coded language are often used to bypass content moderation systems that would otherwise block harmful misogynistic content.

Ian Russell, the father of Molly Russell, who took her life aged 14 in 2017 after viewing suicide material on social media, told the Guardian the lack of progress was “staggering but sadly not surprising”. He blamed “timidity and lack of action” from the regulator and said: “It is time that Ofcom stood up for children and investigated the major flaws in TikTok and Instagram’s design features, not just small technicalities that have been their focus so far.”

An Ofcom spokesperson said: “This is an industry that’s been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years. And so while significant progress is being made – including the introduction of widespread age checks, stronger protections against grooming, and tougher safeguards against child sexual exploitation and abuse – we’re under no illusion that there is much for the industry still to do. We’ve shown that tech firms that don’t comply with their duties can expect enforcement action.”

It said the data did not cover the period from this spring when it said it stepped up pressure on Facebook, YouTube, Snap, Roblox and TikTok over child safety issues. It also said it recorded some reductions in harmful content on platforms including the games Minecraft and Call of Duty and YouTube, Pinterest and Facebook. In July it launched an investigation into TikTok over child safety concerns, including how it checks users are adults or children.

The continuing risks to children come before a planned Australia-style social media ban in the UK for under-16s which is due, from next spring, to cover platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and X, but not messaging services such as WhatsApp and Signal.

However campaigners have warned that must not overshadow the need to enforce protections under the Online Safety Act.

“Children will continue to face risks on services covered by the act but not the proposed ban, including gaming and messaging platforms,” said Mitali Sud, a senior policy manager at Internet Matters, a child online safety campaign. “Sixteen- and 17-year-olds will still use social media. A social media ban cannot replace the need to make online services safer for children.”

A government spokesperson said platforms needed to do more to protect children from harmful content.

“That’s why we are taking bold action to strengthen protections for children from risks of harm online – banning social media from offering their services to under-16s and protecting kids from harmful functionalities like livestreaming and stranger communications on a wide range of services, including gaming services,” they said.

“When it comes to children’s safety, we are not and never will be bystanders. Platforms have both a moral and legal duty to protect children and we expect them to work with us to set a new normal for future generations.”

TikTok, Meta, X and Google were contacted for comment.

Wallaroos complete Scotland sweep as retiring Smith gets standing ovation despite red

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 16:49:27 GMT

Women’s rugby union: Australia 38-31 Scotland

Cecilia Smith ‘sorry’ for red card on final Wallaroos game

The Wallaroos completed their three-game sweep over Scotland with a 38-31 win on Friday in a spicy contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.

Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Canberrabut again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it. The hosts received four yellow cards, with the retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.

Scotland had two players sent to the sin bin and it could have been far uglier if the Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs’ accusations of biting had been verified on review. But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich’s forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.

The Australian prop Eva Karpani was shown a yellow card for a high shot in her milestone game on her 50th cap, while the impressive teenage fly-half Waiaria Ellis was also sent to the sin bin for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.

The win came as a relief for the retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation despite being sent off. “I’m really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess,” Smith said as she embraced her daughter, Ruby, after the match. “She’s been there since day one,” said Smith of her daughter. “Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and put the hard work in.”

A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after making her debut in 2018. “It’s created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for,” she said. “I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can’t be what you can’t see.”

Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against Scotland. The Wallaroos are now out of action until the side transitions to a full-time operation next year under their new coach, Sione Fukofuka, who has previously coached Scotland.

Reform UK braces for Farage standards verdict over undeclared £5m gift

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 16:45:14 GMT

Party insiders say they expect initial verdict to be against leader and are preparing to appeal against adverse findings

Nigel Farage’s Reform is braced for a negative report from the standards commissioner over his failure to declare a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and plans to appeal against any adverse findings.

The party is on tenterhooks over the report, with multiple Reform insiders saying they are readying for a fightback through the appeals process and fully expect the initial verdict to find against their leader.

Any attempt by Farage to oppose a negative verdict could mean the process drags on for months, as an MP under investigation has the right to present further evidence to the standards committee as well as to appeal through the independent expert panel.

After any appeals process, and if parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons, Farage could end up facing a second byelection in his Clacton constituency. This would require a recall petition, triggered by signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over six weeks.

Farage was interviewed by the standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, last month and the party expects to be notified of the verdict at any time.

While it awaits the findings, Reform has been overhauling its HQ operations, having been destabilised by undercover investigations by Channel 4 and ITV in recent weeks and fallen in the polls.

The Channel 4 reporting with the investigative group Verbatim has led to a police inquiry into alleged attempts to orchestrate illegal overseas donations, as well as the suspension of James Orr as head of policy and Dan Jukes as Farage’s communications chief. They deny wrongdoing and an internal party report has cleared them, but the matter remains under police investigation.

The ITV reporting uncovered racist councillors and election candidates for the party caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.

One Reform insider said the ITV documentary in particular was extremely bad and showed the party’s vetting had not been up to scratch, despite its claims to have professionalised.

There have also been departures. Aaron Lobo, its former head of operations, has moved to a new role running a Reform-focused TV channel, which is hiring dozens of “journalists” to increase communications directly to voters.

Amar Johal, a former government lawyer who had been working for the party as head of policy, has taken on the role of acting head of people operations and is said to be a rising force within the party.

Thousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west England

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 16:30:39 GMT

Dozens of schools in Cornwall also affected as Storm Boelo heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of England

Thousands of homes are without power and schools were closed as the first named storm of the year hit UK shores.

Storm Austen brought severe conditions to parts of the south-west, with a gust of 76mph recorded at St Mary’s airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning. Just before 11am, more than 16,000 homes in the south-west were without power, according to National Grid.

Dozens of schools across Cornwall were forced to delay their opening, while others did not open at all. Flights were disrupted at airports in the south-west and on the Channel Islands, and passengers were being advised to check the status of their flight before travelling.

Guernsey airport’s duty manager, Steve Ford, confirmed that normal service was not expected to resume before Saturday morning, with most of the fleet having been stranded on the UK mainland. The Dutch flag carrier, KLM, cancelled dozens of its scheduled flights for Friday and Saturday.

Images showed part of Brighton’s West Pier falling into the sea after it was battered by wind and waves. The pier, first opened in 1866, has grown increasingly derelict since it closed to the public in 1975, with storms and fires destroying much of what remained. English Heritage has previously declared the structure beyond repair.

National Rail reported severe disruption across the rail network, with cancellations across England, Wales and Scotland.

Forecasters have put an additional amber weather warning for wind in place from Saturday into Sunday as the second named storm of the year, Boelo, heads in.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.”

A government campaign aimed at urging people to stock supplies of food and essentials in case of multi-day emergencies made headlines overnight. Burnham was asked whether the government was playing catchup with civil preparedness as he attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires.

He answered: “No. We are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.

“We’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

“It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments [and] we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.”

National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 12,000 properties affected by Storm Austen by 8am on Friday.

A Met Office amber warning for wind covering Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly was issued on Wednesday, taking effect on Friday from 1am until 10am.

The Met Office has now issued a 24-hour amber warning for wind from Storm Boelo from 9pm on Saturday, covering Scotland, the north coast of Northern Ireland, and Cumbria and Northumberland in the north of England.

The forecaster said gusts of up to 80mph could hit exposed coastal areas, with winds of 60-70mph widespread elsewhere, and it warned of danger to life from flying debris. It said there was also a “good chance” of power cuts, damage to buildings, trees being uprooted and travel disruption.

In anticipation of Storm Boelo, train lines in parts of northern and western Scotland are scheduled to close early at the weekend.

Services south and west of Kilwinning in North Ayrshire and the Oban and Mallaig lines will shut on Saturday evening, while the line between Kyle of Lochalsh and Achnashellach in the Highlands will be out of service on Sunday. Trains are expected to run at reduced speed elsewhere in the country.

The Republic of Ireland’s weather agency, Met Éireann, issued six warnings of varying severity for Saturday, mostly affecting counties along the west coast.

Trump again invokes claim he has the ‘right’ to run for third term as president

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 16:18:17 GMT

US constitution unequivocally states that he can’t campaign again, which the president also seems to acknowledge

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump joked with rally-goers on Thursday evening that he had “the right to run again” for president, invoking a claim he has repeatedly made that he may seek a third term despite it being unconstitutional.

“I don’t know who is going to be your next president and I think the law said, I’m not 100% sure, but I think the law says I’m not allowed to run again,” Trump said in Sioux City, Iowa.

Trump went on to seemingly acknowledge that the 22nd amendment prohibits presidents from seeking a third term but then invoked his familiar false claims that Democrats “stole” the 2020 presidential election from him.

“Well, the one thing is different: they cheated us on the second one because we won it three times. So I think I have the right to run again,” Trump said, laughing.

“I think I have the right to run again because they cheated,” Trump added with a coy smile, drawing applause from the crowd.

Trump has consistently teased that he will run again for president, which would be a direct violation of the US constitution.

In October 2025, Trump told reporters he “would love” to run for a third term. At a rally in Texas in February, the president told the crowd, “Maybe we should do one more term,” claiming he was “entitled” to it.

Last year, the Trump store started selling “Trump 2028” hats. The US president went as far as to wear one during the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in July.

His allies have dismissed the president’s claims as a joke.

Mike Johnson, the speaker of the House, told reporters last year that Trump “has a good time with that, trolling the Democrats” with claims of a third term. Johnson said he didn’t see a way to amend the constitution to allow Trump to run again.

But opponents have raised concerns that Trump is being serious.

Trump himself has recognized the restrictions imposed by the US constitution.

Even during Thursday night’s rally, he said, “I’ve studied that phrase for ever. Unfortunately, it’s quite concise. There’s not a lot of wiggle room. It says something to the effect that ‘under no circumstances and for any reason will you even consider thinking about running for president if you had – ’.”

The president, who enjoys wide support thanks to his loyal Maga base, has urged supporters to vote as though he is on the ballot in November’s US midterm elections to help Republicans pick up more seats. The impact of this unconventional strategy remains to be seen as Trump’s approval ratings fall to new lows.

Which is really England’s oldest pub? Tree-ring dating helps settle debate

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 16:17:00 GMT

Historic England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest is from 1430

With their low ceilings, timber beams and roaring fires, many of England’s inns lay claim to being the oldest in the land and to have been visited by Vikings and Saxons.

But an archaeologist who worked on behalf of Historic England says not one of the more than two dozen pubs that make this claim is being accurate.

While many claim origins dating back 1,000 years, Dr James Wright, a buildings archaeologist, said it was difficult to verify whether any pubs were built and used as inns or ale houses and kept in continuous use prior to the 1400s.

After painstaking investigation, including tree-ring dating on the wooden beams of pubs – a process known as dendrochronology – Wright named the George Inn, of Norton St Philip, Somerset, as the oldest pub in England. It has fabrics dating from the late 14th century.

He told the Guardian: “Not one of the claimants to be the oldest pub (and there are over two dozen of them) are even vaguely close to being so in reality.”

Of the George, he said: “The architectural history of the George Inn’s stone and timber suggests that this building has been in continuous service for over 600 years.” He said the pub was set up in the 14th century by the monks of nearby Hinton Priory.

Tree-ring dating had helped “to understand scientifically exactly how old the timbers are,” he said. “Because we know medieval carpenters didn’t muck around at all and they would fell the timber when it was green and build almost immediately afterwards, the actual date of felling gives us the near date of construction.”

Ye Olde Fighting Cocks in St Albans, Hertfordshire, claims to have been established around AD800, and the Bingley Arms in Bardsey, West Yorkshire, declares on its site: “It’s the original English pub – officially the oldest in Britain – dating back over 1,000 years to a time when Vikings were conquering parts of the country.” Similarly, the Royal Standard in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, boasts that it was a favoured watering hole of King Alfred the Great’s West Saxons in around AD880.

Wright said most of these claims seemed to be “modern marketing strategies”. “The Fighting Cocks is often said to date to AD793. This date was probably not arrived at until 1926 when it appeared on a postcard. Prior to that, it was speculated to date to 1030, 770 and 672,” he said. “There does not seem to be a basis in reality for any of those claims. Instead, the building started as a monastic dovecote, built around 1400. The earliest date when we can say for sure it was active as a public house is the first decade of the 19th century.”

Many of the pubs claiming to be the oldest say they were mentioned in the Domesday Book, but the historian said: “There are no pubs mentioned – at all – in the Domesday Book, so any pub claiming to be in it is having you on.”

Wright added: “The claims are likely to originate less in folklore and more in canny marketing strategies by landlords, tenants, breweries and pub companies. The claims potentially rely upon the public not being aware of how to accurately date historic buildings.”

He provided the Guardian with a list of the pubs he believes to be the oldest in the country. His methodology was to determine that it was purpose-built as a public house, that it had been in continuous service and that there was archaeological, archival or dendrochronological evidence for the existence of significant primary fabric remaining from the original construction.

“I did consider buildings which had been converted and others which had periodically changed in land use,” he said. “Even with those taken into consideration, there are only about 12 to 16 genuine contenders which have been doing trade since the medieval period. Of these, the oldest date to the 14th and 15th centuries.”

George Inn, Norton St Philip, Somerset: late 14th century and 1430-32.

Bull Hotel, Ludlow, Shropshire: 14th and 15th centuries.

King’s Head, Shrewsbury, Shropshire: 1426, 1430-31.

New Inn, Gloucester, Gloucestershire: 1432.

White Hart Inn, Hook, Hampshire: 1419-51.

George Hotel, Dorchester-on-Thames, Oxfordshire: mid 15th century.

Angel Inn, Andover, Hampshire: 1445-55.

Kings Head, Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire: 1445-55.

Angel, Grantham, Lincolnshire: circa 1450.

George and Pilgrims Inn, Glastonbury, Somerset: 1461-83.

Saracen’s Head, Southwell, Nottinghamshire: 1460s.

George Hotel, Odiham, Hampshire: 1486-87.

This article was amended on 23 October 2026. A previous version said the Saracens’s Head is in Lincolnshire; it is in Nottinghamshire.

Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 16:10:34 GMT

People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds

The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.

In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.

Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.

Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.

The White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump, and her representative worked directly with ​Russian and Ukrainian ‌leadership to define the ​terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.

Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.

Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe. As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.

Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.

Lubinets ⁠told Reuters on Friday that the mission to Oleshky would involve ⁠demining roads leading into the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians. “A sufficient ​quantity of ‌humanitarian ‌aid will be delivered to ‌meet the needs of everyone who requires it. What’s more, we are working to ensure ‌that this is not just a ​one-off event, and that it is not limited to Oleshky alone,” ⁠he said.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.

The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.

The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.

“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, “underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access” to Starlink in a phone call with Trump on Friday, Downing Street said.

Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.

“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.

“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.

The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.

The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.

Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday, and on Friday the Russian deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, said three tankers were en route to the US and claimed Russian companies could supply 500,000 metric tonnes in October.

Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.

The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.

Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.

Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.

The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

Bavuma’s nine-hour masterpiece was art we risk losing in Test cricket’s great purge

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 16:00:08 GMT

T20 franchise cricket is trash sport and killing the five-day game is cultural vandalism. What would Orwell have made of this?

Have you read George Orwell’s review of Mein Kampf? This might not sound like a grabby reference, or a killer hook for the algorithm. But Hitler is always hot. Hitler is legacy brand. Hitler is eyeballs. Also, it’s just a great review, even more so because it was written at a time when the world didn’t quite know what Hitler was “all about”.

True, you get a vibe off people. The invasion of France. The ranting, visceral hatred. There were signs, clues, indications that this guy, this guy is not my kind of guy.

But the full Hitler-verse had yet to reveal itself. And for a while you worry Orwell’s going to get it wrong, not go hard enough, misread the full history as we now know it. He writes about how much he likes Hitler’s face because he looks pained and sad, like a wounded dog, giving off that sense of eternal injustice the German people really went for.

By this point you’re trying to catch his eye, coughing loudly, saying “Holocaust” into your fist. No, George. Don’t start talking about charisma.

Luckily, it all turns out fine. Orwell says that he would definitely kill Hitler if he got within arm’s reach of him. Then he describes, better than anyone before or since, the terrifying nature of the world Mein Kampf is proposing, above all its utter boredom, the eternal grey repetitions, same struggle, same triumph, same boot stamping on same face, same pitch of willed and empty hysteria.

And yeah … you’re thinking about T20 franchise cricket, aren’t you? I didn’t say it. You did. It’s fine. The mind goes where the mind goes.

You’re picturing a year-round cycle of brain-flooding noise. An endless will to power. The Kansas City CheeseSteaks v the Reykjavik Unmentionables live from the Jakarta T5 Megascream, injected straight into your eyeballs by a robot replicant Danny Morrison.

It’s fine that you want to make this connection. It’s even deeply fitting given the greatest story of the sporting week by an absolute mile, a story so big, so sweeping, so viscerally personal, that most people seem to have completely ignored it, comes from the polar opposite place.

This is of course Temba Bavuma’s match-winning nine-hour hundred in the second Test against Australia in Gqeberha, one of those episodes where sport and the life of the nation seem to cross, blend and become indistinguishable.

Mainly Bavuma in Gqeberha was an incredible feat of skill, resilience and constant adaptive intelligence, in the way only Test Cricket can deliver. Bavuma walked out to bat with the summer running away from him. Thrashed in the first Test, South Africa were 12 for two, faced with one of the great bowling attacks.

Bavuma has been a transformative Test captain, with 12 wins in 14 matches, four hundreds, a world championship mace, all stretched over three broken years. But he is still always, always chasing legitimacy and affirmation, in a way that is unique to cricket, but also unique to this man in this role in this sporting nation. First black middle order batsman. First black captain. How is this going to fall? How strong is that ice underfoot?

Two days later Bavuma was last man out for 179 in a total of 425 for nine, sprinting off with a kind of light around him, waving his bat giddily, 36 years old, wife and kid in the crowd, the greatest moment of his sporting life.

There were so many parts to this. First, the survival period, with that endearing tic of gently jutting his chin out at the bowler, mixed in with the odd deliciously clean whip or push or clump. Bavuma has really quick hands. I remember seeing him in east London in a white-ball game against dark skies and low stands, and all you could really see was his hands whizzing with thrilling speed, like fireflies in the night.

In Gqeberha he was all poise and measured severity. When he plays a cover drive he seems to lean at 45 degrees, knees bent, entire body easing into the oblique, perfectly contained in his own little square of time and space.

The game changed with the partnership of 106 with Marco Jansen before lunch on the third day, brilliant counterattacking Test cricket, but also an amazing tableau. At one end the gangling Dutch farmer with the easy, guileless stride, a cricketer who always seems to be running in with a bushel of radishes over one shoulder and a bolt-action rabbit gun in his waistband. At the other the tiny, super-smart black captain. It’s no more than an optic, unrelated to the nation’s real-world struggles. But it’s also real. Sport is, as ever, saying: how about this version of things?

Bavuma got to his hundred with a release of pent-up power, swivel-pulling Pat Cummins through midwicket, holding the shot, one of those moments where the batter feels what has happened a second before anyone else, allowed in that microsecond to exist all alone inside his own little pocket of private triumph.

But then Bavuma has always had to be aware, to hold himself a certain way. There was surprise in some corners that he turned out to be such an unflappable captain. Try being Temba Bavuma for a bit. You think this stuff is going to faze you?

Bavuma is a child of the transition period, born three months after Nelson Mandela left Victor Verster Prison, the same day (get this) the government finally opened up all its public hospitals to black citizens. He grew up a township boy in Langa, playing in the street, learning which strips of local tarmac had the most carry and bounce.

Plucked out aged 10 on a scholarship to one of South Africa’s top schools, he struggled. Ten is relatively late to start trying to become an elite batter. How about still perfecting your English, learning how to act, what to put on your plate at dinner? Even his height, which we must always talk about, is a thing. Bavuma is the 10th shortest man ever to play Test cricket. Yeah, pour it on. What else have you got?

There was the slow-burn start to his career. For years the quota talk circled, the weird dual burden of innate outsiderdom and suspicions of favour. Then suddenly you’re the first township captain of what has always been an anglophone, military-elite kind of sport.

Sign up to The Spin

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

It sounds overwhelming. Right up until you hear him speak, at which point you just want him to talk about all the stuff in that soft voice, gentle but deliciously insistent. It’s no surprise to learn Bavuma has a normal life away from this, that his wife is founder of a luxury real estate firm, he takes his kid to school, doesn’t do celebrity, that he’s never really made a point of making a point, but made it all the same by being relentlessly himself.

Why talk about this here? Why bring endless grey, smothering repetition into it? First because even without the Bavuma story this was just an epic piece of sport, one of those occasions where every detail feels meaningful.

Steve Smith getting actual whiplash, literally wearing a foam neck-brace after whirling around to see if an edge had carried. Marnus Labuschagne whirling at the crease, acting out his own thoughts in the air like a tortured pantomime horse, while his career self-suffocates in real time. Here is Anrich Nortje, the perfect composite of shoulders, glower and vengeful moustache, looking on like the hand of fate from a deserted balcony, groin-knacked but somehow still profoundly present.

The whole thing heads on to Newlands on Tuesday and the sandpaper reunion game, an impossibly fine piece of narrative work, slow-cooked over eight years, the kind of storytelling the human brain just thirsts for.

Although now it is also time to zoom out and feel the whiplash. On the fifth day of the first Test in Durban, as Australia wrapped up their own victory the TV commentator talked about the fine sporting spirit of the contest and how “it’s credit to the people of South Africa”, at which point the camera panned back with perfect comic timing to show: a completely empty stadium.

So, back to Orwell and being on the right side of history. Because a great thing, a carefully woven cultural exhibit, is being overtly encouraged to die here. South Africa hadn’t played a Test before this series for 11 months. They played eight last year, two a second-string trip to Zimbabwe.

The hard game, the actual game that still produces the short-form TV offshoot, is being sacrificed mercilessly. And the thing that is replacing it is not just demonstrably inferior, but self-dooming in its basic inanity.

In the intervals of the Test, South African TV showed a mouthwatering banter-table chat-along featuring all of South Africa’s craggy modern greats, Polly, Makhaya, AB, the Steyn Gun, sat around just telling stories, doing everything but hug each other, conjuring up moments of beauty, gold, legend.

This will not be allowed to happen in the future. T20 cricket can’t produce these stories. It’s throwaway content, parasocial celebrity fawning. What are we going to have 20 years from now? Lhuan-dre Pretorius telling bardically embroidered tales about the time he slash-hoicked 37 off 12 balls in the now defunct North American Mega-Lurch?

There is still a fear of saying this out loud, of making the unarguable observation that a form of sporting hyper-capitalism is dictating that nothing can matter if it’s not monetisable right here and now. Half-understood arguments about demand and supply will justify an act of cultural vandalism. Well, yeah, but look at the way this entity in a state of managed decline appears, believe it or not, to be in a state of managed decline.

The reality is something beautiful is being extinguished. It feels like the sporting arm of a process that has been called the enshittification of modern life, where the bottom line is the only line, where everything must be reduced to stupidity and profitable chaff.

Orwell was also good on the “machine worship” of the early 20th century. He was, in the best way, a luddite. Inefficient, human-scale elements have a right to exist too. The mechanised loom made a few things better. But mainly it made a few people quite a lot richer.

We can resist this, and not just in the realm of trash sport, but trash life generally. Humans still know what’s good. We crave these things, still hunger for stories like the Bavuma supremacy, which may never happen again, not in the current timeline, because its structures are being peeled away even as it plays out.

Allegations against Thomas Markle Sr challenge media’s Meghan narrative

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:57:45 GMT

Duchess of Sussex’s decision to cut ties with elderly father cast in new light as he faces sexual abuse image claims

Meghan ‘deeply distressed’ by allegations against father

The depiction of the Duchess of Sussex by certain sections of the media has often been one of a fame-hungry daughter casting off an elderly father in his declining years and keeping him from his grandchildren as she embraces the international celebrity stage.

Their estrangement has been the subject of countless headlines since her marriage to Prince Harry. But her statement today, released after child sexual abuse image allegations made against Thomas Markle Sr, 82, suggests deeper, darker fears as the cause.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she said.

It has been speculated that the source of the estrangement between Meghan and Markle Sr, an award-winning TV lighting director, was over his decision to collude with a photographer and be paid for setting up shots of him preparing to attend the Sussexes’ wedding at Windsor Castle where he was due to walk her down the aisle.

In the end, Markle Sr pulled out of the wedding due to health issues, and it was Harry’s father, now King Charles, who lent the bride his arm on her final steps to the altar of St George’s chapel after she walked the first part of the aisle alone.

Since that day in May 2018, the relationship between daughter and father has never recovered. Now it appears the reasons why are contained in a letter from the same year, sent to the Metropolitan police and containing “troubling and disturbing allegations” against Markle Sr and shared with Meghan in the summer after her wedding.

The precise nature of those allegations has not been clarified, though they were enough for Meghan to want to keep her own family at a distance from him, her statement makes clear.

The fact she says that “the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine”, suggests the 2018 letter did not go as far as what has now been alleged.

Markle Sr has vigorously denied the latest allegations, which are made by his son Thomas Markle Jr, 60. First published by the Sun newspaper, they claim Markle Sr downloaded child sexual abuse images to computers and mobile phones found at his former home in the Philippines.

He has called the accusations “sick lies” from a son with whom he has a troubled relationship, and claims to have had no access to the computers and phones in question in the two years since he left Mexico, where he was previously living, for the Philippines, according to the Daily Mail.

Meghan clearly hopes to reframe the narrative of her estrangement from her father, which has often been shaped by his loquacious tendencies in many media interviews.

When speaking to journalists, Markle Sr has frequently lamented the breakdown of his relationship with his youngest daughter (he has two other children, Samantha Markle and Thomas Jr, from an earlier marriage). He has spoken of how he has been unable to reach Meghan, and of how he has never been allowed to meet his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

The media depiction has often leaned towards that of an uncaring daughter, whose father paid for her education, helped her to cultivate her interest in acting through his television work, and found himself abandoned in his time of need.

For the most part, Meghan has not publicly acknowledged his many health woes – he has suffered a series of strokes and recently had a leg amputated due to complications with a blood clot – and she clearly believes this has been weaponised against her.

However, in 2025, Meghan’s spokesperson confirmed that the duchess had “reached out” privately to her father when he was hospitalised and very unwell. He is now understood to be in a rehabilitation centre in Florida undergoing physiotherapy after the amputation of his leg.

Whatever the outcome of this latest development, it adds a new dimension to the complicated, fractured relationship between Meghan and her family.

Tinned mackerel, hand-crank radios and bags for poo: crisis-prepping guides around the world

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:52:29 GMT

UK allies have long urged people to stockpile supplies for a crisis. How are people from France to Australia being advised to prepare?

The UK has told people to fill their pantries with food for three days in case of catastrophe, joining a host of countries urging citizens to ready themselves for core systems failing.

Such advice, once dismissed as the preserve of preppers, has become more common in government circles as climate breakdown worsens weather extremes and geopolitical tensions turn cyber-attacks and sabotage into a regular occurrence.

Even in countries with national strategic food stockpiles – a buffer the UK lacks – authorities have asked individuals to play their part in societal resilience.

What actions do Britain’s allies – from the US and Europe to India and Australia – recommend people take before disaster strikes?

France calls the first 72 hours a “decisive period” in which people should monitor TV and radio news for official updates, and keep an emergency kit close by in case they have to get out fast.

In addition to the essentials, such as food, water, medicine and cash, the guidelines recommend filling the go-bag with photocopies of documents, spare sets of house and car keys, and even games to pass the time.

The strategy emphasises the need for solidarity and calls on people to be in close communication with loved ones, resist rumours and disinformation, and consider volunteering as a reservist or with civil protection organisations. Experts have warned that maintaining societal cohesion is crucial during crises.

As far back as the 1960s, households in West Germany were encouraged to stockpile 14 days of canned food – a target that few seem to have reached despite cold war tensions.

About a decade ago, the recommendation fell to 10 days, and guidance issued last October said households should do this “where possible”, describing even three days’ worth of supplies as “a big help”. Almost half of Germans fail to meet this threshold, a YouGov poll for the German Press Agency found in January.

Guidelines from the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance recommend stockpiling durable foods that are ready to eat, in case cookers stop working, and foods that have short cooking times, allowing fuel for a camping stove to last for more days in a blackout.

The checklist of items also features a hand-crank or solar-powered radio, a paper list of important phone numbers, and a well-stocked medicine cabinet.

The US emergency readiness campaign, launched in 2003, recommends people “make a plan today”, noting that members of a family may not be together when disaster strikes.

Its toolkit foresees people storing enough water for each person to have one US gallon (3.8 litres) a day, both for drinking and sanitation, as well as items such as a whistle to call for help, a dust mask to filter contaminated air and plastic sheeting for shelter.

Food supply advice varies between states, ranging from a few days in California to more than two weeks in Hawaii.

The guidance suggests families rethink the contents of the kit each year as their needs change. It also calls for storing supplies at home, at work and in the car.

Nordic countries have ramped up emergency preparations since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The Finnish advice describes home emergency supplies, including backup power and hygiene articles, as an “excellent basis” for many situations, while warning against hoarding.

It recommends people have enough for at least three days and says these supplies can help even when mundane obstacles such as illness keep one from going to the shops.

Secure silos of grain that make up Finland’s ample strategic reserve provide an extra layer of security, designed to feed the population for nine months if supply chains collapse or domestic production fails.

The Swedish advice, which is framed around conflict but also covers pandemics and extreme weather, says people can “contribute to collective preparedness” if they can manage on their own for at least one week.

It includes specific tips such as growing berries on windowsills, freezing bottles of water, which can function as ice packs if freezers break and then be drunk once the ice melts, and, if the toilet will not flush, disposing of excrement in plastic bags covered by sawdust.

The Norwegian guidelines, which are offered in 30 languages, also encourage people to be able to “fend for themselves” for at least a week when systems such as the internet, mobile phone networks and bank payments are down.

The country is particularly reliant on electricity for home heating, and recommends people store warm clothes, sleeping bags and candles, and keep fireplaces and chimneys clean.

“In a crisis or war, people must be prepared for the fact that not everything will work as normal,” it warns. “The help will first go to those who need it most.”

The Danish advice gives a sample three-day meal plan, which includes 500g of crispbread, 300g of canned mackerel in tomato sauce, 300g of chickpeas and kidney beans, 500g each of pasta and groats, and 1.5kg of tinned vegetables, as well as 100g of nuts and some vegetable oil.

The Australian government can declare a national emergency but individual states and territories are mainly responsible for management.

Most authorities recommend storing supplies to last three to seven days, though the New South Wales health service recommends planning for two weeks. Its “pantry list” recommends giving special consideration to family members with special needs, such as babies, pregnant women and those who are old or ill.

Its fire services also have detailed guidance on preparing for bushfires, ranging from trimming vegetation to wearing a wide-brimmed hat to protect the head from falling embers and respirator masks to avoid the worst of the smoke.

India’s disaster preparedness checklist, prepared by the National Centre for Disease Control, recommends finding out which hazards threaten your home and finding safe spots for each type of disaster.

It calls for storing at least a three-day supply of water and food, prioritising products that require little cooking or refrigeration, while avoiding very salty or spicy ones.

The recommended emergency bag includes a battery-operated torch, chlorine tablets to purify water, a first aid book, and thick ropes. It recommends practising evacuation drills with all family members twice a year. The checklist also explicitly warns that the climate crisis is likely to lead to more frequent and severe disasters.

We are reclaiming real life after getting rid of Instagram

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:41:58 GMT

Readers on taking back their lives – and brains – from social media algorithms

I couldn’t agree more with Georgina McNamara (The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life, 19 October).

Reading about the sheer relief of stepping away from Instagram resonates deeply with my own feelings over the last few years. There is an incredible quiet joy in reclaiming a truly private life, entirely free from the pressure to document, curate and perform our daily routines for an invisible audience.

This shift immediately brings to mind Jaron Lanier’s compelling points in his 2018 book Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now. Lanier warned us that these platforms aren’t just neutral tools; they are behaviour-modification engines designed to hijack our attention and slowly erode our autonomy.

His argument that social media algorithms inherently reward outrage, tribalism and comparison to drive engagement feels truer today than ever. By participating, we unwittingly allow algorithms to alter our moods and warp our sense of reality, stripping away the simple contentment of just being.

In my own life, stepping back from that digital noise has been incredibly grounding. I’ve found that my most meaningful moments – whether I’m spending a few focused hours woodworking in my workshop, sitting down to figure out a new arrangement on the guitar, or just out walking the spaniels – are vastly richer when they exist solely in the present, without the impulse to photograph or share them.

Getting back to tangible, analogue realities has felt like taking a long, deep breath. Even organising a recent social evening at the local pub in Hipperholme reminded me how much more genuine our connections are when we are physically present, sharing a pint and a conversation rather than a screen.

A private life is not a smaller life; it is an unmediated one. As Lanier suggests, opting out isn’t just rejecting technology; it’s reclaiming our free will and our peace of mind. Guy Edmondson Hipperholme, West Yorkshire

Georgina McNamara’s article really resonated with me. I haven’t deleted Instagram, but I check it very infrequently now. While I didn’t post all that often, the compulsion to document experiences and turn moments into posts or stories, rather than being in the moment, was always there – and with it, the eventual anxiety about whether anyone had liked what I had posted.

I also realised that comparing my day-to-day life with others’ carefully curated highlights was making me unhappy: an endless stream of holiday photos made me keenly aware of how long it would be until I would next have a break, while other fitness instructors posting photos taken from strategic angles made me worry that I wasn’t as flexible as them in comparison, or that my technique was poor.

After reading some books and articles on cutting back on smartphone use, I took a number of steps to reduce my phone use, and used the One Sec app to trigger a breathing exercise whenever I opened Instagram.

It made me realise how often I checked Instagram as a reflex, and that I could be devoting this time to other activities that I found more fulfilling. The few occasions that I do check it these days, I find it a bit overwhelming.

I find that my mind is a lot quieter now and that I pay more attention to what is around me, appreciating what I see as a moment that doesn’t have to become a post or a story. And if I take a photograph of something, it’s because I like it, not because I’m concerned about whether someone else will. Laura Dobie Glasgow

I deleted my Instagram account after getting pregnant with my second child. At first, I muted it; when I returned, the algorithm had decided that, with all the information it had gathered on me, I must have taken a break due to baby loss. It bombarded me with images and messages about baby loss, until it realised this wasn’t the reason and started to fill my algorithm with “two under two” narratives. The juxtaposition was stark and insensitive. It felt awful.

I realised I didn’t want this platform having information about not just me but my family as well, and I hated that by feeding into it (with likes on obsessed-over images and funny captions), I was allowing it to dictate some of my parenting decisions through algorithms and advertised content. Since leaving it, my motherhood journey has been much happier, simpler and in my control. I completely agree that it’s the change that works! Stefanie Withey-Jones London

I enjoyed Georgina McNamara’s account of leaving Instagram, particularly her observations about the time spent checking reactions and seeking validation.

However, there is an important distinction to be made between sharing our lives and seeking approval for them. I use social media to share photographs with friends and family because I enjoy letting people I know see what I have been doing. For me, that is about connection, not validation.

There is another pleasure too that is rarely mentioned: unexpected reminders of photographs posted one, five or even 10 years ago. A holiday, a familiar face or an ordinary moment that I had forgotten suddenly reappears, bringing back the feelings associated with it.

It’s not just the memories themselves I treasure, but the unexpected joy of being reminded of them, often when they’re furthest from my mind.

The problem, perhaps, is not posting our lives online, but allowing other people’s reactions to determine how much we value those experiences. Nicky Atkinson Shoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex

I lasted only six weeks on Instagram. Unlike Georgina McNamara, I came to the party late, in my 60s. Almost immediately, I resented the way that posts were pushed into my feed. In no time at all I was spending hours watching posts of horse sanctuaries in the US and feeling depressed and resentful at whole sections of society. So I deleted my account – no small feat in itself, as the process is determined to keep you there.

Afterwards, I felt relief at getting back hours of my own brain time, but for months, I would think: “I could just pop on and look at x, y, z.” I’m glad that I’m off, and scared at how quickly I became addicted. Now when I look around I see that I am the only person on the bus or train who is not looking at a screen but at the outside world, and thinking for myself. Dr Hilary Redden Aberdeen

The one change that worked? I deleted all social media from my phone and instead installed the Guardian app with a subscription to news and well-curated content. No more time-wasting, bottomless doomscrolling for me. Do it, kids! Cecilia Scott Woking, Surrey

A tender sporting moment with Alex ‘Hurricane’ Higgins

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:41:52 GMT

Paul Mitchell recalls snooker champion Alex Higgins tearfully celebrating his win with his young daughter

While I enjoyed your photo feature with its “groundbreaking images [that] have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power” (Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad), 17 October), I felt that a more fitting sporting example than Gazza’s tears would have been Alex “Hurricane” Higgins at the 1982 World Snooker Championship.

On winning the title, Higgins, a notoriously erratic and divisive figure, broke down in tears and pleaded for his wife and infant daughter to join him. It was not an act of image management, popularity-seeking or virtue- signalling. Rather, it was the spontaneous reaction of a man who simply wanted to share the greatest moment of his career with his young daughter.

The scene was made all the more poignant by what followed. With the benefit of hindsight, and in light of Higgins’s subsequent decline into sporting wilderness and personal hardship, that moment stands as a fleeting glimpse of unguarded joy and human vulnerability. In that respect, it remains one of sport’s most moving displays of emotion.

And if Alex Higgins, a man renowned for his toughness, volatility and refusal to conform, could openly weep in public and clutch his baby daughter at the pinnacle of his career, perhaps it serves as a reminder that showing emotion diminishes neither the man nor the achievement. Paul Mitchell Belfast
