‘I always think my head will fall off when Traitors turn on each other’: the inside story of the world’s biggest TV show

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:00:26 GMT

Celia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owl

It all began on a Dutch trading ship in 1628. No, really. When the Batavia set sail from Amsterdam, it crashed and the shipwrecked survivors were left stranded on a tiny island off the coast of Western Australia. As mutineers eyed the Batavia’s stash of silver, shipmates, friends and families turned on each other. About 100 people were brutally murdered, making it one of the most violent chapters in maritime history.

Nearly 400 years later, in 2015, creative entrepreneur Marc Pos had a lightbulb moment while reading about this “adult Lord of the Flies” atrocity. It gave him the idea for a reality TV show – the game of trust and treachery we now know as The Traitors. It was originally envisaged to take place on a boat, with banished players jumping overboard into the sea.

Co-creator Jasper Hoogendoorn joined Pos to develop the idea, The Mutineers. After 20 rejections, they fine-tuned the game further. Filming it on a boat was too limiting, so they shifted the action on to dry land – and looked for more aesthetic inspiration. Pos was once a choirboy in a 14th-century cathedral, gazing up at its spooky gothic architecture. This became the template for the show’s setting: cue cloak-clad figures walking silently down torch-lit corridors to a secret tower. The Traitors was finally born in 2021, now known as De Verraders.

UK production company Studio Lambert – maker of superior reality TV from Gogglebox to Race Across the World – soon clocked this new Dutch show. “We watched it in the office and couldn’t stop talking about it,” says creative director Mike Cotton. “Reality TV goes in cycles. At the time, it was in a phase of dating shows. This felt totally different. It wasn’t about love, it was about trust.” He and executive producer Sarah Fay visited the Netherlands to witness the phenomenon first-hand. “We went straight to the set,” says Cotton. “All these people in a castle were discussing how someone had been murdered and taking it very seriously. Even unedited, it was fascinating to watch.”

Snapping up the UK and US rights, Studio Lambert began adapting it. “The Dutch version was smaller, so we supersized it,” says Cotton. “We tweaked the format. Changed the endgame. We decided to film the British and American shows at the same castle in the Scottish Highlands.” Each episode is estimated to cost £1m, almost double a normal reality show, enabling it to splash out on cinematic flourishes such as exploding pirate ships and creepy cabins.

Now all it needed was a worthy host. Enter Claudia Winkleman, clad in covetable knitwear. “[BBC One controller] Kate Phillips said she had a show for me,” recalls Winkleman. “It was in Scotland for four weeks. But I don’t leave the kids or my bed, so I said no thanks and forgot all about it. Then Kate said: ‘You should rethink. I’m going to send you the original series they made in Holland.’ I watched two episodes and called back to say I was booking my train to Inverness.”

“Once we had Ardross Castle and Claudia, everything fell into place,” says Cotton. “The UK version quickly became its own thing.” Launching in 2022, it pulled in ratings of about 4 million. As buzz spread and punters caught up on iPlayer, audience figures grew exponentially. The second series leapt to 7 million, the third to 9 million, the fourth to 11.5 million. The inaugural celebrity edition last autumn peaked at 14.9 million, making it the year’s most-watched show.

Did Winkleman ever imagine such stratospheric numbers? “Not a chance,” she laughs. “But I don’t like knowing about ratings. My BBC boss Ed [Havard, director of entertainment] called me a couple of weeks ago to say ‘10 million’. I told him it was a clerical error and never to call me again.”

Fay believes Winkleman is key to the show’s success. “As much as possible, we wanted The Traitors to feel like a drama,” she says. “That was our approach in every department, be it set design, music or Claudia’s wardrobe. It needed to feel like a premium show. Claudia’s integral to that. It’s not your usual reality host role, where they’re slightly removed from the action. She’s embedded as queen of the castle and obsessed with the game. Right from the start, she begged to have screens in her dressing room so she could watch the footage.”

Ever modest, Winkleman plays down her importance. “I disagree with that quite viciously,” she says. “At first, I couldn’t bear being mean or cold. I loathed not smiling and telling everyone they were amazing. But under Sarah’s guidance, I learned to trust that I could be a bit strict. It’s hard because I feel protective and maternal – is that weird? – towards all our players. I want them to know they’re smashing it. Then again, I’m dressed like Chewbacca and throwing portraits on the floor, so I’m hard to take seriously.”

Now airing in more than 40 countries, The Traitors has officially become the most successful TV show on the planet. It has won Baftas and Emmys, while spawning board games, stage shows, escape rooms, even a Prom. Did TV insiders expect the show to strike global gold?

“Nobody saw it coming,” says Deadline’s TV expert Jake Kanter. “Viewing figures growing steadily is always a good sign because it means word of mouth is strong. The best definition of a hit is that you don’t need to tell anyone how well it’s performing, they just know. Your friends, family and colleagues are talking about it.”

When Pos and Hoogendoorn shopped the show around, they resisted pressure to compromise and dug their heels in over certain core principles. One was that gameplay should take place in a self-contained bubble with minimal interference.

“The Dutch always talked about it as a game, not a TV show,” says Cotton. “This is the game, these are the rules. After that, they’re very hands-off. That’s something we’ve adopted. We set up the game and just let it go. That’s rare nowadays. We never want producers to come up at the round table or be the reason someone’s suspected as a Traitor. If you interfere, they’ll latch on to it. We plan certain elements but have no way of controlling what happens.”

Another cardinal rule was that the identity of the Traitors isn’t hidden from the audience. Wouldn’t it be better if viewers played detective, too? “We did dabble with the audience not knowing with the Secret Traitor twist in series four,” says Fay. “But what’s delicious for the viewer is that they’re in on it all. They see the strategies and paranoia on both sides. Imagine if you didn’t know Alan Carr was a Traitor last year. You’d have missed out on the hilarity of him sweating, panicking and going: ‘What am I doing?’”

Winkleman finds the psychology of the game endlessly fascinating. “It’s about gut instinct,” she says. “Turns out it doesn’t exist. It’s about what happens when we try and ‘read’ people. It’s about trust, betrayal, friendship, all of it.” It’s no coincidence that The Traitors was conceived during the era of fake news and social media manipulation. In a post-truth world, it offers insights into conspiracy theories, herd mentality and groupthink.

“What still wows me is that every series is completely different,” says Fay. “That’s the beauty of a murder mystery. We’re just back from filming the seventh UK series and, again, there are things coming up that you’ve never seen before.”

When did the makers realise they had a smash hit on their hands? “For me, it was episode four of the first series,” says Fay. “The Red Breakfast, when Tom stood up and went: ‘Alex isn’t a Traitor, she’s my girlfriend!’ We were watching the rushes with our mouths wide open.”

“It’s rare to find a format that’s multi-generational,” says Fay. “Remember when we walked down the street and pubs were showing the series one final on big screens, like a football match?” grins Cotton. “That blew our minds.”

What have been Winkleman’s highlights? “There are so many I could bore you for 18 months straight. I often have to stop myself gasping out loud at the round table. When the Faithful catch a Traitor, it’s electric. If Traitors turn on Traitors, I always think my head is going to fall off. And I still get a total buzz from going into the turret. It feels very special to be allowed in there.”

For its award-garlanded host, The Traitors has been transformative. “It’s the greatest job I’ve ever been given,” says Winkleman. “It has changed my life and my career, no question. I’ll be there with Barry the owl long after they’ve fired me. I’ve also told the peacock to make room in the shed where he roosts.”

The Traitors has overtaken Strictly Come Dancing as the BBC’s crown jewel but it’s a mutually beneficial relationship. From Celia Imrie’s guff to Richard E Grant’s gaffe, from Ross Kemp’s twitching paranoia to James Acaster’s trembling terror, the franchise thrives on communal talking points. It wouldn’t work nearly as well being binged on a streamer. “The Traitors demonstrates the power of television to bring people together,” says Kanter. “At a time when there’s lots of existential hand-wringing about the health of the broadcast industry – and the BBC particularly – it’s a reminder that when terrestrial TV is good, it’s something to treasure.”

The chaotic second celebrity series reaches its climax this week, with 17 million expected to tune in. What can they reveal about Friday’s final? Fay laughs. “I’m trying to work out what we can tell you without ruining anything.” “It’s stressful and unpredictable,” says Cotton. “Genuinely surprising, even for us,” adds Fay. “With real heart-in-mouth moments.”

“I always cry at the endgame, regardless of who wins,” concludes Winkleman. “Whoever is left standing has played the best game. I feel incredibly proud of them. This series is no different. It feels momentous.”

The Celebrity Traitors climaxes at 8pm on Thursday 29 October and Friday 30 October on BBC One and iPlayer.

‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:00:25 GMT

The auteur’s new film – a study of labour, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he says

A quintessential 21st-century horror story: a private equity firm has set its sights on your company. That’s the premise behind director Lee Chang-dong’s new film, Possible Love, and the idea for it first came more than a decade ago, when mass layoffs resulted in a standoff that “fundamentally changed the Korean labour movement”.

In 2009, workers at Ssangyong Motors company protested against plans to lay off between 37 and 43% of the workforce, staging a historic 77-day strike and occupation of the factory that was eventually broken up by riot police. “Until that point in time in Korea, labourers’ rights were widely accepted,” Lee says, speaking through an interpreter in a central London hotel; “however, afterwards, the basic rights of labourers changed; to the public, they couldn’t be seen as more important than market profitability or corporate competitiveness.”

At the time, Lee shelved the project. “The more I examined the pain of these individuals” – after the violent crackdown on the Ssangyong Motors strike, there were several suicides, and reports of long-term mental health issues – “I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story? And if I am, how do I tell it? Do I stand close to the workers, or keep my distance?” Later he and his co-writer Oh Jung-mi, wrote “many different” scripts, including one with post-apocalyptic elements, before Oh suggested introducing a character who is a documentary film-maker, thereby finding a way to work in Lee’s ambivalence about his intentions.

The result is a sharply observed Russian doll of a film that places a narrative about “labour and its relationship to capital” within a broader story about the ethics of film-making, and the tensions and desires that emerge when a working-class couple collide with an astronomically wealthy one. It has, like many of Lee’s previous films, been received to great acclaim: it recently won the grand jury prize at Venice film festival, and has been hailed by critics as one of the best films of the year.

The film’s opening title shows the 10th commandment, “Thou shalt not covet”. You can already guess that it will be swiftly broken. Soon we see the depressed Ho-seok, who has been fired from his job at a metal factory, reprimanding his free-spirited wife Mi-ok for caring about her clothes. They’re on their way to a funeral of Ho-seok’s former colleague, who killed himself after being made redundant, and meet the ambitious film-maker Lee Ye-ji and her financier husband Sang-woo. They radiate the kind of glow afforded by wealth. After a stay at a luxury resort in Qatar made Ye-ji reflect on the nature of hidden labour, she’s making a film about the state of labour in Korea, and believes she’s found her ideal subjects; if only Ho-seok, who refuses to go to therapy let alone talk about his experiences in front of a camera, would agree.

Since his first feature in 1997, Lee, now 72, has made luminous yet unsparing films about disempowered people swept up in brutal economic and political circumstances: his protagonists include blue-collar workers, ex-prisoners, people with disabilities. In his previous film Burning, an adaptation of a Haruki Murakami short story, a poor writer battles for a woman’s affections with a wealthier rival. (Possible Love brings together two lead actors from Lee’s most acclaimed films; Secret Sunshine’s Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu who starred Peppermint Candy and Oasis.) Class tensions bristle throughout his work: now, however, he’s wondering whether we’ve outstripped the usefulness of the term.

“It’s difficult to use the word ‘class’ because it is so vast,” he says of the difference between the couples in Possible Love. He describes Sang-woo, who moves about the world with possessive ease, an allure and emptiness, as a “symbol of capital … It’s not even that Sang-woo is a wealthy man. It’s about how he is capable of moving and controlling a huge amount of capital. And that capital creates further wealth. It’s almost as if you can’t really grasp how much wealth it creates. It’s just something of a different dimension.” At the same time, “I didn’t want to show that the two couples belong to completely different worlds, because they do live in the same world.” It is, after all, the abstract financial machinations of people like Sang-woo that materially overturn the lives of people like Ho-seok. Making the characters interact together at restaurants, their homes, and on a charged summer holiday “was going to naturally bring out the tension, the hidden power difference between them. There is a gap that just cannot be crossed.”

The film exposes the audience to many different kinds of looking: we are shown Ye-ji’s documentary footage; a CCTV feed; newsreel-style clips of a violent police crackdown on a workers’ strike. Lee wanted to study the “issue of the gaze”; “the ethics of capturing and observing the lives and pain of others”. Ye-ji has a habit of holding her camera up at inappropriate moments, often to the discomfort of Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s young son, Cheol. I wonder if she’s supposed to be a sympathetic character. “Anyone who’s really hardworking, they tend to overdo it,” Lee says. He feels a “closeness” to her, “and cameras by their nature search for drama.” Can there ever be equality between a film-maker and their subject? “It’s very hard to be equal because the person holding the camera without even realising it is given power. And it’s a one-sided relationship.”

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

In his telling, Lee became a film-maker almost by accident. He was a writer in 1980s South Korea, then under a military government, feeling called to draw attention to human suffering: “That was our moral responsibility.” As the country moved towards democracy and into the new century, he felt that although the suffering still remained, “that moral responsibility among people in literature began to disappear. Literature that dealt with the close pains of reality were treated as if they were expired goods. I was disappointed with that change.” He took up screenwriting to try something new, before working as an assistant director, “because I almost wanted to punish myself in a way, make myself go through something very tough. I worked so hard at it that people around me were moved, and they said: ‘Oh, you should be a film-maker.’”

South Korean films today are known globally for their confronting depictions of capitalism, though unlike, say, Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite (which also features a class divide between two families) or Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice (also about the misery of corporate layoffs), Lee’s characters are not schemers who attain pyrrhic, depraved victory against the system. We instead are often left to observe how they are marginalised by the world around them; we witness their small disappointments, the cruelties they endure, and how they strain to hold on to their hopes.

Yet his films also reveal the small but significant moments of solace and grace these characters find: in nature, other people, or their own willpower. Lee has previously described his films as stories about people taking on impossible fights against large, impenetrable entities. “However, despite that, I think the fight itself has meaning. I think these fights the individuals take on against the world is quite possibly the only way they are able to reclaim dignity. Regardless of your chances of winning, I think the fight itself is significant and meaningful.”

You could say that his latest film was made after a fight of sorts. Lee struggled to find domestic funding for the film, given the “structural crisis” facing the Korean industry, caused by the economic losses from a strict Covid 19 lockdown, and the rise of streaming services. Netflix stepped in to fund it, granting the film a theatrical release in some countries worldwide. “The character Ye-ji has a wealthy husband. She lives with someone who holds that capital but still tries her best to be independent,” Lee says. (Her husband, Sang-woo, somewhat disparagingly describes an independent film as a “film independent of capital”; “I thought it would be very amusing to have him say that line,” says Lee.) “I feel like she and I are in the same shoes. I am also dependent on capital to get my films made. You could say that I am also someone who is married to capital, but trying to protect my own voice, which I almost think is the fate of all film-makers.”

After its victory at Venice, there are already whispers about the Oscars; it is South Korea’s submission for best international feature. I ask what success means to him. “I’ve always made films wanting to connect with audiences. It’s always meaningful for me when my audiences accept the questions that I ask through my films and try to find their own answers. And hopefully that leads to a very small change in their lives.” It’s a fitting answer for a film-maker who has long portrayed the subtle acts of resistance people can mount against a hostile world; who finds in small changes, causes for hope.

Possible Love is in cinemas now, and on Netflix November 6.

Slegers and misfiring Arsenal badly need a result in WSL north London derby

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 11:58:27 GMT

Gunners’ title hopes have seemingly evaporated and their under-pressure head coach faces her latest test against Spurs on Saturday

It says much about Arsenal’s predicament that the team who have conceded 12 goals in two games are not the side whose head coach is under most pressure before a north London derby. Tottenham, four points above their neighbours before Saturday’s meeting, may have been humbled in consecutive Women’s Super League matches but all eyes are on Renée Slegers.

Arsenal are winless in five WSL matches for the first time, and the most decorated club in English women’s football desperately need a turning point. Their failure to beat Birmingham at home last Saturday, dropping points against a promoted side for the second time this season, again demonstrated the team’s inability to convert possession into goals. They increasingly look like a team stuck in Groundhog Day.

The Arsenal hierarchy are understood to remain behind Slegers, but for how long? The answer may hinge on Saturday lunchtime’s result. However much goodwill the Dutchwoman gained for guiding Arsenal to Champions League glory in May 2025, the simple truth is, it is unacceptable for a club with one of the biggest budgets in the world to be 12 points behind the leaders after six games.

That gap is why the draw with Birmingham not only pretty much extinguished Arsenal’s title hopes but also burned a hole in their secondary domestic objective – Champions League qualification. The unthinkable prospect of failure appears a genuine possibility: they are nine points adrift of third-placed London City. Arsenal need a derby win on Saturday but also a winning run to reverse the slide, and there is little evidence to suggest such a turnaround is close.

Arsenal have the worst shot conversion rate in the league (4.1%) and, according to Stats Perform, the third-worst shooting accuracy (30.6%) and third-lowest average xG per shot (0.09) despite averaging over 60% possession. Slegers’s persistence in deploying Alessia Russo – widely regarded as one of Europe’s best No 9s – in the No 10 role has baffled supporters and commentators alike. Russo has scored more WSL goals against Tottenham (eight) than any other player so Saturday’s game may be the perfect moment for that to change.

Arsenal have struggled against low blocks for a number of seasons, though, so not all fault lies at Slegers’s door. Nonetheless, the 37-year-old was substantially backed in the summer, with Arsenal enjoying perhaps their strongest transfer window in recent memory. So far though they have looked confounded tactically, bruised mentally and lacking the self-belief to grab a game by the scruff of its neck.

Asked if she was surprised to still be in her job, Slegers said: “That’s not something I think about. It’s about, ‘where are we as a group?’ and ‘what are we working towards?’ It’s absolutely not what we expected [our recent results] or what we wanted. But I’m in the here and now, and we are preparing for the north London derby. We have the group together. Everyone is going in the same direction and the fuel and motivation is sky high, because of the fans that will be there for us. That’s where my focus will be.”

Asked how imperative it is that Arsenal climb back up into a Champions League place this season, Slegers added: “Of course that’s in the back of our heads, but what we need right now is to get back to winning ways. We can only do that with the next game in front of us so that’s why the next game in front of us is the most important right now.”

Slegers has maintained after last weekend’s draw that Arsenal will recover when they fix some “details and margins”. Perhaps taking on a Tottenham side who have become only the second team in history to concede six or more goals in consecutive WSL games is the perfect opportunity.

after newsletter promotion

“It is a little bit of game intelligence and smartness in moments,” said the Spurs head coach, Martin Ho, insisting he is not worried about his team’s defending in the long-term. “There have been certain aspects that, collectively, players and staff, we were not happy with in certain moments, and we have to make sure we correct them. At the moment we’re getting heavily punished for some small errors with the ball that we’re making.”

The Englishman also only had praise for Arsenal’s qualities when speaking on Friday morning. “If you try and underestimate a team with Arsenal’s quality you’re in for trouble,” he said. Asked about Arsenal’s poor run, Ho added: “Arsenal aren’t a bad side. Their possession stats are probably the highest in the league, alongside Manchester City. Their goalscoring chances and touches in the opposition box are very, very high. They have world-class players.”

Last season’s runners-up do have world-class players but it is high time for them to play like a cohesive team.

Digested week: Finally gen Alpha discovers Nicole Kidman – via Adéla’s corset lyrics

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 11:32:12 GMT

Plus, King Charles’s unusual gift to Aung San Suu Kyi, Larry David’s provocative essay and Andrew Scott in Elsinore

“Who’s Nicole Kidman?” asked my 11-year-old. For God’s sake. “You know Nicole Kidman,” I said. “She’s in ...” I tried to think of a single thing she might have seen her in. “She’s that witch queen with the hair in Aquaman.” Blank stare. “She’s in … she’s an icon, she’s really famous. She used to be married to Tom Cruise.” A pause. “Oh for God’s sake, Tom Cruise, from Top Gun.” “Oh yes.” “She was the villain in Paddington!” Thank God.

Kidman had come to her attention, and that of every other 11-year-old girl in the land, via Adéla, the Slovakian singer whose song, Nicole Kidman, from her debut album, Prima, has caused a minor TikTok sensation and went to No 1 on Spotify earlier this month.

“Do you mean Adele?” I said, when we got to this part of what already seemed like a very long conversation. Excoriating, alright-grandma look. “It’s Adéla. With an ‘a’. She was in Dream Academy, she went out in the first round.” I knew what this meant and got briefly excited. “So she’s a Katseye reject!” More stern looks. “She’s in trouble for mocking Christians.” I gave up at this point.

The Nicole Kidman song, given a discreet nod by Madonna in a TikTok, was inspired by a corset Adéla wore to the Golden Globes and contains the lyrics: “Babygirl in control / I feel like Nicole,” and: “Every single night / I pray that my tits are sittin’ right / Moulin Rouge, my corset is so tight.” Hmm.

Kidman has graciously accepted the compliment and this week, when the song played at a runway show for Victoria’s Secret in LA, the actor, in the front row, laughed and put her head in her hands. I thought the whimsy of the song was quite clever, then made the mistake of watching the video and, after having a full Mary Whitehouse moment, am rehearsing remarks I intend casually to launch over dinner on the relationship between thongs and UTIs.

What do we think of King Charles sending Aung San Suu Kyi, the imprisoned Burmese leader, two books about soil? Suu Kyi, who is 81 and has been under house arrest at an undisclosed compound since her government was ousted by a military coup in Myanmar in 2021, was pictured receiving the books and smiling in a photo apparently staged by her captors.

It’s either a genius move on the part of the king – bringing to the gated leader visions of rolling English countryside and vistas she has, at present, zero chance of enjoying – or else, a little tactless. Soil to Table by gardeners Bridget Elworthy and Henrietta Courtauld, has been described as “a celebration of soil and its connection to the food we eat”. And the second title, Soil: The World at Our Feet, is a catalogue from an exhibition held in London last year.

Gift diplomacy is, of course, always tricky. You may recall the king’s father’s blunt knockback of a gift from a wellwisher during a walkabout with his wife in 2016. Offered a framed picture of Elizabeth II, the then Duke of Edinburgh snapped: “I don’t want that and neither does the queen. She knows what she looks like.” (The Lady Mayor of Windsor briskly stepped forward to accept the gift and smooth things over.)

Larry David’s new essay in Air Mail, the online newsletter, caused enough division this week to provoke coverage in the New York Times. “In our Socialist America,” David went after the Democrat Socialists of America (DSA), aping the style of Jonathan Swift’s A Modest Proposal to write: “Everyone will be so fulfilled spiritually and financially that the police department will be dramatically reduced to where an officer’s only job will be to adjudicate domestic disputes. Toward that end, stands will be set up at local farmers markets, where they will work to resolve marital issues in a folksy, farm-to-table manner. Fresh berries will be provided.”

It’s a weaker effort on David’s part than when he went after Bill Maher in the New York Times last year, savaging him in an essay entitled My Dinner with Adolf for approving remarks made after a meeting with Donald Trump. (“This private Hitler was a completely different animal. And oddly enough, this one seemed more authentic, like this was the real Hitler. The whole thing had my head spinning.”) Predictably, it’s David’s final section on the Middle East that has triggered a lot of take-the-phone-off-gramps fury from gen Z.

“We strongly believe in a two-state solution,” David writes in his mock manifesto. “To this end, we propose that Palestinians should be given all the land currently occupied by Israel and that Israel should be given Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, where the weather is beautiful and grapefruits are aplenty.” Zohran Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are great advocates for the DSA, but for a fuller picture it’s worth returning to DSA co-chair Megan Romer’s side-splitting efforts to explain her party’s policies to David Remnick, earlier this year. “Yeah. You know, again, I don’t have, like, a solid …”

Andrew Scott is everywhere promoting Elsinore, his Oscar-bait movie about the Shakespearean actor Ian Charleson, who died of Aids in 1990, and which I can’t wait to see. (Even though, occasionally, I feel about Scott the way I have come to feel about Nicola Walker – that the acting tics are visible enough to pull me out of the performance.)

Elsewhere in gay content, it’s worth stopping by a much-overlooked and very good show, Fellow Travelers, currently airing on Channel 4, in which Matt Bomer and Jonathan Bailey’s characters fall in love in 1950s Washington, right in the middle of Senator Joe McCarthy’s various purges. Alongside the well-known anti-communist witch-hunt, McCarthy also went after gay and lesbian federal workers in what came to be called the Lavender Scare, ruining lives as he went. Bailey, who looks like a young Gregory Peck and as an actor just gets better and better, is heartbreaking in this show about an underdocumented episode of history. Highly recommended.

News this week of Andy Burnham’s appearance on Gogglebox raises the happy, theoretical spectre of what previous incumbents at No 10 might have looked like on equivalent shows. Thatcher on The Weakest Link? Churchill on Bake Off? One feels that Blair would have actively enjoyed scaling the bouncy houses on It’s A Knockout. Someone alert the AI!

The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 11:30:24 GMT

People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans

Jack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.

Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”

For generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting for less than 10% of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.

According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is $765 for a new car and $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay $1,000 or more a month, according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.

For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”

Y2K cars don’t encompass everything produced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect become mortgage payments on wheels – they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.

The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunk from 21% of inventory a year ago to 15%, according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”

On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlander with a screwdriver. “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”

In a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.

At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access to owners and even independent mechanics. Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.

Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ’em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”

Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘What is going on?’” Price says. Generally speaking, he says, “the fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”

Twenty-five miles north-west of downtown Atlanta, a half hour’s drive in optimistic traffic, sits Town Center at Cobb, a typical suburban mall in recession. But on the first Sunday of every month, the mall parking comes alive for Caffeine and Octane, a sprawling car show that’s open to the public, free to attend and also has long lines for coffee and donut trucks. And even though the usual turnout of 2,000-plus cars was winnowed down to a few hundred on the gray, showery morning of October’s show, it was still an impressive array of vintage American muscle, Japanese domestic market (or JDM) unicorns and multimillion-dollar exotics. The Y2K cars stood out, too.

Sitting right at the entrance of the show was Anthony DeNaples’s 2000 Buick Regal GS, a sleeper sedan that has become a cult classic. He bought it four months ago for $18,000 on Facebook Marketplace, a price he considered a bargain for such a rare commuter. “Person didn’t really know what they had,” says the 37-year-old custom car builder, who uses the car to ferry his two young daughters. His oldest is constantly goading him to do burnouts, which she calls “making stripes”. Modern cars, he reasons, have become so laden with safety systems – for keeping the car in lane, or slamming on the brakes when sensors detect an obstacle – that they’re less fun to drive hard. “A lot of newer cars, if you want to drive it how it’s meant to be driven, you’ve gotta shut off all these things, and a lot of times it doesn’t completely shut off.”

A few rows down from the Buick were Mike and Kate Landaverde in his-and-hers Honda Civics from the 90s: a barebones CRX coupe called Dirty Gertrude and a slightly less spartan wagon called Tatiana. The couple bought them cheap, in keeping with the Y2K ethos. Mike, 34, treats having to bump-start the CRX and his sweat-soaked commutes in summer traffic as part of the thrill ride. “I’m smiling the whole time,” says Mike, who manages a local Wendy’s. They keep a 2021 Toyota Corolla hatchback in the garage as a backstop. That car’s got AC.

When young Wendy’s customers pull up to the drive-through in newer barges he assumes carry huge monthly payments, Mike can’t help feeling a bit smug. The couple’s Hondas, however, haven’t necessarily come cheap. Kate, 39, reckons the money she has put into modifications on Tatiana alone could buy a new car. But the occasional outlays – on an engine swap, most recently – can be done at a self-directed pace. “You can do the mods at your own wallet bracket,” says Kate, a software specialist who does her own wrenching. “You can go eBay parts. But all my friends call me bougie because I’m not gonna do anything cheap.”

Meanwhile, making a case for best in show was Alex Jimenez in a 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan tricked out to look like the Scooby-Doo Mystery Machine. “My family is growing,” said Jimenez, a 32-year-old facilities manager, as his 14-year-old daughter Izel sat shotgun scrolling through her phone while a Scooby-Doo cartoon played on the aftermarket infotainment display. Beyond the extra space, he says, “we love it because I can literally fix everything at home. I don’t need special equipment or tools or a computer to diagnose what’s wrong with it. And it puts smiles on people’s faces everywhere we drive. I mean, everybody’s taking pictures.”

Y2K cars have their charms, sure. Barry, of Consumer Reports calls it “survivorship bias” – seeing the most durable makes and models still on the road contributes to assumptions that all from the era must be rock solid. But there’s a reason the automotive industry moved on. “If you go back to cars in the 1990s, our road-test data and reliability surveys were showing problems that were unheard of on modern vehicles: defective paint, parts falling off; the steering wheel would be on crooked,” Barry says. Rust is another scourge of Y2K cars, though it’s less of a concern in the Sun belt. Newer models are far better protected against corrosion. “The technology that allows a car’s body and frame to survive longer is just so much more advanced,” says Barry, adding that a modern car from a manufacturer that prioritizes reliability can reasonably be expected to last 200,000 miles or more with proper maintenance. To his point: the average car on American roads is now 13 years old.

Still, some young Y2K-car owners welcome the opportunity to get their hands dirty. Che Bidal, a 19-year-old Pit operator who also belongs to the furry community, was idling inside his 2004 Mazda6 as the rain poured on Caffeine and Octane. He takes immense pride in having bought the broken sedan for $900 and getting it running again with another $1,500 in parts and help from AI chatbots and YouTube tutorials. Having Frankensteined a Y2K car back to life, the prospect of taking on a new car payment – in this economy – only to be discouraged by the manufacturer from making his own repairs seems ridiculous. “Car companies are banks now,” says Bidal, who was further emboldened by his positive experience under the hood to start a wrenching group for furries. “Coming from fandom into the [auto enthusiast] community is a whole different thing – pretty amazing.”

Nevertheless, there’s a critical difference between a car that’s gratifying to restore and one that can protect you when something goes terribly wrong. Modern cars are subject to increasingly demanding safety standards, and the differences in structural reinforcements and accident-avoidance features between models just three years apart can be dramatic. Consumer Reports has long recommended that drivers prioritize safety as much as their budget allows – advice that its largely Boomer readership can more easily take onboard, naturally.

Barry went through an old-car phase too. “When I was driving around in my 1988 Renault Medallion, I’d see someone come across the center line as they’re looking on their phone and think, ‘I would not stand a chance in an overlap collision,’” he says. “You might think that the older car you’re driving is a tank. Well, the car might be fine. It’s the things inside the car, the new safety features, that help you survive.” Features like blind-spot monitoring, driver attention monitoring and electric stability control, which intervenes to maintain traction in a skid.

The US auto industry has made some effort to address young consumers’ affordability concerns. In 2021, Ford introduced the Maverick, a four-door compact pickup with an available hybrid powertrain and a starting price below $30,000. A startup called Slate, which offers an infinitely customizable electric truck with a starting price of about $25,000, hopes to begin fulfilling orders at the end of this year.

In China, buyers can get new cars with features that would seem extravagant at the same price point in the US – the payoff from decades of Chinese investment in innovation and American offshoring of manufacturing. An affordable, widely available Chinese car with modern features would give young US car buyers something truly tantalizing to consider. But Chinese automakers are in effect shut out of the US market. Even if they weren’t, Barry cautions: “We’re still not getting one for $8,000. Think closer to $20,000. You’re still going to have a car payment. And even if the interior is simple, it’s a different kind of simplicity than someone driving a 99 Camry is looking for.”

Ultimately, young consumers just want cars that deliver on the industry’s fabled promise of independence – and right now, Y2K cars are meeting the brief. These days, Price’s Pewter Pebble struggles with a leaky sunroof, and the headliner is still drooping. “It’s a Volkswagen so it’s coming back to bite me in the butt,” he says. “I’ve probably had to put three grand into it this year.” But with more than 150,000 miles on the clock, it’s taken him further than even he could have imagined.

The absence of a car note helped him become a homeowner in his 20s. It softened the blow of Alex Vindman’s upset loss to Democratic socialist Angie Nixon in Florida’s August Senate primary. Rather than scramble for another job, Price took a European vacation to decompress and plot his next move. As it happens, he spoke to the Guardian from the Spanish Pyrenees. “If I had a car payment and I lost my job,” he says, “I wouldn’t have the flexibility to hike a mountain.”

This man has quit Badenoch’s increasingly hard-right Tory party – others should be brave enough to do the same

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 11:16:16 GMT

The London Assembly’s Andrew Boff is one of many who reject Kemi Badenoch’s authoritarian position. They are the only chance for the party’s future

The chair of the London Assembly, Andrew Boff, resigned this week from the Conservative party after 53 years of membership. He quit after being blocked from entering the race to be Tory candidate for London mayor because he supports the European convention on human rights (ECHR), putting him at odds with Kemi Badenoch’s hardline position.

Messages of support for one of the capital’s longest-serving Conservative politicians quickly poured in from fellow Tories. Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s Downing Street chief of staff, has backed Boff, warning Badenoch that others would follow him over the ECHR edict. But the rest sent messages privately, not daring to reveal themselves under a leadership that doesn’t tolerate dissent. In an interview last year, Badenoch decreed that rebels “should not and cannot stand as a Conservative candidate” if they do not agree with leaving the ECHR. She also bars anyone supporting net zero.

When Boff applied, for the seventh time, to be considered as Conservative candidate for London mayor, he didn’t really expect to be selected – but nor did he expect to be summoned to be told he was barred from entering the race. In a statement he pointed to the fact that Winston Churchill helped found the ECHR after the second world war, arguing “it was never a leftwing project” but a “safeguard against arbitrary government”. What’s more, he points out to me, the “convention doesn’t even mention asylum seekers”, Badenoch’s main justification for leaving the treaty.

The time may come, he warned, when extremists win an election on an even smaller vote share than Labour’s 34% in 2024 – and overturn all human rights legislation without the protections the ECHR affords. “That’s what authoritarian governments do,” Boff said. But he insisted that the committee, which vets Conservative candidates, didn’t listen. “They just repeated the same tropes, that activist judges are using the ECHR against parliament.”

Now he is free of the party straitjacket, Boff is planning to stand for London mayor as an independent, allowing him to say what he thinks about Badenoch.

He complains to me that the energy and resources that should promote the party “all go to promoting Kemi, Kemi, Kemi”. Thinking well of her in 2015, he says he had encouraged her to stand for the London assembly, where she served until 2017 before being elected to parliament. He says he found her “lazy and combative”.

Few will be surprised by Boff’s departure. But many will be wondering what took him so long. He was ejected from the Tory conference in 2023 for quietly heckling the then home secretary Suella Braverman’s speech, accusing her of homophobia and transphobia. “It is a signal to people who don’t like people who are LGBT+,” Boff, who is gay, said at the time as he condemned her speech as “trash”. Boff said that Braverman “was basically vilifying gay people and trans people by this attack on LGBT ideology”.

He was not alone in voicing criticism over the party’s direction. The former Tory MP Robert Buckland, fellow one-nationer and director of the Tory Reform Group, hurried out to defend Boff after his ejection from the conference, saying heckling was “part of the democratic debate” and that his treatment by security staff was “heavy-handed”.

Buckland was among the many one-nationers who lost their seat at the 2024 general election. But that traditional strand of Conservatism has not vanished – nor have those who used to vote for the Tories but now turn to the Liberal Democrats or simply boycott the ballot box.

Boff’s views represent a growing centre-right moderate strand that has been expelled or silenced under Badenoch’s leadership. Facing this hostile climate, one nation Tories have gone to ground in parliament; but outside the Commons, Prosper UK, a centrist Tory grouping led by the former mayor of the West Midlands, Andy Street, and the former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson quietly gains strength.

Its mission statement is to win back moderate voters who snubbed the Conservatives at the last general election, and this message seems to have struck a chord, with the group attracting nearly 30,000 supporters since its launch in January.

It is worth examining Boff’s views, as many Conservatives who have signed up to Prosper UK are likely to share them. He calls himself a Thatcherite, strongly opposing Labour’s renationalisation plans, backing low taxes and a small state. He voted for Brexit, believing the words of the likes of Daniel Hannan, who claimed “absolutely nobody is talking about threatening our place in the single market”. But instead the Tories delivered a hard Brexit after what he calls an “atrocious” campaign.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Times have changed; as the political analyst Peter Kellner pointed out this week, Britain’s pro-Brexit majority has literally died out. Any so-called betrayal of the referendum is only betraying the dreadful legacy of the departed.

If the Conservative party has any future as a government, it won’t be under its present leader. A small bounce for improved performance in parliament will never overcome Badenoch’s growing distance from voters, including those who should be natural Tories.

Boff may be a throwback to an irretrievable, more moderate Conservative brand, like that of the Macmillan era – a voice from the good old days when traditional party allegiances were clearly defined. Or possibly he and Prosper UK are the vanguard of a reconstituted centre-right able to attract new voters as well as those who have deserted the Tories.

That won’t be easy: already there are gloating Spectator-aligned Tories who say that the party is better off without the likes of Boff, or any real concession to centrism. But we should have a care. The success of a respectable right matters to all in the left bloc of progressive parties, too. A centre right is needed to fight off the dark forces of the hard right and worse, here and across Europe. That Overton window framing politics needs a firm shunt towards a more rational debate on our future in Europe – and on saving the planet.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Taika Waititi’s Star Wars film is the latest to hit the buffers. At some point Lucasfilm is going to have to actually make a movie

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 10:39:45 GMT

Waititi joins a long list of movie-makers who were expected to bring a new direction to the franchise, before the studio appeared to get cold feet

Movie-making these days is a very expensive endeavour. In 1977, George Lucas’s Star Wars cost $11m to make, which would be approximately $60m in today’s money, and has since amassed $775m at the global box office, including rereleases. Fast forward to 2026 and the most recent film in the long-running space saga, The Mandalorian and Grogu, cost a reported $165m and brought in $346m worldwide. If there was ever a Hollywood gold rush, the mines ran dry long ago.

Perhaps this is one of the reasons why Disney-owned Lucasfilm seems to be so terrified of making new Star Wars movies. Since 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker, only one Star Wars film, the aforementioned Mando and Grogu movie, has actually made it into cinemas. But that has not stopped the studio announcing a small armada of other projects – sometimes via press release, more often at various high-profile celebrations, conferences or other corporate jamborees – that have so far failed to reach multiplexes.

This week, Taika Waititi revealed in an interview with Inverse that his proposed Star Wars film, announced six years ago, has been “put on ice”. No clear explanation was offered, but frankly nobody should be surprised. It now joins mooted projects from Patty Jenkins, Kevin Feige and Game of Thrones creators David Benioff and DB Weiss on the list of Star Wars movies that we were once told we were definitely (probably) getting, but that we never actually did. Some, such as Rian Johnson’s proposed trilogy, have spent years receding into the distance, while others – Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy’s film about Rey’s new Jedi order, anyone? – have never been officially cancelled.

The failure of Waititi’s project may be the most damaging of the lot. Why hire a film-maker with such distinctive, punky sensibilities, only to leave them announcing to the world that their movie is now frozen in carbonite? Surely Lucasfilm teed up this film in the first place because it thought it might be an idea to shift away from dynastic daddy issues and planet-sized weapons with inexplicable design flaws, towards something whose plot couldn’t be guessed halfway through the opening crawl?

There is every chance that Waititi’s movie would have focused on an annoyingly genial Kiwi stormtrooper who insists on interrupting vital lightsaber duels to ask whether anyone fancies a sandwich. Johnson might have delivered 500 minutes of space opera in which the Jedi council are eventually forced to admit that the feeling of a disturbance in the Force is usually just trapped wind. But at least nobody watching the opening crawl would have known what kind of Star Wars movie they were about to witness – and that alone would have been worth the price of entry.

At some point, Lucasfilm has to let somebody make one of these films that might go wrong. Familiar faces and established audiences did not guarantee Mando and Grogu the kind of triumphant return we all wanted to see, and bringing back the saga’s big bad, Emperor Palpatine, more than three decades after he fell down an Imperial reactor shaft, was very far from a smart move. The forthcoming Star Wars: Starfighter, starring Ryan Gosling, may yet surprise us, but any film that already has Star Wars in its title and still needs one of Hollywood’s most famous faces to get us through the door isn’t exactly venturing into the Outer Rim.

Surely somewhere out there in a galaxy far, far away is a film-maker who can bring something fresh to this venerable old saga. Disney needs to find them, commission them to make a movie, and then actually let them get on and do it.

‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seas

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 10:03:02 GMT

When thousands of dying crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverups

It was an otherwise typical day on 25 September 2021 when thousands of dead and dying crustaceans washed up on beaches in Yorkshire and the north-east of England. Early morning walkers and swimmers were aghast to find a sickening carpet of twitching, fitting crabs.

It would be the first but not the last die-off, which would see the disappearance of vast swathes of integral native sea life along an extended stretch of coast, including seal pups. It would also see the decimation of the local fishing industry and, with that, a way of life.

Environmentalists, fishers and ordinary local people wondered what could have possibly caused such a rare catastrophic incident. Meanwhile, hours before – completely coincidentally, the authorities said – a major dredging operation was carried out in the mouth of the River Tees, disturbing sediment where decades earlier highly toxic pollutants from heavy industry had been pumped.

The authorities, after carrying out a series of their own tests, denied there was a causal link, blaming an algae bloom and then, later, a novel pathogen. But those who live and work around the Tees estuary disagreed.

In All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea, the critically acclaimed documentary film-maker Jeanie Finlay is not setting out to find out what killed the crabs and lobsters. “I can’t offer an easy answer to what happened,” she says. “There isn’t an official cause. But what I can do is show the audience what that feels like.”

To do so, Finlay followed Stan Rennie, a fisher off the Teesside coast, over four years. What emerges is not an investigation into what destroyed precious marine life along a whole coastline but a story about the people searching for those answers. And it has won critics over. Mark Kermode called the film “a life-affirming treat – funny, poignant and profound”, and it was awarded early film festival gongs at Bristol and the Mediterrane.

Rennie is, according to Tina Brown, “the next Mr Bates”, and much like the Horizon Post Office scandal, it is a story of ordinary working people whose livelihoods have been destroyed, who are doggedly trying to get to the truth amid cold, uncaring powers that be.

In fact, it was the ITV series Mr Bates vs The Post Office that helped Finlay gain the trust of the group of jaded fishers, who by then had begun to believe nothing would change and resisted having their first meeting filmed. “After that came out, they were like, yeah you can film it,” says Finlay, who plays down her own role in endearing herself to the men, none of whom had seen – or, she says, had a particular interest in seeing – her 10 previous films.

They include Seahorse (2019), following Freddy McConnell, a transgender man who gave birth, and, the same year, a documentary following the filming of the final series of Game of Thrones, lauded by critics as better than the season it documented.

But it was important too that Finlay is a local lass, having grown up in Stockton-on-Tees. When she first came across the story, it “made me think about the coastline that I knew and loved, the place that made me”. “I didn’t have to research it because I knew them. I knew them really, really well because this is my home,” she says.

We are introduced to Rennie in the opening scenes, as he explains from his boat, “All my life’s just been about fishing.” This is palpable over a video call from his home in Teesside, as he rattles off fishing jargon, in among complex scientific explanations and legal and bureaucratic terms in a whirlwind, telling the story of the past five years of his life.

He had pulled in some lobster pots that day in 2021 to find only dead lobsters in there. “We just knew that there was something wrong. Within a couple of days, the life had disappeared totally.”

It was disturbing, he says, to speak to his friends and realise they too had seen the devastation. “I got involved from then onwards, doing everything I could to campaign to get to the truth.”

Rennie has spent decades caring profoundly about the sealife on his doorstep. He would fish a mile away from the entrance of the Tees, in what had been some of the richest lobster grounds in the UK, thanks to sustainable fishing practices. “In all my life I’ve never kept a big lobster,” he says, explaining the process of cutting a v-shaped notch in the tails of large females and returning them to the sea. V-notched lobsters are illegal to sell in parts of the UK, so this act prevents them from ever being eaten, protecting them their entire 50-year lifespans.

“We could have landed thousands of lobsters, but we thought we were doing our bit and it certainly seemed to be working. And then overnight, all of them years, you think, what have we achieved? Because everything was dead.”

He is both the natural and reluctant leader of the North East Fishing Collective (NEFC), a group made up of about 60 fishers, many of whom found themselves swamped with debt and unable to take care of their families. Rennie is joined in his quest by Dr Sue Wilson from Tara Seal Research, who watched all the seal pups born along that same coastline perish, , chemist Dr Simon Gibbon and marine biologist Dr Gary Caldwell.

Another key figure, snippets of whom we see interspersed throughout, is the Tees Valley mayor Ben Houchen, now the Conservative Lord Houchen. He led the concerningly fast demolition of the old steelworks – featuring the largest UK explosion in 75 years – and rapid construction of the Teesside Freeport project in its place.

His denials, as evidence grows that this work may be what caused the die-offs, are a constant frustration for Rennie and the gang. Many of them believe he was involved in corruption and a cover-up, while Houchen denies this, labelling the fishers “activists” and refusing contact with them.

“You can say it’s done,” says Finlay. “It’s not done for Stan. It’s not done for Sue. It’s not done for the scientists … or for Simon Gibbon, the chemist who’s trying to get the dredge licence put on hold.”

That is something the viewers have understood better than the authorities, as money has poured into an NEFC £100,000 fundraiser for the next round of scientific testing. “Someone in Glasgow donated £1,000 during the Q&A on the night, and people have been putting £5 in the pot, it’s pretty amazing.”

Rennie says audience members have been angry on their behalf, and some have cried. “For strangers who aren’t from the area to have that same reaction, it blows your mind.”

Finlay says: “People are becoming infuriated by elected officials who use their enormous platform, their enormous loudhailer, to tell you stories that are greatly at odds with lived experience. Our lives are dominated by tech bros and platforms and conglomerates and people that shout very loudly. And that can often feel disconnected from real life.”

On top of that, Finlay says, people are simply disgusted by the state of the UK’s waterways. “You can sell off all the utilities in the country, and now we’re living with the consequences of that. You can make as many promises as you like, you can promise as many jobs as you like. But the reality is, the trains aren’t working and there’s poo in the river and everyone’s pissed off with that.”

All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea is in cinemas from 23 October.

The Trump-Putin love story’s next chapter: selling out Ukraine

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 10:00:31 GMT

The US president is portraying Zelenskyy as the villain as he strives for Russia’s approval

If Donald Trump could, he would fly to Munich to sign away Ukraine to Vladimir Putin, and return to wave the document as “peace in our time”, hoping to claim at least the second Fifa peace prize.

Whatever the complicated motives of Neville Chamberlain, his well-grounded fear after the carnage of a world war of another apocalypse and his wishful thinking that Hitler would be satiated after carving up Czechoslovakia, Chamberlain had not sent his son-in-law and former golf partner and real estate partner in advance to cut back-end deals with the Nazis to profit for his family and cronies.

Though Chamberlain is judged as grievously misguided in history, Winston Churchill eulogized his “perfect sincerity according to his lights” and declared his mistaken gesture as rooted in the “noble and benevolent instincts of the human heart”.

Putin has proposed a meeting with Trump and Xi Jinping to settle the Ukraine war on Russian terms without the presence of the troublesome Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Wall Street Journal described such a meeting as “unprecedented”.

As a historical matter, that would be untrue. The Czechs were not present at Munich when their country was delivered to Hitler.

Part of Trump’s urgent reason for selling out Ukraine is to cast blame before the midterm elections for the inflation wrought by his tariffs and Iran war. Panicked by plunging polls, he has ramped up his rhetoric against Zelenskyy as the alleged source of the crisis that Trump himself has created.

Portraying Zelenskyy as the villain, Trump projects himself, as usual, as the victim. His perceived political need and irreducible pathological neediness dovetail with his longtime admiration of Putin as the unconstrained strongman he has always wished to be.

Since Trump’s first visit to Moscow in 1987, he has dreamed of the bonanza of Russian deals to be lavished on him from Putin. Upon his return, he paid for full-page ads in major newspapers calling for the US to stop funding the defense of countries capable of defending themselves and to cease defending the flow of oil through the Gulf. “The world is laughing at America’s politicians as we protect ships we don’t own, carrying oil we don’t need, destined for allies who won’t help,” the ad said.

From the start, the ideology has been a token of his greed, decades before he hawked his “America First Collection” of digital tokens. Putin has been the unwavering object of his aspiration, one of the few people he has not betrayed or sought to humiliate, but to whom he bends his knee.

“Together,” tweeted Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s head of the Russian sovereign wealth fund, over a graphic showing the Russian bear and the American eagle on the same side poised to fight against the British lion and a shattered European Union flag. He was celebrating on 16 October what he conceived as the new axis against the western allies the same day that Trump waived sanctions against Russia under the Lindsey Graham Act.

Graham, who died in Washington just hours upon returning from a visit of support to Ukraine, was hailed as Trump’s closest friend in the Congress, which passed the bill overwhelmingly, Democrats and Republicans in rare unity.

Graham’s sister, Darline Graham Nordone, whom Trump imposed on the South Carolina governor to be appointed as the martyr’s replacement, was prominently made the marquee sponsor, lending the novice senator a credential. In a Republican primary debate, she said: “National security is not my thing.”

When Trump tossed aside the Graham Act without bothering to consult her, she was left to sputter an ineffectual objection, leaving her vulnerable in an unexpectedly close race. Her prospect and dignity were shards of Trump’s collateral damage.

Trump vehemently blamed Zelenskyy for supposedly prolonging the war, called him “not a good guy for us to deal with”, and said that the Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries were a “disgrace” and had “better damn well stop”, and that Ukraine needed a “new leader who can make a deal”.

After an hour-and-a-half phone call with Putin on his 74th birthday, so friendly that neither wanted to hang up the phone first, according to Yuri Ushakov, Putin’s aide, Trump announced his sweetheart deal for 300,000 metric tons of diesel from Russia, followed in November by 500,000 and an additional million. For this, Trump waived sanctions.

The stunt gives Putin hard cash to continue operating his war machine, while the diesel will be statistically insignificant to the price in the US market. The US consumes 300,000 tons within 14 hours. Zelenskyy called this a “happy birthday gift to Putin”. The effect of Trump’s transaction could not help struggling American consumers, but is a practical help to sustain Putin’s aggression.

Trump’s giveaway was followed by the sudden restriction of Ukrainian access to the Starshield network, managed by Elon Musk for the Pentagon, that is indispensable to Ukraine’s defense. For a week, in an Abbott and Costello routine of “who’s on first”, Musk blamed the Pentagon, while Trump claimed to be out of the loop. “It wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said.

Ukraine’s frontline communications were immediately degraded. The outage directly preceded barrages of Russian missile strikes that knocked out energy infrastructure and left 600,000 Ukrainians without power. Slowly, after outraged reaction from the Europeans and Congress, connectivity was mostly but not completely restored.

Musk, whose businesses are dependent on federal contracts, is the largest donor to the Republican campaigns in the midterm elections, spending $366m so far, exceeding the $276m he spent to elect Trump in 2024.

The diesel deal was a successful ploy as part of Putin’s larger scheme to leverage Russian energy assets as bait to Trump in order to end US support for Ukraine. In early September, Putin pitched Trump’s self-interested envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, on the vast international assets of Lukoil, Russia’s second-largest oil company, requiring a treasury department waiver, thereby opening the door for a host of shadow agreements.

The Abu Dhabi royal family and the Qatari Al-Khayyat brothers would hold a large part of the equity, the New York Times reported. The Qatari investors are simultaneously partnered with Kushner on his luxury real estate project in Albania, which has provoked a popular uprising called “the Flamingo revolution”.

Another partner in the Lukoil consortium, Todd Boehly, CEO of Eldridge Industries, a holding company, and co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers and Lakers, has donated $2m to Trump’s political action committee, Maga Inc.

The negotiator on the Russian side, Kirill Dmitriev, is the one who enthusiastically tweeted: “Together.” But the Lukoil deal is hardly the only one apparently in the pipeline; Trump laid the groundwork for an array of post-sanctions opportunities. “A classified report produced by a European intelligence agency states that Trump and people around him have discussed several potential contracts in Russia,” Dexter Filkins reported in the New Yorker. The document detailed 10 ventures after a “peace deal” – that is, after forcing a Ukrainian surrender on Russian terms.

Against this background of the Russian strategy, large and small movements of Trump and his family become clarified, from the Kushner-Witkoff-Dmitriev negotiations to Don Jr’s wedding party in the Bahamas paid for in part by a Putin thug, Umar Kremlev, head of the Olympic-banned International Boxing Association.

A “large” contingent of Russians was present at the intimate wedding party, according to ProPublica, but their identities remain unknown. Kushner was also present at the celebration.

Fiona Hill, who served as Trump’s director for Russian affairs on the national security council in his first term, has described Trump as awestruck in his relationship with Putin. Trump envied him as the “ultimate badass”. She observed how Trump’s pathetic need to be seen as a peer to the autocrat allowed him to be played like a fiddle.

At the 2018 Helsinki summit, she was horrified when Trump dismissed the findings of the US intelligence community that Russia had interfered in the presidential election of 2016 on his behalf, deferring to Putin by saying: “President Putin says it’s not Russia. I don’t see any reason why it would be.”

Hill thought she might stage a fake medical emergency or pull a fire alarm to stop Trump from humiliating himself and the US.

But that was during the first term, before Trump grasped how to use the presidency, with official immunity granted by the supreme court, to forge his own kleptocratic state to achieve his highest aspiration: attaining the exalted law-free status of Putin. Trump’s effort to become the full partner with Russia makes his pay-for-play ballroom seem a mere bauble by comparison.

Among Trump’s infinite abuses is his suborning of the Department of Justice to pursue his retribution snark hunt of a “grand conspiracy” of his alleged enemies of the “deep state” for perpetrating the “Russia hoax”, those national security officials who asserted the factual truth that Russia interfered in the 2016 election to benefit him.

In early October, however, the key man appointed to run this operation, the veteran Washington attorney deep into rightwing causes, Joe diGenova, resigned, “saying top department officials were pressuring the team to bring criminal cases before they were ready”, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Nobody now observing Trump’s relations with Putin is accusing him of “collusion”. There is no secrecy. Trump brazenly proclaims his aspiration to partner with Russia and to become the equal of Putin. “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much,” he said.

After Russia released an American schoolteacher imprisoned for four years on what the state department called false charges, a human chip to personify Putin’s gratitude to Trump, Witkoff praised Putin: “You are a humanitarian.”

Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press that if Trump “will take the side of Russia”, it would be a “a historic mistake and big tragedy”. Dmitriev tweeted Trump’s remark: “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given us nothing.” Dmitriev added his comment: “Clarity.”

Nobody in retrospect will eulogize Trump for “noble and benevolent instincts of the human heart”.
