Lawmakers Plan to Block Trump Nominees Over Ukraine Satellite Network Restrictions

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Senators have warned the White House they will withhold confirmation votes until the administration ensures the restoration of communications capabilities used by Ukraine’s military.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from Washington

Republicans and Democrats in the Senate have told top White House officials they will block President Trump’s nominees pending on Capitol Hill until the administration ensures the restoration of critical satellite communications capabilities used by Ukraine’s military, according to three people familiar with the discussions.

The move, described on the condition of anonymity because it has yet to be publicly announced, would escalate a bipartisan confrontation over the White House’s increasingly conciliatory approach toward Russia. It would play out in the lame-duck congressional session scheduled for after the midterm elections, when Republicans are expected to seek the confirmation of dozens of Mr. Trump’s nominees before the current Congress ends.

The standoff comes after Ukrainian officials reported last week that they had encountered new limits on their ability to operate the military drones that have become essential to their war against Russia, and suspected that a Trump administration official might have deliberately throttled the Starshield satellite communications network that enables them to function. It was not clear whether such an action was taken or by whom, but Mr. Trump last week called Elon Musk, the billionaire whose SpaceX runs the network, and asked him to restore Ukraine’s full access, according to a senior administration official and a person briefed on the exchange.

The episode has highlighted a widening gulf between the White House and Congress over Russia, with even senior Republicans increasingly willing to challenge Mr. Trump’s policy positions. And they pointed to a potential change in posture after the midterm elections, when control of Congress could shift to Democrats and lawmakers in both parties may be more aggressive about using their leverage and oversight on the matter.

Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican fighting to defend his seat in a highly competitive district, threatened to pursue the firing of U. S. officials responsible for the disruptions and budget cuts for their agencies, saying he doubted the problems had been accidental.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

“I’m personally not buying the coincidence argument,” Mr. Fitzpatrick, a former F. B. I. agent who worked on Russian counterintelligence in Kyiv, said in an interview, citing mounting hostility by Mr. Trump toward President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.

Mr. Fitzpatrick recently spoke with Mr. Zelensky and said he was concerned about delays in the delivery of ballistic missile interceptors, disruptions to early-warning intelligence and Starshield restrictions.

Similar concerns were raised during a separate bipartisan call with Mr. Zelensky this week organized by Senators Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, and Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina. They said the Ukrainian leader told them that critical satellite services remained degraded, including on drones traveling faster than 100 miles per hour, hampering Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones.

“Funding Russia’s war machine, disabling Ukraine’s satellite communications, and crippling its air defense are all impediments to peace,” the senators said in a joint statement.

The disruptions have also endangered American personnel in Ukraine, according to a U. S. official who traveled to Kyiv this month and witnessed Russian drones and missiles overhead. The official said warnings of incoming attacks arrived so late that American diplomatic personnel were unable to reach hardened bunkers and were instead instructed to shelter in hallways. At least 230 American military and diplomatic personnel remain in Ukraine, relying on Ukrainian air defenses for their protection.

A Senate aide who agreed to speak on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive information said the Foreign Relations Committee had approved several transfers of critical air defense interceptors that had yet to reach Ukrainian inventories, raising concerns about delays in assistance already cleared by Congress. Staff members also are considering potential investigations of SpaceX over the satellite disruptions and have asked companies involved in Russian diesel transactions to preserve documents in anticipation of possible congressional investigations, the aide added.

Starshield service abruptly cut out last week, sending Ukrainian drones en route to their targets falling to the ground. The outage risked disastrous repercussions on the battlefield and thwarted Ukrainian efforts to disrupt Russian logistical routes in occupied Ukraine.

As of Friday, the service continued to face major disruptions, commanders and officials said, with the speed limit still in place and some troops reporting connectivity problems even at slower speeds. Washington still has not provided any answer to Ukraine as to why the service was cut, several officials briefed on the matter said.

Mr. Zelensky has repeatedly raised alarm that the outages are leaving civilians vulnerable to Russian drone attacks.

“Starshield/Starlink speed restrictions remain in place. Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters,” Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in Washington, wrote on X. “Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives.”

Senator Roger Wicker, Republican of Mississippi and the chairman of the Armed Services Committee, separately pressed Mr. Trump earlier this week to accept Mr. Zelensky’s offer to suspend attacks on Russian petroleum infrastructure in exchange for American targeting assistance against Russian missile launches.

“President Trump can lower prices at the pump today by simply agreeing to this deal!” Mr. Wicker said in a statement on social media. “MR. PRESIDENT, PLEASE TAKE THIS WIN!”

Siobhán O’Grady contributed reporting from Kyiv.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

The Meaning of the Republican War Over Ramaswamy’s Vile Ad

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Michelle Goldberg

By Michelle Goldberg

Opinion Columnist

It’s quite a feat, in this numb and debased era, to create a political advertisement so shocking and indecent that people from across the political spectrum feel the need to denounce it. The Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has long fashioned himself as a kind of Donald Trump 2.0 — younger and brainier but just as brash — has managed it.

By releasing what may be the most disgusting ad in American political history, he’s done more than just reveal his own low character. He’s opened a kind of proxy debate on the right about whether a post-Trump conservatism should try to reclaim some base-line morality or continue along its current smash-mouth course.

As you might know by now, the story behind Ramaswamy’s ad involves child sexual abuse. His Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, was 12 when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, known as Bud, was arrested and indicted on charges of raping her, though he skipped town before he could be tried. Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, stood by him and lost custody of her children; she never saw her daughter again. (Bud Arthur died in 2004.)

In 2020, when Acton was serving as Ohio’s health director, Donna Arthur, fashioning herself as a concerned Christian, gave an interview to the anti-abortion group Operation Rescue attacking her estranged daughter. It was deeply if unintentionally self-incriminating. Arthur speculated that Acton got the idea to say Bud Arthur raped her from his daughter from a previous marriage, who’d made a similar claim. By Donna Arthur’s own account, then, she brought a man accused of sexually abusing his child into her children’s home.

Now Ramaswamy’s campaign has dug up this elderly woman to make a video calling her daughter a liar who can’t be trusted to lead the state. At first, the ad featuring Arthur circulated online, without attribution. As outrage about it grew, Ramaswamy’s campaign admitted that it created the spot, and then, in Trumpian style, doubled down, saying it would spend millions to air it on television and promote it online.

By tacitly siding with a man indicted on charges of child rape, Ramaswamy has shown us all who he is. But he’s also given conservatives space to reckon with the ethical degradation of Trumpism, though without quite admitting that that’s what they’re doing.

Take, for example, the conservative magazine National Review. Early in 2016, it put out an issue with the words “Against Trump” emblazoned in gold on its cover. “Donald Trump is a menace to American conservatism who would take the work of generations and trample it underfoot on behalf of a populism as heedless and crude as the Donald himself,” said the lead editorial.

Over the following decade, some of the issue’s contributors remained anti-Trump stalwarts, but several — along with the magazine as a whole — turned into apologists and bootlickers for the president. As long as Trump offered the right new peaks of political power, many of his onetime conservative critics were happy to swallow their qualms. Now, as the whole gaudy edifice of MAGA crumbles — with Trump so unpopular that Republicans risk losing states like Texas and Kansas — at least some of his enablers may be feeling ashamed.

Denouncing the Ramaswamy ad gives conservatives a chance to try to drag their movement out of the Trumpist gutter. National Review, tellingly, has helped lead the charge. It ran a sober article backing up Acton’s story, and then several columns lambasting Ramaswamy, including one titled “When Character Was Obliterated.”

The conservative broadcaster Erick Erickson has taken a similar line. He was one of the contributors to “Against Trump” who then turned around and endorsed Trump for re-election. “I still struggle on the character issue,” he wrote in 2019, but argued, “We cannot have the Trump administration policies without President Trump, and there is much to like.” Now Erickson is back to believing that character is crucial. “We keep being told we must surrender our decency to win and then we lament how indecent the country is becoming,” he wrote about Ramaswamy, as if he had not been one of the ones counseling such surrender.

If conservatives were to suddenly decide that moral depravity is disqualifying, it would be bad news for Trump and those closest to him. It’s not surprising, then, that on Wednesday, JD Vance praised Ramaswamy’s “audacity” in running the spot, declaring himself “disgusted” by Republicans who are “whining” about it. Trump, on Thursday, celebrated the ad on Truth Social, writing, “I only wish the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse.” Both men seem to understand that Republicans who criticize Ramaswamy are also implicitly criticizing them.

That’s particularly true of Vance, because he and Ramaswamy are such similar figures. The two men were friends at Yale Law School. Both worked in venture capital and developed ties to the tech right before positioning themselves as inheritors of the MAGA movement. Both have to contend with anti-Indian bigotry — Vance’s wife is Indian American — which has cost Ramaswamy some far-right support. And both are charmless, awkwardly imitating the president’s cruel provocations without his dark charisma or comic timing. If Ramaswamy loses a state as red as Ohio despite Trump’s imprimatur, Vance might start to look like a bad bet in 2028.

Seventy-two years ago, Joseph Welch, the attorney representing the U. S. Army, rebuked Joseph McCarthy with the immortal line, “Have you no sense of decency, sir, at long last?” Despairing observers have been asking the same thing of the Republican Party for the last 10 years. Both Ramaswamy and Vance had better hope that the answer is still no.

Michelle Goldberg has been an Opinion columnist since 2017. She is the author of several books about politics, religion and women’s rights and was part of a team that won a Pulitzer Prize for public service in 2018 for reporting on workplace sexual harassment.

Under U. S. Watch, Venezuela Grapples With Tensions Over Democracy

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump says Venezuela is not ready for elections, and he focuses instead on its oil. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio is nudging talks between opposing politicians.

By Edward Wong and Julie Turkewitz

Edward Wong reported from Caracas, Venezuela. Julie Turkewitz reported from Bogotá, Colombia. Both have covered U. S. policy on Venezuela for many years.

The two combatant politicians shook hands on a stage at a hotel in Caracas after signing an accord. It was a sign that they were willing, for now at least, to keep talking about finding common ground for Venezuela.

Their aides and supporters surrounding them clapped, encouraging the notion that the authoritarian state might move toward democracy — in months or years from now, and under the watch of the country’s new chief authority, the United States.

No one addressed the central questions looming over the talks: Are President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and the leaders in Caracas who now answer to them, ready to commit to a timeline that would result in elections?

And when should they take place?

One of the politicians on the stage, Jorge Rodríguez, in glasses and a gray sports jacket, serves as a top official in the government formerly led by Nicolás Maduro, who was seized in January in a U. S. military assault that killed scores of people.

Mr. Trump now supports that government, lavishing praise on its new leader, Delcy Rodríguez, long a commanding figure in the apparatus of repression under Mr. Maduro, who is imprisoned in New York.

The other politician onstage, Dinorah Figuera, standing next to the Venezuelan flag in an electric-blue suit, returned from exile in Spain to represent opposition groups in the negotiations over what American officials call a gradual political transition. She and Mr. Rodríguez had just spent a week doing their third round of talks, ending with the signing ceremony and news conference on Wednesday.

The next day, in a small group interview, Ms. Figuera made it clear who wielded much of the power in the process.

“I recognize Marco Rubio as a democratic figure for the United States and for Venezuela,” she said. “I recognize how he has supported a path toward free elections, transparent elections, freedom of expression and respect for human rights.”

After the interview, Ms. Figuera went to the Miraflores presidential palace to meet with Ms. Rodríguez, a signal of reconciliation. After the meeting, Ms. Rodríguez acknowledged “the effort of the parties seated at this dialogue table to make progress regarding political guarantees for all.”

She also criticized dissent.

“There are still very, very small groups that resist and believe that by setting fires — or attempting to set the country on fire — and blocking streets, they can help Venezuela move forward,” she said.

If the talks move too slowly, that could work to the advantage of Ms. Rodríguez. Over two days this week, Ms. Figuera told reporters from Washington there had been steady progress, but declined to give a notional timeline for elections.

State Department officials had encouraged the reporters to fly down to observe the end of this round of talks.

For Mr. Rubio, the eventual outcome in Venezuela has an important personal and domestic political dimension — he is an ambitious Cuban American politician from Florida, home to many Venezuelans who fled the country over the decades and long for a new government there. Any suggestion that Mr. Rubio is not working toward democratic change ignites criticism from them.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly asserted that the country is not prepared to vote. “I don’t think they’re ready yet. You know, it’s very new,” he said last month. At the same time, he boasts that he is taking Venezuelan oil and its revenues for the benefit of Americans.

“The president expresses himself colloquially,” Ms. Figuera said. “Of course, it leaves us uncertain. But when I see his tangible policies in the process of investing in Venezuela in the oil sector, and alongside that, he’s in the process of democratization, I value what he has done more than his words.”

In a follow-up conversation, Juan Miguel Matheus, a member of Ms. Figuera’s negotiating team, said he hoped that by the end of the year, the country could finalize plans to set up a new Supreme Court — a key step in building an election framework.

On Thursday, Venezuela’s legislature approved a committee that would help select new justices.

Decades ago, Venezuela was a working democracy. After Ms. Rodríguez’s party took power in 1999, leaders ravaged that system.

For its part, the United States has been criticized for poor outcomes after orchestrating some foreign democratic elections, notably in Iraq during the American occupation and civil war.

Mr. Rubio has emphasized that the United States has a three-stage plan for change in Venezuela: stabilization, economic recovery and political reconciliation leading to a democratic transition.

“To have a peaceful transition — which is what we desire, a peaceful transition to a permanent and enduring democracy — will require a lot of hard work, a little bit of patience, free and fair elections,” Mr. Rubio told reporters when he met with Ms. Figuera in Washington on Oct. 9.

Mr. Rubio was an outspoken champion of democracy in his former role as a U. S. senator, but has avoided putting any deadlines on the process. Mr. Trump rarely talks about democracy or human rights, and openly admires authoritarian leaders.

Absent from the talks is María Corina Machado, Venezuela’s most popular opposition leader and the recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize last year. Ms. Machado, who lives in exile in Panama after leaving Venezuela to receive the prize, would be Ms. Rodríguez’s most competitive electoral challenger if she were to return.

Ms. Machado has called for elections by July 2027. She has said she is trying to get back into the country, but has been blocked on at least seven occasions by authorities she has declined to name.

The Trump administration has not expressed enthusiasm for her return.

“The United States does not facilitate the return of opposition figures,” the State Department said in a statement when asked why the United States had not helped Ms. Machado travel back to Venezuela.

In an interview with The New York Times in Panama last week, Ms. Machado said the United States left her out of the dialogue. The State Department has said her party was invited to participate.

In the Thursday round-table discussion with reporters, Ms. Figuera said she had no interest in running in a future election and continued to see Ms. Machado as the leader of the opposition.

Ms. Figuera, a doctor by training, is a relatively little-known figure in Venezuela. She assumed the role of dialogue leader because she was a lawmaker in what the United States recognizes as Venezuela’s last democratically enshrined legislature, elected in 2015.

“I have no interest — to use a Venezuelan expression — in ‘barking in María Corina’s cave,’” Ms. Figuera told reporters. “Rather, as I told her, my goal is to help pave the way. And to me, it is inconceivable to be the one who establishes the institutions while simultaneously being a candidate.”

At one point, Ms. Figuera wept softly when she spoke about the isolation from her family while she was in exile and having to return to sit across a table from Mr. Rodríguez, a leader in a government that she said had tortured and killed political prisoners.

Some tangible results have emerged from the talks and other negotiations.

In recent months, the government has released hundreds of political prisoners, restored access to blocked media websites and proposed changes to the country’s repressive anti-hate law, used to imprison those deemed to have incited hate. Human rights groups say the law has been applied to punish government critics.

Still, the moves are incremental. More than 320 political prisoners remain behind bars, according to the human rights group Foro Penal. And other repressive laws remain on the books.

One goal of the talks is to confirm new justices to the Supreme Court, which validates election results. The next step in establishing the election framework would be the legislature under Mr. Rodríguez selecting members of a new National Electoral Council, which administers elections.

Both parties have also agreed to work together to try to recover Venezuelan gold stored in the Bank of England.

American diplomats and Ms. Figuera say the U. S. government is the “facilitator” of the talks. It has drawn up a road map for the negotiations. And it helps pay for hotels and other travel expenses for some members of the opposition, a senior State Department official said.

Most of the people on the opposition’s side still live in exile and have been flying to Caracas for the talks.

A fourth round of negotiations is scheduled for November.

All parties face pressure from Venezuelans, who are increasingly taking to the streets to demand better living conditions. A Bloomberg poll released this month showed that 65 percent of respondents disapproved of Ms. Rodríguez.

Although talks in recent years have not resulted in democratic change, Mr. Matheus, the ally of Ms. Figuera, said he thought this round would be different — because the reputations of several Republican politicians, including Mr. Rubio, were now closely tied to Venezuela.

They have to make it work, he said, adding, “I think this process is irreversible.”

Sheyla Urdaneta contributed reporting.

Edward Wong reports on global affairs, U. S. foreign policy and the State Department for The Times.

Julie Turkewitz is the Andes Bureau Chief for The Times, based in Bogotá, Colombia, covering Colombia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru.

Palestinian Gunmen Open Fire on Israelis in the West Bank, Officials Say

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Israeli military said two soldiers and two attackers had been killed, and three soldiers wounded. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to launch a major offensive in the Israeli-occupied territory.

By Adam Rasgon

Reporting from Tel Aviv

Palestinian gunmen opened fire on Israelis in the West Bank on Friday, prompting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to promise a major offensive in the Israeli-occupied territory, days before a pivotal national election.

The Israeli military said that two soldiers had been killed and that its forces had shot dead two Palestinian assailants near a checkpoint in Hebron, the most populous city in the West Bank. Three other Israeli soldiers were wounded in the attack, the military said.

Mr. Netanyahu visited the site of the attacks and said Israel would carry out a major operation in a neighborhood of Hebron, where he said the attackers had come from. “We will evacuate the residents; we will go home by home and remove weapons,” he said. “All of the weapons infrastructure will be dealt with and demolished.”

“We are going to implement the successful and aggressive model that we employed in the refugee camps,” Mr. Netanyahu said, referring to the Israeli military’s offensives in Jenin and Tulkarm, in the northern West Bank. Since early 2025, the military has conducted a massive crackdown there, displacing tens of thousands of people, demolishing homes and tearing up roads. The military has said it was targeting militants. The offensive has left parts of those cities bearing resemblance to destruction in Gaza.

On Friday, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the Israeli military’s chief of staff, said that Israeli “troops’ swift action prevented an even more serious attack and further harm to civilians and security forces.” A large amount of ammunition was found in a vehicle used by the attackers, the military said.

Soldiers and police officers have launched “offensive counterterrorism operations in the Hebron area,” the military said, adding that soldiers were operating in the homes of the assailants and other suspects. Mr. Netanyahu ordered the security forces to cordon off Hebron, and to prepare for a “lockdown” of the territory starting on Friday. He added that security forces were conducting extensive arrests.

Israeli analysts expressed concern that Mr. Netanyahu’s calculations in responding to the attack could be influenced by the election next Tuesday. His hard-right coalition is in a close race against opposition parties.

“The losses were heavy and painful, but the characteristics of the terrorist attack are not unusual,” said Michael Milshtein, a former Israeli military intelligence officer specializing in Palestinian affairs. “This isn’t the first time we’ve faced such an attack.”

Mr. Milshtein said he worried Mr. Netanyahu was seeking to escalate in the West Bank for political considerations, but he emphasized that it was too early to tell whether the military would carry out the action the Israeli leader outlined.

Gadi Eisenkot, Mr. Netanyahu’s leading challenger and a former military chief, praised the “heroism” of the Israeli soldiers for preventing a bigger attack.

Bezalel Smotrich, a hard-line minister in Mr. Netanyahu’s government and a settler leader, said that the Israeli authorities were demolishing Palestinian homes near the site of the attack, asserting that they had been constructed without permission.

“It will be clear that there’s a very high price for terrorism harming Israeli citizens,” he said.

The homes being demolished were located in Area C, a part of the West Bank under Israeli control, according to an Israeli security official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details.

Palestinian landowners have long said that the Israeli authorities refuse to provide them permits to build in Area C, which makes up roughly 60 percent of the West Bank.

Yousef Jabari, the mayor of Hebron, said that the Israeli authorities had closed off every entrance and exit to the city and shut down the Palestinian-run part of the Ibrahimi Mosque, a shrine in the city revered by Jews, Muslims and Christians as the burial place of Abraham. Jews call the site as the Tomb of Patriarchs.

“This is collective punishment against innocent people,” Mr. Jabari said in an interview. “Why should the entire city be besieged? Why should people with health appointments or social events in other cities be forced to stay home?”

Garbage trucks were unable to reach a dumpsite outside the city on Friday because of the Israel restrictions on movement into and out of the city, according to Tareq Shuqair, an adviser to Mr. Jabari.

The shooting took place amid a broader rise in violence in the West Bank since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and the devastating war in Gaza that followed.

Palestinian gunmen have shot and stabbed Israel civilians and soldiers. Last month, an Israeli man was shot and killed in the central West Bank, according to Israeli authorities, who said they had detained a Palestinian suspect over the attack.

Extremist Jewish settlers have carried out attacks on Palestinians, setting mosques and homes ablaze, stealing livestock and cutting down olive trees. That aggression has forced entire Palestinian communities to flee.

Settler attacks against Palestinians have intensified in recent weeks during the annual olive harvest, a cultural touchstone for Palestinians and an economic lifeline for many families. More than 1,000 Palestinians have been injured in settler attacks in 2026, according to the United Nations.

Hamas praised the attack on Friday as a “heroic operation,” but it stopped short of taking responsibility.

The militant group also called on Palestinians bearing weapons to shoot “bullets at the chest of the occupiers, their soldiers and their criminal settlers.”

Aaron Boxerman and Johnatan Reiss contributed reporting.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Are Fewer Teens Identifying as Gay or Bisexual? It’s Complicated.

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

New data have prompted questions about changes in teens’ sexual orientations. But researchers disagree on how much the numbers can really tell us.

By Azeen Ghorayshi

Jean Twenge has made a career out of studying generational differences. Central to her work is analyzing federal survey data on youth and adults, looking for shifts in how successive generations see themselves and behave.

Some of the most notable changes between generations have involved gender and sexuality, where there has been a steady increase in young people identifying as L. G. B. T. Q. over the decades. But as culture and attitudes evolve over time, Dr. Twenge has wondered if that trajectory will hold.

Her analysis of new federal numbers on youth and sexual identity suggests there may be a change: In a recent post on her Substack, Generation Tech, Dr. Twenge argued that lesbian, gay and bisexual identification was in a “free fall” among U. S. high schoolers, with the clearest declines among ninth-grade girls. After peaking at 26 percent in 2021, the percentage of ninth-grade girls identifying as bisexual dropped to 13 percent in 2025.

The change caught her eye, Dr. Twenge said, because “pretty much every other indicator for a very long time was going in the direction of more same-sex relationships, more acceptance of same-sex relationships, more identification.” Those patterns were evident ever since the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began surveying youth about their sexuality in 2015, incidentally the same year gay marriage was legalized in the United States.

“It’s a reversal of very longstanding trends,” Dr. Twenge said.

The data were collected as part of the C. D. C.’s Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which is administered every two years in all four high school grades across the country. Understanding how young people identify is important to researchers like Dr. Twenge because it can help predict broader cultural shifts that may shape society in the future.

Dr. Twenge’s analysis immediately prompted speculation about the forces driving the change.

Conservative commentators argued the nation’s rightward swing had swayed young people, suggesting that the prior rise in L. G. B. T. Q. identities had been a product of progressive institutions promoting them. “Amazing what happens when you cut the Department of Education and USAID,” Terry Schilling, the director of the American Principles Project, posted on X.

Others argued that the findings reflected an increasingly hostile climate for L. G. B. T. Q. people in the United States, making teenagers afraid to disclose their sexual identities, especially in surveys conducted by the federal government.

Dr. Twenge disputed both interpretations, arguing that smaller declines had first been observed under the Biden administration. She said that neither theory could explain why the number of ninth-grade girls identifying as bisexual had fallen by half between 2023 and 2025.

Still, other researchers questioned how much the data revealed at all.

Andrew Flores, a demographer at American University and the Williams Institute, stressed that it was difficult to draw broad conclusions about trends in young people’s sexual identities given that most of the change showed up only in ninth-grade girls.

The data showed a clear increase in high schoolers saying they identified as heterosexual, up to 78 percent in 2025 from 73 percent in 2023, Dr. Flores said. But most of that shift could be explained by the drop in ninth-grade girls identifying as bisexual. Across all grades, the share identifying as lesbian or gay remained relatively stable, at roughly 3 to 5 percent.

Christopher Julian, a postdoctoral researcher in demography at Vanderbilt, questioned whether the data told a story about a “free fall,” or whether the increases in gay and bisexual identification that preceded it were more noteworthy.

Dr. Julian noted that there had been a sizable decline in the share of teenagers identifying as heterosexual, to 73 percent in 2021 from 85 percent in 2019. But that had coincided with changes to the survey’s wording, with new answer options including identifying “Some other way” or “Do not know what this is asking.” Those changes made it difficult to draw direct comparisons between the two data sets.

The argument that lesbian, gay and bisexual identification was more broadly falling is “not statistically there — it’s a sensational claim,” Dr. Julian said. “Some people have suggested that there was a going back into the closet or a revoking of identity, but that’s not evidenced in the data.”

Young people are still identifying themselves under the L. G. B. T. Q. umbrella much more than previous generations, said Phillip Hammack, director of the Sexual and Gender Diversity Lab at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

Data from 2025 Gallup polls of youth and adults showed that, overall, levels of L. G. B. T. Q. identification remained mostly stable, with a slight recent dip, at about 9 percent of the general population.

“That’s a huge uptick from when they first began tracking this in 2012,” Dr. Hammack said. Looking at that data, Gen Z is clearly the biggest driver of the increase across cohorts, with more than 20 percent identifying with some kind of L. G. B. T. Q. label. (Members of Gen Z are now 14 to 29 years old.)

But he acknowledged that the signal emerging among ninth-grade girls was something researchers should pay close attention to in future surveys.

“I think this is something we need to watch,” Dr. Hammack said, “precisely because these are young people who are starting to experience these questions about their gender and sexuality in such a hostile moment.”

Dr. Twenge agreed that understanding what’s happening among girls is important. Research has shown that girls and women are more likely to have sexual identities that fluctuate over their lifetimes and are much more likely than boys and men to identify as bisexual. That makes the political and cultural environment even more salient.

“Their sexuality just changes more,” Dr. Twenge said. “And I think that’s exactly what’s showing up here in both the increase and the decrease. But why it’s so big for the ninth graders, I don’t know.”

What is clearer is how young people in these groups are faring. While the 2025 C. D. C. survey showed promising mental health improvements among high schoolers more generally, lesbian, gay and bisexual students reported high rates of sadness and suicidal thoughts.

The survey did not include questions about gender identity, complying with an executive order from President Trump declaring that the federal government would acknowledge only two sexes.

The prior version of the survey had shown that transgender students had among the highest levels of sadness and suicidal ideation in their peer group.

“To me, it’s just a sad loss of information about people,” Dr. Flores said. “Simply erasing that data doesn’t mean the problem stops, it just means it can’t be tracked.”

Azeen Ghorayshi is a Times science reporter.

Israeli Settlers Turn a Palestinian Rite Into a Gantlet of Violence and Fear

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Israel’s Election

This year’s olive harvest in the Israeli-occupied West Bank is the most violent in years, as settlers have attacked farmers and besieged homes, drawing condemnation from U. S. officials and others.

This year’s olive harvest in the Israeli-occupied West Bank is the most violent in years, as settlers have attacked farmers and besieged homes, drawing condemnation from U. S. officials and others.

Palestinians harvesting olives last week in Khirbet Abu Falah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Israeli settlers attacked a group of Palestinians there last week, injuring several people, including an American journalist. Credit...

Supported by

By Fatima AbdulKarimGabby Sobelman and Azam Ahmed

Photographs by Ivor Prickett

The families had only just begun harvesting olives when the attack started. Clad in all black, bearing metal batons and guns, Israeli settlers materialized without warning.

Ilham Al-Bazari, one of the Palestinians farming, froze. It was too late to run, she said.

Her husband was shot in the leg, and settlers attacked her teenage nephew. Believing they might spare a 50-year-old woman, Mrs. Al-Bazari said she jumped on top of her nephew to protect him. They broke her arm instead.

Her cousin, Ali Al-Bazari, an off-duty captain in the Palestinian Authority’s security forces, raced to help and was shot in the back by a settler.

The Israeli military showed up shortly after, Mrs. Al-Bazari and other witnesses said, as her cousin lay on the ground dying.

“We called on the soldiers to allow an ambulance,” she said. “But they refused.”

Mr. Al-Bazari, 44, died on Oct. 7, the first person killed in this year’s harvest — the most violent olive season in recent history, still weeks from ending. The Israeli military did not respond to requests for comment about Mr. Al-Bazari’s case or other incidents described by Palestinians or seen by journalists from The New York Times.

The violence of this year’s harvest is a distillation of the turmoil upending Palestinian life in the Israeli-occupied West Bank since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, which killed as many as 1,200 Israelis. As the country plunged into war in Gaza, Israeli settler expansion sharply accelerated in the West Bank, as extremist settlers — Jewish Israelis living in areas that Israel occupied in the 1967 Arab-Israeli war — push Palestinians off the land by intimidation and force.

Each year, the olive harvest has grown more tense but endured as both a social and economic rite for Palestinians. Families gather in groves, serving coffee brewed over open fires as several generations pick olives together. As many as 100,000 families rely on revenue generated by the harvest, which typically runs from mid-October to mid-November, Palestinian officials say.

In the last three weeks alone, armed Israeli settlers have launched hundreds of attacks, according to the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, the United Nations and the Palestinian Authority. Settlers have lit trees ablaze, shot farmers and bludgeoned men, women and children. On Friday, Palestinian gunmen opened fire on Israelis: The Israeli military said that two soldiers and two Palestinian assailants were killed.

In at least three instances witnessed by The Times in the past week — in the villages of Khirbet Abu Falah, Turmus Ayya and Deir Abu Masha’al — soldiers stood by as settlers stopped Palestinians from harvesting olives.

The far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vigorously supported settlers seeking to redraw the map of the West Bank. It has also allowed extremist settlers to operate with near impunity, even as violence has soared ahead of Israeli elections that could determine Mr. Netanyahu’s political fate.

Entire communities sit empty, residents run off by marauding settlers who have established more than 100 outposts over the last three years and are rarely stopped by Israeli troops. Hundreds of prominent Israelis, including former top-ranked military and intelligence officials, have accused Mr. Netanyahu’s government of allowing what they describe as ethnic cleansing.

Mr. Netanyahu’s office has rejected those accusations. Asked for comment about settler violence, an office spokesman, Doron Spielman, said: “While there is Jewish crime, it is not state-sponsored or state-supported. It is condemned; people are arrested and brought to court, and if they are found guilty, they are prosecuted.”

Three Palestinians have been killed in recent weeks, one during an olive harvest, with many others wounded and trees destroyed. A series of exceptionally brazen attacks have drawn condemnation from U. S. and other officials, some of whom have called them acts of terrorism.

In one attack last week, settlers assaulted European officials on a visit to a Christian village. In another, they badly beat a 63-year-old photojournalist from The Washington Post, breaking two of her ribs and fracturing several vertebrae.

Then, on Wednesday, a delegation of rabbis joined by several Americans, including Brad Lander, a Democratic nominee for U. S. Congress, were detained by Israeli authorities while accompanying Palestinian farmers near Bethlehem. The Israeli military said they were detained because of “the security risk posed by conducting an uncoordinated harvest near an Israeli community.”

Military aggression has also sharply increased in the West Bank: the Israeli military have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians in the last three years, a sum greater than the previous 17 years combined, according to U. N. data, a figure that includes combatants.

In many cases, the soldiers appear to protect their fellow Israelis while detaining the Palestinians who come under attack.

The Israeli military has rejected accusations that it supports “the actions of violent groups” in the West Bank. It says its mission is to “protect all residents,” and that any soldier who takes part in settler attacks or stands by while they occur is “acting in complete disregard” of their orders.

“The season is not starting off well,” said Ramez Obeid, head of the Palestinian Agriculture Ministry’s olives department. “We estimate 50 percent of the land will be inaccessible.”

Indeed, as settlers paralyze harvesting, some communities like the village of Jalud can barely harvest enough to produce oil for themselves.

Jalud and its surrounding areas stretch between several hills, nearly all of which have become home to new settler outposts since 2023. The settlers’ presence has made accessing more than 1,000 acres along the village’s periphery impossible.

“They stole my equipment just a few meters away from our home,” said Raed Al-Naser, the mayor. “And they are doing this to many others.”

Fearing for their lives, residents let the olives hang from trees, untouched.

Except where the settlers take them.

“It’s not the olive harvest season,” said the mayor. “It’s the olive stealing season.”

The attacks typically follow a pattern and are executed with precision, as Palestinians described them and as we saw ourselves.

Settlers have claimed the high ground in much of the West Bank, placing encampments above the olive groves that terrace up and down the limestone bluffs.

From the ground below, one can see the settlers preparing, usually dressed in black hoodies with masks and armed with rifles and other weapons.

They descend with speed, sometimes on foot, fanning out across the groves and hiding among the trees. In other cases, they barrel down roads into the lower ground.

This was the case in Khirbet Abu Falah last Friday, when 50 or 60 settlers laid siege to farmers harvesting crops before a group assaulted the veteran Post photographer. Mr. Netanyahu’s office said the “facts surrounding the confrontation” were being investigated.

Where they can, Palestinian lookouts scale unclaimed hillsides so they can warn their neighbors about attacks. Without them, the farmers would have no chance to flee before the settlers came storming down, like what happened with Mr. Al-Bazari.

By Israeli law, Palestinian villagers cannot be armed. Even throwing rocks at settlers could land a Palestinian in prison, often meaning that the only recourse available is to flee their own lands.

On Monday in Turmus Ayya, a Palestinian village filled with the homes of dual U. S. citizens, settlers attacked one such house while its owners were out harvesting olives.

We arrived after the assault began. Settlers burned cars, smashed a neighbor’s windows and beat an American citizen to the point of hospitalization, his family said. In the aftermath, we saw Israeli soldiers threaten the Palestinians outside of the home with tear gas if they did not disperse.

“But this is where I live,” said one Palestinian man, in English. “Where is your warrant saying we must leave our own lands?”

“For the Palestinians, we don’t need a warrant,” the soldier said. “We can just tell you to go.”

Everyone pressed inside the destroyed home, where glass crunched underfoot.

Hanan Mousa Hamayel, who was inside during the attack, shouted in despair.

“How long will it be like this?” she asked, adding, “We live in fear 24 hours. We cannot find peace even in our own homes.”

In some cases, the mere threat of violence and the apparent complicity between settlers and soldiers was enough to halt the harvest.

We saw this in the village of Deir Abu Masha’al on Monday morning, when a farmer, Mahmoud Rabia, arrived at his olive fields to find a half dozen settlers already there.

Mr. Rabia, 60, expected the worst as he trundled into his grove, and the fear was palpable as settlers walked among the farmers, despite the presence of journalists and Israeli activists trying to help the farmers. A young settler jumped into an SUV, using it to block the road back to the village.

The crowd braced for an attack as four more settlers walked up the road to join the others.

And then the army showed up.

Only it wasn’t to push the settlers off the private land; it was to evict everyone else.

The soldiers forced the farmers and others away, brandishing a military order closing the zone. The settlers stood around laughing and smiling.

As one farmer attempted to drive away, another young settler jumped in front of his car to stop him. He told an officer to arrest him, claiming the Palestinian had attacked him. The military detained the man.

The boy then called out another Palestinian for holding a hand saw, and soldiers detained him, too.

Mr. Rabia fumed.

“My ancestors farmed this land,” he said. “And I have harvested these trees through the intifadas, through hard times and violent times.”

Through it all, he had never been kept from his own land.

“I don’t care if they have their outposts,” he said. “I just want them to leave me be.”

Gabby Sobelman is a reporter and researcher for The Times, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs, based in Rehovot, Israel.

Azam Ahmed is international investigative correspondent for The Times. He has reported on Wall Street scandals, the War in Afghanistan and violence and corruption in Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.

Ivor Prickett is a photographer based in Istanbul. He covered the rise and fall of ISIS in Iraq and Syria while on assignment for The Times. More recently he has been working on stories related to the war in Ukraine.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Trilobites

The discovery may hint at the roots of human norms around fairness and friendship.

Yoyo, left, and Pasa, best friends living in the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. Chimp friendships are largely initiated by grooming. Credit...

Supported by

By Taylor Mitchell Brown

Pasa and Yoyo, two female chimpanzees, are best friends. They spend their afternoons lounging together in the warm grass of the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda, grooming and sharing food. Sometimes they even try to escape the grounds together.

They are also less likely to steal food from each other, according to the results of a new experiment that pitted friendship against pineapple slices.

The new study is the first to find that primates can prioritize friendships over tasty treats, revealing an ability to squash selfish impulses previously undocumented in our hairy ape cousins. The discovery, which may hint at the roots of human norms around friendship, was published in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

“It wasn’t obvious to us that chimpanzees would steal less from their friends,” said Oded Ritov, a social psychologist at the University of California, Berkeley and lead author of the study. The discovery shows that chimps, like humans, have social expectations of each other, he added. “We think that these expectations might be a basic building block that later evolved into fairness and other types of morality we see in humans.”

Notions of “friendship” in nonhuman primates have a contentious history. Many researchers have claimed that attributing the term to relationships in primates like chimps and bonobos is a kind of anthropomorphism, imposing ideas familiar to us onto distantly related animals, where they don’t belong.

“For a long time, it was like this F-word,” said Laura Lewis, a biological anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara and coauthor of the study. But over the past few decades, primatologists have uncovered increasing evidence of friendships in social primates, finding that they show more trust and support toward the peers they feel close to.

In the wild, chimpanzee friendships mostly develop between males, where they nurture bonds primarily to defend against alpha male tyrants or provide backup in fights against other troops. In bonobos, friendships are common among females, who must vie for power in the prevailing matriarchy. In captivity, for both species, friendships develop more broadly across a troop, with fewer sex differences.

“In captivity, you sort of have to deal with each other all the time,” said Zoë Goldsborough, a behavioral ecologist and primate expert at the Max Planck Institute for Animal Behavior, who was not involved with the research. Because captivity removes some of the normal constraints on a chimp’s life based around food, and conflict, you see many more relationships, including friendships, flourish.

Once established, friendships afford many privileges. Friends hang out, hold hands, nest together at night, protect each other in battles and console each other after fights or if an infant dies. Sometimes chimps even get jealous when they see a friend grooming another chimp, intervening to prevent them from bonding with someone else, said Dr. Goldsborough.

In the new study, the researchers wanted to see whether chimp friendships encouraged self-restraint regarding certain bad behaviors, in this case, stealing.

The team scrutinized 800 hours of video recordings of the Uganda sanctuary to figure out which chimps were friends. Then they set up trials in which the chimps were placed in pairs. One of the chimps in a pair had the option of being a thief who could steal fruit from a victim; the victim was either a friend or a neutral acquaintance. The chimps sat in adjacent rooms, one with metal trays stocked with pineapple slices and the other with ropes attached to the trays, which the thief could pull to steal the treats for itself.

“Sometimes the thieves would come in and they’d rip that tray,” said Dr. Lewis. But other times they came in, inspected the rope, then dropped it in an act of protest. When Yoyo was faced with the opportunity to steal from Pasa, she rejected the experiment altogether, turning her back to the ropes and refusing to enter the room at all.

Overall, the results revealed that friends were less likely to steal from one another, and pulled the pineapple trays away only 61 percent of the time, compared with 70 percent of the time with acquaintances.

When a chimp did steal from a friend, the result was chaos. The betrayal induced the victimized chimp to do things like pound its fists into the ground, screech loudly or scratch itself in a fit of anxiety, showing that it had expected more from its pal.

But after these betrayals, researchers found that the same chimps were quicker to forgive their friends, eventually acquiescing to such swindling in later trials. Nonfriends received no such grace, and were met with the same degree of anger throughout the experiment.

“The fact that they’re able to attenuate this behavior depending on their social relationships is incredibly important,” said Dr. Lewis, “and we think it’s critical for the maintenance of these social relationships over time.”

As humans, “we put a lot of weight not just on the nice things people do for us, but also the lack of mean things they do,” said Dr. Goldsborough. “This study shows very nicely that chimpanzees also do this.”

Melania Trump Says She Brokered a Cease-Fire in a Starving Ukrainian City

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

The first lady, who is positioning herself as an intermediary between two warring nations as her husband sides with Russia, said the agreement would allow residents to evacuate.

By Katie Rogers

Katie Rogers is a White House reporter and reported from Washington.

Melania Trump, the first lady, said on Friday that she had brokered a cease-fire between Russian and Ukrainian forces in Oleshky, a southern Ukrainian city that is occupied by Russia and whose citizens are cut off from food and medical aid.

Mrs. Trump said the cease-fire would allow residents of the frontline city to leave “through a designated safe passageway.” The city, in the Kherson region of Ukraine, has been occupied by Russia since it began its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

“It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she said in a statement, adding that the “localized cease-fire” would begin on Thursday. Pope Leo XIV also lobbied Vladimir V. Putin for a cease-fire in recent days, calling the Russian leader from his hospital bed after undergoing lung surgery.

David Arakhamia, the head of President Volodymyr Zelensky’s party faction in the Ukrainian Parliament, said in a statement that the cease-fire would begin in “the near future,” with the goal to establish “permanent humanitarian corridors for the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of aid.” He offered “sincere gratitude” to Mrs. Trump and the pope.

Dmitri S. Peskov, a spokesman for the Kremlin, said in statement that the Russian military was “working on agreeing upon the timing of a cease-fire in that area to enable this humanitarian mission.” The first lady “made a significant contribution” to the negotiations, he said.

The unusual announcement by the first lady, who has tried to position herself as an intermediary between the warring sides, underscored the Trump administration’s freewheeling and unorthodox approach to diplomacy. It came as Ukraine and U. S. allies try to head off a turn toward Russia by President Trump that they fear could alter the course of the war.

In recent days, Mr. Trump has defended Mr. Putin and demanded that the Ukrainians replace Mr. Zelensky. He has also arranged to purchase diesel from Moscow and insisted to reporters that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” even as Russia attacks civilians with missiles and drones.

Earlier this week, Mr. Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, called Mr. Putin a “humanitarian” for releasing an American held for more than four years on what the State Department called fabricated charges.

Mr. Zelensky, for his part, has accused Mr. Trump of pushing Ukraine to surrender. He has also asked for the administration’s help in unblocking Starshield, a military version of the Starlink satellite network run by SpaceX that enables Ukrainian drones to attack against Russian forces. Mr. Trump has since called Elon Musk, who controls SpaceX, and asked him to restore communications.

Mrs. Trump has ramped up her own diplomatic efforts. During a rally in Iowa on Thursday, the president said that his wife is “actually becoming the next Eleanor Roosevelt.”

The first lady has “a direct line” to Ukrainian and Russian leadership, her adviser, Marc Beckman, told the pro-Trump Newsmax network in an interview on Friday. Mr. Beckman is directly in contact with both governments, two people familiar with his involvement said, and is a primary representative for Mrs. Trump on negotiations.

“Both sides formally recognized her as an intermediary and in writing, and they gave her the power to negotiate this cease-fire,” Mr. Beckman said. “And she’s been working tirelessly now for over a month to make sure that this occurs.”

In a statement, Mrs. Trump said that she would send “an impartial American media organization to accompany and document Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground.” The network is Newsmax.

Oleshky is separated by the Dnipro River from the larger city of Kherson, which Russia captured in early 2022 and surrendered later that year. Russian forces strike Kherson from across the river in Oleshky, and Ukrainian forces strike Oleshky from Kherson. The circumstances are among the worst anywhere in Ukraine. Swarms of drones, ubiquitous mines and destroyed infrastructure make it exceedingly difficult for residents to leave or for help to arrive.

In the past, Ukrainians have fled Oleshky by traveling deeper into Russian-occupied Ukraine, then crossing through Russia and Belarus to re-enter Ukrainian-controlled territory. It was not immediately clear how evacuees could leave the city, and what route they would take. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.

In her statement, Mrs. Trump said she was made aware of the conditions in Oleshky during a private meeting in New York while attending the United Nations General Assembly in late September. For more than a year, she has also made direct appeals to Mr. Putin to reunite dozens of Ukrainian and Russian children with families that were separated after Mr. Putin began the invasion.

According to the White House, at least 34 children have been returned to their families, but officials have not said how many children were returned from each country.

In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Mr. Putin for war crimes, saying he bore criminal responsibility for the abduction and deportation of Ukrainian children. Since the beginning of the war, Ukraine has accused Russia of abducting more than 19,000 children, according to humanitarian groups. Mr. Beckman said on Friday “that there are some Russian kids that have come back from Ukraine to their families in Russia as well.”

Mr. Putin has been invited to the Group of 20 meeting in Florida later this year, where the first lady is hosting an event. On Friday, Mr. Trump was asked if the first lady would take a larger role in peace talks between Ukraine and Russia. The president said no, before adding, “It’s not the worst idea I’ve ever heard.”

Reporting was contributed by Siobhán O’Grady, Marichka Varenikova and Liubov Sholudko from Kyiv, Anton Troianovski from Fort Myers, Fla., and Valerie Hopkins from Berlin.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Tech Fix

The first-generation Apple foldable may feel awkward, but it’s an intriguing step toward merging phones and tablets into one.

Credit...

Supported by

By Brian X. Chen

Visuals by Camille Cohen

Brian X. Chen, the personal tech columnist for The Times, owned the first-generation iPhone in 2007 and has waited years for one that folds.

Whenever I take a plane to go on vacation, I have a renewed appreciation for my iPad. Its roomy, bright screen makes movies, books and comics look great.

But then I return home, where I rely on a laptop and a phone. The iPad goes in a drawer. Only occasionally, like when I’m taking public transportation, do I wish I had my tablet to read a book.

How often you find yourself in that situation — yearning for a tablet when it is impractical to carry one — should be the central question you ask when considering whether Apple’s $2,000 iPhone Duo, which the company released on Friday as its first two-in-one, foldable tablet phone, is worth your money.

Because that’s the whole point of it. The Duo is a miniature tablet that can be folded up into a phone that fits in your pocket so you can carry it everywhere. To that end, what’s most important to evaluate about the Duo is its usefulness as a tablet. Everything else, including the camera, is secondary.

If having a tablet everywhere is not important for you, stop reading this review and continue enjoying your old-school, rectangular phone. You have plenty of time to think about it anyway. In a sign that this is the iPhone of our K-shaped economy, people eager to have every shiny new Apple thing bought all the iPhone Duos minutes after online orders opened last week. Any orders placed on Friday are estimated to ship in 2027.

I had a day to test an iPhone Duo before its release, so I mostly used it the way I use a tablet — for watching movies, reading books and doing some lightweight work.

My verdict is that commuters and business travelers who spend a lot of time on trains, buses and planes will probably like the Duo, as will avid book readers and people who watch lots of TV. Everyone else may feel frustrated with what is otherwise a funky, so-so smartphone.

Here’s what to know.

The Duo’s name refers to two devices. Closed up, it has a 5.4-inch outer screen for people to use as a normal smartphone. It opens up to reveal a 7.6-inch inner screen to become a tablet.

Every foldable phone released in the last eight years has had compromises, and the Duo is no exception. Its 5.4-inch phone screen looks like a cute, dainty device resembling a passport. But when used, it feels thick and stubby, which makes it cumbersome to operate with one hand. While trying to type a text message with one hand, I could not reach some letters with my thumb.

The Duo’s camera also lacks a so-called telephoto lens, which means it cannot zoom in as much as Apple’s other expensive iPhone, the $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro. (This is not a deal breaker because photos taken with the Duo’s camera looked quite good.) More annoyingly, the Duo doesn’t have a face scanner for unlocking the device, relying on a fingerprint sensor embedded in a button on the side of the phone, and it takes longer to unlock.

So the question comes down to how often you would use the Duo as a tablet to forgive the trade-offs, because the device begins to shine when it is opened up to take advantage of its bigger screen.

For watching movies, reviewing photos, reading books and writing emails, the Duo excelled. As an owner of many iPads of different sizes over the years, I found the Duo to be the most versatile and interesting tablet I’ve used.

As soon as I set up the Duo, I fired up the Amazon Prime Video app to stream some movies and shows. Some videos looked better than others. “The Expanse,” for example, was shot in an aspect ratio that took up most of the Duo’s screen and looked nice. But movies in widescreen, like Christopher Nolan’s “Memento,” showed thick black bars, detracting from the viewing experience.

Still, the screen felt roomy enough to satisfyingly stream videos, which I rarely feel compelled to do on my normal iPhone.

When I got tired of holding the tablet, I simply folded it 90 degrees and set it down as if it were a miniature laptop to continue watching hands-free.

I opened the Photos app on the Duo to scroll through the thousands of photos I had taken of my family, including Homer, a golden retriever, and Max, a corgi. Having grown accustomed to reviewing photos on a phone, I had forgotten how much better they look on a larger screen. I realized I hadn’t noticed details captured in past photos, like a chip on Homer’s tooth.

E-books, which are no fun to read on a tiny phone screen, were a delight to consume on the Duo. Even better were comic books. Graphic novels produced in color looked crisp and vibrant, and the screen’s matted texture reduced glare from ambient light.

While my book reader of choice is still a Kindle, I’d consider a Duo if I wanted to get into the habit of reading more often, because it would become a book reader that I carried with me everywhere.

Tablets for years have not been conducive to productivity, but are great for lightweight tasks like email. Apple’s Mail app made good use of the Duo’s software interface. With the Duo folded shut, the small outer screen showed a simple list of emails. With the Duo unfolded into tablet mode, the app adapted to list the emails on the left side and show their contents on the right side.

The biggest plus to productivity is the ease of typing on the larger screen. As a tablet, the Duo is thin and compact enough to easily compose emails and Slack messages with two thumbs, which was very difficult to do with larger iPads.

Many tech reviewers have dunked on the iPhone Duo’s smaller screen because it diminished the experience of using the device as a normal smartphone. But when the Duo arrives to customers, I expect people will prefer to unfold it for use primarily as a tablet.

This is a new beast and should be treated as such. It may not be as fun to mindlessly scroll through TikTok using one hand with the Duo, but perhaps that means you will end up opening it up to consume deeper content, which would be a win.

While the Duo probably isn’t for me (a person who commutes on a motorcycle and tries to minimize screen time), I’ve been sold on the concept of foldables after testing many in the last few years because they help us get larger screens without adding much bulk.

I’m quite fond of my rectangular iPhone, but wish it were thinner and more compact in my pocket, which would mean it would have to fold up into a tiny square. That feels like the inevitable next step for the quintessential phone.

To tell the truth, when foldable phones first arrived about eight years ago, I was skeptical they would ever be appealing because of their high cost but also because of their trade-offs. Their bendable screens were less durable than normal phone displays, which are protected with hard glass; folded up, they can feel bulkier and heavier in a pocket.

But over the years I’ve warmed up to foldable phones as brands like Samsung, Google and Motorola managed to make them thinner and also rejiggered the software to take advantage of their novel design. I‘ve been holding out for Apple to make one simply because I prefer iOS to Android.

Brian X. Chen is the lead consumer technology writer for The Times. He reviews products and writes Tech Fix, a column about the social implications of the tech we use.

Connections Coach

Violet Clinton is doing award-winning entomological field research. Her dad still has to buy the beer for her moth bait.

Credit...

Supported by

By Callie Holtermann

Visuals by Hilary Swift

Reporting, with bug spray, from the Eugene and Agnes Meyer Nature Preserve in Armonk, N. Y.

As the sun went down one night in September, 16-year-old Violet Clinton marched into a meadow of goldenrod with her butterfly net.

Every few minutes she flicked it toward a speck in the air. She knelt to examine a bug that looked like a toasted pecan with antennae.

“This is a three-lined leafroller moth,” she said. “There’s one kind of woodgrain leafroller moth that looks similar, but those came earlier in the year.”

She snapped a picture with her smartphone, then set the moth free. Onward she went toward a cluster of pines where an even greater variety of insects awaited.

“That’s a pug moth. That’s an elegant grass-veneer moth. And that’s a wasp.”

Violet is a high school junior by day and a moth researcher by night. While many of her Gen Z peers scroll through TikTok or fret about college applications, she spends two or three evenings a week “mothing” — think birding, but without the feathers — in the Eugene and Agnes Meyer Nature Preserve in Westchester County, N. Y.

She has cataloged more than 11,300 insects so far as part of a seven-month study she is conducting of moth diversity and abundance in the area. Her goal is to identify which species are present in three habitats under different weather conditions and moon phases — information that can be used to aid conservation efforts for moths and the plants they pollinate.

Violet’s findings have placed her in a league with researchers decades her senior: At this summer’s annual meeting of the Lepidopterists’ Society, she took second place in a research competition among a field of college and graduate students.

Her work is filling in gaps in scientists’ knowledge of where moths can be found, especially common moths that do not attract as much research funding as pest species, said Jason J. Dombroskie, an entomologist and the manager of the Cornell University Insect Collection.

The decline of the global insect population has put key pollinators, like bees, in jeopardy. Violet wants to know just how much moths can help pick up the slack.

“Realistically, this data will outlive her — it will be useful well into the future,” Dombroskie said.

Beyond the data, Violet hopes to persuade others to be a bit kinder in their estimation of moths — not exactly the prom queens of the insect world.

“A lot of people think that moths just eat clothes,” she said. (Their larvae are actually to blame, she added, and it’s only a couple of species.) They tend to be seen as drab brown pests, perennially overlooked in favor of flashier, more charismatic winged insects like butterflies.

Violet wants people to appreciate that moths are important. If you look closely enough, she said, you may even find them beautiful.

Her research takes up a lot of her free time, although she also plays cello and has written a draft of a novel about a girl who loves moths. It is rare for her to come across a moth she cannot identify. But that night, the woods were full of surprises.

“Oh, I’ve never seen this species before,” she said, brightening with excitement as she crouched to take a picture. “I’ll figure it out.”

Violet was dressed like a typical teenager, in Saucony sneakers and a teal zip-up fleece. As we walked, she showed me moths the size of Oreos and moths that looked like splinters, moths with brilliant red underwings, moths that disguise themselves to resemble bird poop. She treated each one with affection, as if it were an adorable newborn kitten.

“I feel comfortable picking up and touching every bug,” she said.

She moved through the woods with the seriousness of a seasoned entomologist, pausing occasionally to record the temperature, air pressure and humidity in a spreadsheet. Soon she reached the first of three data-collection stations she had set up earlier that evening, where a sheet of canvas glowed purple under two UV lights.

Violet had bought one light with money from her after-school job shelving books at the local library; the other was technically a Halloween decoration. A gardening cage nearby was draped with a damp T-shirt that Violet had soaked in her homemade moth bait: a mixture of mushy bananas, brown sugar and beer.

“I have to buy the beer,” said Brian Clinton, Violet’s father, who trailed behind her.

“It’s just for the moths,” Violet added.

Brian, a physician, drives Violet to and from her mothing expeditions, but does not help with data collection. The outings are a nice way to spend time together, he said, even though he admittedly does not know very much about moths.

“She can see it flying, and she’ll say, ‘That’s a clover looper moth,’ and I’m like, ‘What?’” he said.

Violet has been curious about insects since she was a child with a habit of poking around for grasshoppers. Her first memorable brush with a moth was when she was around 7 years old and brought home two woolly bear caterpillars that she had found inching their way across a sidewalk. In the winter, she thought they might have died, but in the spring they hatched as Isabella tiger moths with vibrant orange wings.

By the summer between middle and high school, she was studying field guides about insects to compete in entomology events as part of her school’s Science Olympiad team. Her family has been supportive, allowing her to raise hornworms from a pet store until they hatched into Carolina sphinx moths.

Still, there are limits: The beer-and-banana-soaked T-shirts have to be washed outside with a hose, not in the washing machine.

At the beginning of her sophomore year, Violet’s science research course at Horace Greeley High School required her to pick a subject for study. While many students chose to work with publicly available data sets about A. I. or mental health, she elected to do her own fieldwork.

Her data-collection efforts went well beyond the stuff of a typical school project. Seeking guidance, she sent an email to to Dombroskie, whose research specialty is moths.

“She had what I thought was an impossibly ambitious project, but she was insistent,” he said in an interview. “I said, ‘If you can pull this off, you’ve got something.’”

They began meeting on Zoom in January to refine her research process. Impressed by her drive, Dombroskie encouraged her to attend the Lepidopterists’ Society meeting in June at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh.

There, she presented her preliminary data from three habitats — deciduous forest, pine forest and meadow — on a poster board for the student research competition. “I thought, ‘Yeah, she’ll do a poster, but she won’t win: She’s competing against a lot of grad students,’” Dombroskie recalled.

Afterward, he said, a colleague came up to him and asked, “Where did you find her?”

What’s so great about moths? Violet would love to tell you.

There are 160,000 species, at least eight times as many as butterflies. And while bees tend to get a lot of credit as pollinators, research suggests that moths may actually be more efficient. They carry pollen on body parts including their ventral thoraces (entomology-speak for chests), helping to nocturnally pollinate crops and wildflowers.

“A lot of plants couldn’t exist without moths,” Violet said. The insects contribute to biodiversity and help scientists assess the effects of climate change, she added.

Yet they don’t tend to attract the research attention or cultural fascination that some other insects do. It’s the “Bee Movie,” not the “Moth Movie” — and don’t get a lepidopterist started on the portrayal of moths in “Silence of the Lambs.”

Unlike many people her age, Violet does not use social media — that is, unless you count iNaturalist, the citizen-science app where she identifies moths with the help of other lepidopterists. For her, the study of moths is not about influence or clout.

What is it about, then? It might be tempting to cast Violet’s passion for moths as one teenager’s effort to resist the encroachments of the digital world by immersing herself in a natural one that is fast disappearing. Maybe her work delivers a tidy lesson in the importance of stopping to consider the beauty that exists right under our noses, or the hidden value of those everyday annoyances we so often brush away.

Like any good scientist, Violet resists such sweeping conclusions.

Ask her why she pays such close attention to moths, and she will give it to you straight: “They’re important pollinators that people haven’t thought about already.”

Despite her interest in insects, Violet does not plan to study them professionally. Entomologists often have to trap and kill bugs, which she does not want to do. (“They put them in a jar and the jar has a chemical so they slowly slop flapping and it’s really sad,” she said.) She plans to study animal science and become a zoo veterinarian.

Back in the preserve, it was approaching 10 p. m. Violet had found 373 moths in all, including signate Quaker moths with hairlike scales and aster eucosma moths that shimmered like trout. There had been two pale beauties, a translucent-winged species that looks less like a moth and more like the ghost of a butterfly.

“Sometimes I need to photograph a moth for the data collection, but a praying mantis or a spider is eating it,” she said. She does not like to disrupt the way of nature, so she takes the picture anyway.

Over the next few days, she uploaded the images to iNaturalist and identified them with assistance from other users, as well as her field guides of Northeastern moths and online databases like BugGuide. She will stop collecting data at the end of October, when most of the area’s adult moths will have died. Then she will finish her analysis and submit the results to academic journals.

But even once her official research is done, she will probably not stop mothing.

“I saw a moth today in the hallway at school,” she said when we spoke on the phone a few weeks after our nighttime walk.

“It was a greater red dart,” she continued. “I released it, and it flew away.”

I didn’t know much about moths until Violet Clinton, a 16-year-old, took me out “mothing” in the woods north of New York City. I made the mistake of wearing a green fleece, which meant that a lot of moths landed on me — to them, I looked a little bit like a plant. I learned that moths are important pollinators that need to be studied more closely. I also learned that they like beer. (Same!)

Callie Holtermann reports on style and pop culture for The Times.
