U. S. Government Takes a Cut of Chip Business in Japan-Funded Deal

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump’s novel deal-making is on display in upstate New York, where the administration is funneling Japanese funds into a government-owned chip factory.

By Ana Swanson

Ana Swanson covers international trade and reported from GlobalFoundries factory in Malta, N. Y.

For years, the United States has tried to jump-start domestic semiconductor production through a mix of federal grants and loans. The Trump administration is taking a much different approach — channeling foreign money into the sector, and demanding a cut for U. S. taxpayers in return.

The latest example was an unusual agreement for a semiconductor factory in upstate New York that was unveiled this week. Billions of dollars in Japanese funding has been dedicated toward building a facility that will be operated by the U. S. chipmaker GlobalFoundries.

But unlike GlobalFoundries’ other factories in New York, the upstate project will be co-owned by the United States and Japan through a special purpose vehicle. Japanese financing of $10 billion is expected to accelerate the construction of the factory, which will begin producing chips for cars, factories and data centers in 2029. Another $10 billion could fund a second plant, if the parties later approve it.

Call it the financialization of government investment. The Japan tie-up is the brain child of President Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, a New York financier known for pursuing unorthodox and aggressive tactics to amass a fortune. In Mr. Trump’s second term, Mr. Lutnick has used the threat of tariffs as a cudgel to drum up big promises of international investment, and turned the Commerce Department into a deal-making operation that wields those funds.

With Japan, whose economy depends on exports of cars, technology and steel, Mr. Lutnick and Mr. Trump offered the country lower tariffs in return for setting up an investment fund that the president could direct toward chosen projects. So far, Japan has agreed to fund a natural gas plant in Ohio, a crude oil export facility along the U. S. Gulf Coast and a synthetic diamond manufacturing site in Georgia, among other projects related to nuclear energy, critical minerals and other fields.

Profits from the New York chip project are expected to be split between the U. S. and Japanese governments, with GlobalFoundries also taking a cut. The chip company will also be paid a series of fees for the use of its technology and for operating the site. And the U. S. government will take an equity stake in GlobalFoundries, one of dozens of equity stakes in private companies, including the chipmaker Intel, that the Trump administration has acquired since last year.

Speaking from GlobalFoundries’ New York factory on Wednesday, Mr. Lutnick heralded the project’s benefits.

“Not only does the United States of America make money from the tariffs in Japan, but we also make money on 50 percent of the cash flow profits of this $20 billion investment,” he said. “And then on top of that, because of the scale of this investment, GlobalFoundries has agreed to give us 7 percent of the company, which at current market value is about $2 billion.”

Mr. Lutnick said that Mr. Trump had not yet decided what to do with the equity shares the company had given to the United States, but that Mr. Lutnick personally favored putting them into Trump accounts, new tax-advantage savings accounts for children.

GlobalFoundries, whose majority owner is the sovereign wealth fund of Abu Dhabi, has long had U. S. government funding and contracts. The Biden administration approved $1.5 billion of funding and another $1.6 billion of loans in 2024 to support the company’s chips. The company also operates as a “trusted foundry,” providing semiconductors for the U. S. military.

The company had been pondering the expansion for years, and moved forward after discussions with the government and Japan. The project would increase the country’s capacity for semiconductors, which are used to power everything from cars and toasters to data centers, by 10 percent, and become one of the largest facilities in the country. Both Republicans and Democrats have been pushing to increase domestic chip production in recent years, after pandemic-era shortages slowed car production and stoked inflation.

Mr. Trump and his cabinet officials have been promoting investments in Alaska, Iowa and North Carolina — some of which seem more likely to be realized than others — as they try to buoy their approval rate ahead of the midterms. After an event last month to celebrate what Mr. Trump said would be an Alaskan gas pipeline financed by South Korea, officials there clarified that they had committed to move forward with the project only if it was deemed commercially reasonable.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly made exaggerated claims about foreign investments, including that his administration has brought $20 trillion into the country — a sum equal to more than two-thirds of U. S. gross domestic product.

On Wednesday, Mr. Lutnick ticked through his own accounting: a $550 billion commitment from Japan, $350 billion in promises from Korea, as well as another $500 billion to build Taiwanese semiconductor factories.

“No one has ever seen or heard of these kind of numbers before,” Mr. Lutnick said.

At GlobalFoundries, all the parties expressed their enthusiasm to go forward with the first $10 billion phase of the project. The second phase, which would take the total investment to around $21 billion, is still subject to a “go-no-go decision” between the shareholders before the end of 2028, the company said.

Tim Breen, the chief executive of GlobalFoundries, said in an interview that the company had wanted for some time to expand, but that the government had pushed them to “think bigger.” He added, “so we came up with this concept to expand this site in two phases.”

Pradip Singh, the chief manufacturing officer at GlobalFoundries, said the move would be positive for the company’s shareholders, allowing the firm to provide its customers with domestically produced chips, without bearing the extra cost of capital expansion.

U. S. officials have also described the fact that Japan is footing the bill as a benefit to U. S. taxpayers. Japanese officials, who attended the ceremony Wednesday, emphasized that the facility would use Japanese machinery to make its chips, and supply some of the products to a technology corporation in Japan.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Republicans Cut Taxes to Win the Midterms. It May Not Work Out.

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Among the stakes in next month’s election is the long-running question of whether tax cuts can shape how people vote.

By Andrew Duehren

Andrew Duehren spoke with voters at community events in Briarcliff Manor and Yorktown Heights, N. Y., to report this article.

All across the country, Republicans are campaigning on last year’s tax cuts as they try to retain control of the House and Senate. But none of them are doing so quite like Representative Mike Lawler of New York.

Mr. Lawler has made the higher cap on the state and local tax, or SALT, deduction central to his political identity. He plugs it in ads and at his campaign events. President Trump has taken to calling the congressman “Mr. SALT,” including at a rally in Mr. Lawler’s district this spring. At the Republican midterm convention in Texas last month, Mr. Lawler took to the stage to talk up his work securing the larger tax break, a contrast with the Republicans who shied away from the event and an unpopular Mr. Trump during the campaign.

“It’s not often, out of 435 members of Congress, that a member can point to something very specific that they did, that directly impacted their constituents in a really positive way,” Mr. Lawler said in an interview. “I can do that.”

Whether that pitch is convincing to voters on Nov. 3 will not only determine control of this congressional district in the lower Hudson Valley, where Mr. Trump narrowly lost to Kamala Harris in 2024. It will also inform a long-running debate about whether tax cuts can influence the outcome of an election, a crucial question as Republicans, and increasingly some Democrats, try to win votes by committing trillions of dollars to lowering taxes.

Of all the tax cuts Republicans passed last year, the higher limit on the SALT deduction would seem to be the most politically potent. It was one of the most expensive changes, with its benefits concentrated in places like the suburbs that Mr. Lawler represents. Lawmakers from New York had loudly demanded a higher cap for years, making the policy more salient in the district.

Even then, the tax cut may not sway many of the voters it was meant to convince.

“I mean, I don’t think anybody wants to pay more taxes,” said Emer Flounders, a 43-year-old resident of the district. Still, Mr. Flounders said he would not be voting for Mr. Lawler. “Whatever benefit there was, I’d easily forgo it to have somebody else in there,” he added.

Mr. Flounders was among the parents watching their children zip by on carnival rides at the celebration of the Fire Department’s 125th anniversary in Briarcliff Manor, N. Y., this month. Jennifer Nigrelli, 49, was another. She said she planned to vote for Mr. Lawler — and would have done so whether the SALT cap had been increased or not.

“I know a little bit about the tax relief that he has brought, so that is helpful, but also I always vote Republican,” Mrs. Nigrelli said.

Entrenched partisan loyalties are just one of the barriers to any tax cut’s making an appreciable difference in an election.

The tax system is famously convoluted, and many people may not even be aware of any change. Even those who know about a tax cut, and benefit from it, still may not give credit to the candidate who supported it, research has shown. Other issues — energy prices, immigration policy — may always be more important to voters than a lower tax bill.

Republicans made several design choices to try to overcome those obstacles. They passed a number of buzzy tax cuts that Mr. Trump had championed on the campaign trail, including a deduction for overtime pay. The Trump administration also funneled the savings into larger tax refunds this year rather than marginally lower tax payments, hoping that would be more noticeable to voters.

Nevertheless, the party faces the prospect of large losses next month.

“One of the challenges of tax cuts is that people only interact with the tax system once a year, and it’s in April,” said Chris Faricy, a political science professor at Syracuse University. “It’s a heavy lift for Lawler to say, ‘Hey, I know you’re concerned about affordability and housing, but remember in April when you did your taxes?’”

Not that Cait Conley, the Democrat challenging Mr. Lawler, can ignore the SALT issue. She has argued that there should be no limit at all on the deduction and knocked Mr. Lawler for voting in favor of a cap, even if it was a higher one. The legislation that lowered taxes last year also cut funding for Medicaid, a change that Ms. Conley has repeatedly criticized.

“So for him to say he did us any favors, when he actually screwed us, is really just another sign of how he’s a political operative instead of a public servant,” Ms. Conley, an Army veteran and a former national security official, said in an interview.

Her line of attack draws on the circuitous backstory of the SALT deduction. For decades, American taxpayers had been able to write off, on their federal return, all of the income and property taxes they paid to their state and local governments. That gave people in areas with high taxes, often represented by Democrats, substantial tax savings.

Then, during Mr. Trump’s first term in 2017, Republicans put a $10,000 limit on the deduction, a tax increase that offset some of the cost of legislation otherwise dedicated to cutting taxes. Like many of the other tax provisions in that 2017 law, the $10,000 SALT cap was set to expire at the end of 2025.

Last year, Republicans extended many of those expiring measures but, at the insistence of a small group of lawmakers that included Mr. Lawler, did not continue the old SALT cap. Instead, Republicans imposed a higher limit: $40,400 for people making $505,000 or less in 2026. The larger deduction, which shrinks at higher income levels, snaps back to $10,000 for all filers in 2030.

Even though temporary, the savings could be substantial: The average tax cut from the higher SALT cap was $2,700 among New Yorkers, according to the Treasury Department.

“It was a very big deal,” said Russell Glickstern, a financial adviser in Westchester County, much of which falls in Mr. Lawler’s district. Mr. Glickstern, who supports Mr. Lawler, said his clients under the income limit were able to reap “huge refunds” by writing off their property taxes.

Other voters were less impressed by the seesawing changes.

“I know that Trump put into effect some things that made it hard to get a refund, and then pretended that he fixed it, when he caused it in the first place,” said Erin LeForce, a 39-year-old Democrat who plans to vote for Ms. Conley. “I don’t have a ton of respect for that.”

Because they do not pay as much in state and local taxes, low- and middle-income taxpayers are unlikely to benefit much from a more generous SALT deduction. And in a problem for Republicans, larger tax refunds arrived this spring soon after Mr. Trump launched a war against Iran, which may have overshadowed the tax savings by driving up the cost of gas and other goods. Mr. Trump’s wide-ranging tariffs, effectively a tax increase, have also pushed up prices.

Joe Caldwell, 62, came to the carnival event in Briarcliff Manor from where he lives in Mount Vernon, which is in a neighboring congressional district. He said he thought Republicans were “out of touch with the small things” and too focused on cutting taxes.

“But they aren’t worried about how much groceries we put on the table cost or the gasoline or stuff,” Mr. Caldwell said. “I’m more of a working-class guy.”

Beyond his district’s financial gains, though, Mr. Lawler’s work on the SALT deduction may have helped him present himself as a more moderate Republican. He opposed much of his party on the issue; Mr. Trump has joked that Mr. Lawler was a “pain in the ass” during the negotiations. In a national political environment that heavily favors Democrats, polls show Mr. Lawler and Ms. Conley in a very close race.

Victor Broglia, a 76-year-old Republican in Yorktown Heights in the district, said that while he would not benefit from the larger SALT deduction, his son had taken advantage of it. He said he saw the policy as an example of Mr. Lawler’s helping his constituents.

“He stands up for us,” Mr. Broglia, a retired bus operator, said.

Regardless of the outcome of the election, either Mr. Lawler or Ms. Conley is likely to continue demanding more SALT relief. In general, lawmakers believe that there is too much political risk in ever opposing a tax break for constituents, even if the reward for cutting taxes may not be particularly large, said Andrea Louise Campbell, a political science professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. That’s how an expensive provision like the SALT deduction, a bête noire for tax experts across the ideological spectrum, can reappear in the tax code.

“Even if you manage to get rid of them, they tend to reappear like barnacles on a ship,” Dr. Campbell said.

Andrew Duehren covers tax policy for The Times from Washington.

Ambush of Salvadoran Soldiers Escalates Haiti’s Anti-Gang Mission

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

With four soldiers missing, Haiti’s new Gang Suppression Force, already off to a rocky start, is facing its first crisis.

By Frances Robles

Frances Robles spent 12 days in Haiti, including three embedded with the Gang Suppression Force.

The skies above the slums and hills of Port-au-Prince are buzzing with helicopters.

Some of them are manned by a team of Salvadoran soldiers, medics and technicians who fly with machine guns at the ready in case they are fired upon.

The Salvadorans are deployed to Haiti as part of an international mission called the Gang Suppression Force aimed at eradicating rampant gang violence. Often tasked with evacuating the injured and transporting soldiers over gang territory, the Salvadorans once flew across the country to pick up a Sri Lankan soldier who had broken his legs.

The Salvadoran contingent in the U. N.-backed force is now the focal point of a high-stakes rescue operation after four of its members were ambushed on Sunday and went missing. Hundreds of Salvadoran special forces are expected to arrive in Haiti in the coming days, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.

The episode marks a critical flashpoint in the Gang Suppression Force’s deployment, quickly escalating what critics worried was a slow, underwhelming start to the mission. With El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, warning of a severe military response if his soldiers are not returned alive, the U. N.-backed mission threatens to become a showdown between Haiti’s armed groups and El Salvador’s contentious leader.

For the first time, the understaffed Gang Suppression Force, known as the G. S. F., is conducting operations in Croix-des-Bouquets, a town outside the capital where the Salvadorans were abducted that is one of the country’s most entrenched gang strongholds.

“I think this is a wake up call,” said Louis-Henri Mars, senior adviser of the Institute for Research and Action for Peace, a peace-building organization in Port-au-Prince, the capital. “Wake up call for the international community, for the U. S., for everybody: ‘Hey, we’ve been fooling around here, and those guys are not fooling around. Let’s get it on.’”

The New York Times spent three days last month with the international force, including with the Salvadoran helicopter unit. Troops from a Chadian contingent conducted patrols in armored personnel carriers. The commander of the international mission is from Mongolia.

But the force has been dogged by late deployments and logistics problems, which experts say have led gangs to meet the mission’s arrival with a collective shrug.

Haiti’s gangs control many parts of Port-au-Prince, forcing residents to flee some neighborhoods that have become no man’s lands. In others, gangs are so entrenched that even the police do not dare enter.

More than 22,000 people have been killed in a spiral of gang violence that worsened since the assassination of Haiti’s president five years ago — more than 5,000 so far this year alone. Gangs, once controlled by powerful elites and politicians, outgrew their overseers and banded together, taking over major roads and entire communities.

Touring a former school that the G. S. F. had cleared of gangs, Maj. Tahir Bahar, of Chad, acknowledged that his troops faced a steep learning curve: They’re used to deserts, not cramped urban terrain.

Expectations from Haitians are high, but he promised improvements.

“They want results,” Maj. Bahar said. “We must do it. I cannot promise a timeline.”

Haiti’s ability to hold cleared areas remains a critical obstacle for long-term results, including elections that had been scheduled for December that many here consider an extremely unrealistic goal. The school, in the Tabarre neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, is an area so dangerous that it still lacks residents and basic services.

“We need someone to come in after us,” Maj. Bahar said. “The civilians want to come back. They need electricity, and they need schools. We cannot bring electricity.”

The G. S. F. arrived in April with a mandate to take the fight to the gangs and take back control. Unlike a previous international initiative known as the Multinational Security Support mission, it would be five times larger, conduct intelligence-led operations, have arrest powers and work independently without having to coordinate with the Haitian National Police.

It is also funded by contributions to a dedicated U. N. trust fund. Expected to cost about $400 million a year, the fund has received $194 million, according to U. N. records.

The mission is supposed to have 5,500 soldiers, with contributions from countries around the world. Six months later, it only recently reached 2,000 troops, from six nations.

Troop contributions have been delayed, and moving people, vehicles and equipment across the world has proved a challenge.

The international force has cleared gang roadblocks, seized weapons and regularly conducts patrols in downtown Port-au-Prince, freeing up the Haitian National Police to respond to serious outbreaks of violence.

But of 26 arrests the force has made since its arrival, 18 people were released for lack of evidence. In one city, Gros-Morne, gangs killed civilians in retaliation for G. S. F. operations.

“We’ve got a long way to go, we totally recognize that,” Jack Christofides, the force’s special representative, said in an interview last month. “I don’t believe the gangs can sustain a fight against professional soldiers coming from so many different countries. We’ve got real capabilities coming — not just infantry, but police, we’ve got a maritime unit, we’ve got an air unit.”

The mission should have most of its forces on the ground by the end of this year and be making more progress by early next year, he said.

“We’re not saying that in two years’ time there will be no gangs in Haiti,” he said. “What we’re saying is that in two years’ time the Haitian state will no longer need an international force such as ours, because they can look after their own security and eventually stabilize the situation.”

From his social media posts, it does not appear that President Bukele plans to wait that long. In a message written in Creole directed to the Haitian gang members who abducted the four Salvadorans, he warned military operations would only get more intense.

“We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too,” he wrote.

Mr. Bukele, in office since 2019, is both praised and criticized for a harsh crack down on Salvadoran gangs that put tens of thousands of people in prison. El Salvador used to be one of the world’s most dangerous countries; now it’s among the safest.

The Salvadoran technicians went missing on Sunday after coming under attack while driving back from a supermarket through a gang-controlled area. Their vehicle was discovered burned, but the four Salvadorans have not been heard from since.

Although the attention is focused on finding them, the episode has raised serious questions about what they were doing driving through what is widely considered a “no-go” zone for foreigners and even most Haitians. While the incident is being treated as a kidnapping, many experts fear the men have been executed.

On Thursday, Lanmò Sanjou, a gang leader in the area where the Salvadorans were taken, released a video in which he refers to Mr. Bukele and shows buckets full of bullets.

“We will fight to stay alive,” he said.

Gédéon Jean, the director of the Center for Human Rights Analysis and Research in Port-au-Prince, said Haiti needed an international force to help shore up the local police, but that requires adequate technological and human resources.

“Unfortunately, this is still not the case, although the efforts are commendable,” Mr. Jean said. “We are still waiting for a full and complete deployment, and especially for tangible results.”

The ambush of the four Salvadorans will be a turning point for the international mission, he said.

“The disappearance of the four Salvadorans changes the situation,” he said, “because now it is the G. S. F. that is the victim of gang violence.”

André Paultre and Michael Anthony Adams contributed reporting.

Frances Robles is a Times reporter covering Latin America and the Caribbean. She has reported on the region for more than 25 years.

The Education of Kathy Hochul: A Family’s Rise, a Hometown’s Fall

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Gov. Kathy Hochul’s vision for New York has been largely shaped by her upbringing in a failing western New York town and her family’s move up from a trailer park to affluence.

Gov. Kathy Hochul has won over the real estate community in New York City, but her politics and worldview remain products of her life in western New York. Credit... Hiroko Masuike/The New York Times

Supported by

By Benjamin Oreskes

Benjamin Oreskes, who covers the State Capitol in Albany, N. Y., visited the area where Gov. Kathy Hochul grew up in western New York.

In Lackawanna, a small Rust Belt city in western New York, generations of families have passed through a mobile home community since it opened in the 1950s to house mill and oven workers from Bethlehem Steel.

Working-class tentacles still touch the rows of mobile homes and R. V. s, but there are signs of discord. Among the widespread totems of Buffalo Bills loyalty, a Confederate flag hangs from one window. Well-manicured lawns outside newer homes contrast with rundown double-wides and dilapidated cars.

Kathy Hochul’s origin story begins here, just outside Buffalo, at a trailer where her parents lived right before she was born.

There is no marker or plaque noting the governor’s ties to the community, and the co-owner of the mobile home park, seated atop a riding lawn mower, offered only a tepid welcome. She noted that she planned to vote for Ms. Hochul’s Republican opponent, Bruce Blakeman, in November.

The frustrations of voters from corners of the state like this one animate Ms. Hochul. She has paid particularly close attention to places like western New York, far from the state’s hubs of power and wealth, and filled with people who feel forgotten.

Ms. Hochul asserts that she understands this sentiment better than most.

Her father, Jack Courtney, once worked in the furnaces at Bethlehem Steel, which employed 20,000 people at its peak. He eventually moved to the white-collar side of the company as a computer programmer and systems analyst.

As his career advanced, so did the family’s fortunes. The Courtneys left their mobile home, first for a nearby apartment and later for Hamburg, a fast-growing town about seven miles to the south.

The family’s rise amid a steep manufacturing decline — punctuated by the steel mill’s closing in 1983 — has served as something of a guiding light for Ms. Hochul’s worldview and economic vision for New York.

Her zeal to keep or create jobs in the state has led some government watchdogs, as well as Mr. Blakeman, to question whether the governor has been overly generous in offering state subsidies or other incentive packages to the private sector. Ms. Hochul rejects those assertions, often tying her policy to the economic struggles that she witnessed growing up.

She retells the trailer park story when she introduces public housing investments, and invokes the Bethlehem Steel shutdown as she heralds the opening of a bus plant in Plattsburgh or a technology center in Rochester.

“I have the memory of being a child who watched Bethlehem Steel close down, the place my grandpa worked, my dad worked, my uncles worked,” she said this summer at an event commemorating a construction milestone at Micron’s $100 billion semiconductor manufacturing campus in central New York.

“All of a sudden, because of foreign competition and decisions made back in the ’70s, all that was gone,” she added later. “My memories were of people saying, ‘Last one here, turn out the lights.’”

Ms. Hochul was thrust into the political limelight in August 2021, when she suddenly found herself in the governor’s mansion after the shocking resignation of Andrew M. Cuomo. She has since won attention for resisting some of President Trump’s agenda and has won over New York City’s powerful real estate titans while achieving a surprising political partnership with Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Despite her prominence, Ms. Hochul remains a diner-counter populist, and she says her upbringing is at the root of it all.

Jack Courtney met his future wife, Patricia, in church when they were in the eighth grade. They married when she was 19 and he was 20, working in the furnaces of Bethlehem Steel while attending Canisius College in Buffalo.

They made their home in the trailer park, briefly raising the first of six children, Dennis, there. Their daughter Kathleen followed in 1958, her imminent arrival prompting the family to move to an apartment in nearby Woodlawn.

After about a decade at Bethlehem Steel, Mr. Courtney left what appeared to be a secure job in 1968 to join Computer Task Group, which had just been founded by several former IBM employees. By 1973, the firm named him marketing chief.

Mr. Courtney was known for tracking new technological trends that could be taught to the firm’s employees, positioning the company to win lucrative contracts to help others build systems that incorporated these innovations.

By 1980, the company employed roughly 600 people and made $20 million in revenue, and Mr. Courtney shared in that success. In 1979, The Buffalo News reported that he was the 20th highest-paid executive in western New York, earning roughly $127,000 at the time, the equivalent of $626,000 after adjusting for inflation.

David Campbell, a former colleague who ran the company when Mr. Courtney was its president, characterized Mr. Courtney’s ascent as “an amazing American success story.”

“Having the boldness to leave Bethlehem and take a chance on a new company that ended up being a tremendous success,” he added. “Obviously, his daughter saw that whole path.”

As Computer Task Group prospered, western New York declined.

Facing increased foreign competition, Bethlehem Steel, then the nation’s second largest steel producer, lost close to $500 million in the third quarter of 1977. At the time, it was the largest quarterly loss for any American company ever.

That same year, one of the worst blizzards in western New York’s history killed 23 people. The following year, the local N. B. A. team, the Buffalo Braves, relocated to California.

“To understand Hochul, you need to understand Buffalo of the 1970s and 1980s,” said Sean Ryan, the mayor of Buffalo who has known Ms. Hochul for decades. “The deindustrialization of Buffalo and western New York stuck in everyone’s head.”

In public appearances across New York, Ms. Hochul frequently describes how the economic downturn of this period morphed into a psychological malaise as well.

“When those big employers left, it meant you had no value in people’s minds,” she said in an interview.

“That was hurtful, and it gives us a chip on our shoulder — one that I still have today,” she added. “People look down on us. You’re the Rust Belt. Your team loses four Super Bowls. You have the Blizzard of ’77, which was on Johnny Carson late-night jokes. People mocked us all the time. So that’s been our psyche. And I just thought, ‘But we’re not losers.’”

As her father climbed the corporate ladder, Ms. Hochul also observed the social activism of her parents, who were the children of Irish immigrants and were Democrats.

In 1971, Ms. Hochul, her brother and her parents participated in a daylong fast protesting the Vietnam War. The event was a “gesture of personal penance for supporting it through your taxes,” according to a local newspaper ad.

In Hamburg, the family delivered turkeys to Puerto Rican families on Thanksgiving and took leadership positions at their church. News accounts from that time also show that the Courtneys sought to integrate the town, which had no Black residents in 1965. To accomplish this, Mr. Courtney coordinated a survey gauging local sentiment on “racial attitudes.”

Ms. Hochul said in an interview that her parents were “social justice Catholics.”

“You were taught that you were put on this earth to make profound change in the lives of others,” Ms. Hochul said. “They found different vehicles to do that. I follow that same philosophy today.”

She began working in local politics in high school and, at Syracuse University, immersed herself in student government and activism. Syracuse was not her clear-cut first choice. A small women’s college was also in the running, and Ms. Hochul sought her father’s opinion.

He told her that one of those schools was where a congressman’s wife goes, she recalled. The other — Syracuse — was where a congressman enrolls.

After interning for a state legislator and working on local campaigns in New York, Ms. Hochul found her way to Washington, D. C., to attend the Catholic University of America for law school, moving there with her future husband, William Hochul, another Erie County native. She landed jobs with John J. LaFalce, a former 14-term congressman from western New York, then with Senator Daniel P. Moynihan.

She married Mr. Hochul, a lawyer, in 1984, and the couple returned to Hamburg in 1991 to raise their two children. She joined the Hamburg Town Board, where she served 13 years before becoming deputy clerk and then clerk of Erie County. After winning and then losing a seat in Congress, she was elected lieutenant governor in 2014, when Mr. Cuomo won his second term.

In her many references to her father, who died in 2023, she rarely details the extent of his financial success story, but it played a concrete role in her electoral rise. He contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to causes benefiting her political career. The donations included a $110,000 loan to her campaign for county clerk, which he later forgave, and a $250,000 contribution to the House Majority PAC, which spent around $660,000 supporting her failed congressional re-election run in 2012.

Her early focus as an elected official trended toward the quotidian: efforts to rejuvenate Hamburg’s downtown business district; fights over the locations of cellular towers; and a yearslong battle to remove tolls from the State Thruway.

Ms. Hochul once appeared at a forum lugging a bag with $200 of coins to showcase “the average amount western New York residents pay every year in New York State Thruway tolls,” according to local news reports.

She also started a downtown neighborhood improvement association with her mother, who had opened a flower shop in Hamburg. And she led campaigns against big-box stores like Walmart coming to town and usurping customers from local businesses. (When Walmart did eventually arrive, Ms. Hochul proudly trumpeted the concessions she wrangled regarding aesthetics.)

“They knew that it would be sucked dry if Walmart came in,” said Sheila Courtney, Ms. Hochul’s only sister. “They were worried about all the villages, all the little towns closing out, particularly Hamburg.”

Friends and former colleagues of Ms. Hochul say that as much as she is shaped by her upbringing, her agenda also reflects her political environment.

When a resolution in support of same-sex marriage came up for a vote before the State Democratic Committee in 2003, she declined to take a position. In 2007, as the Erie County clerk, she promised to report undocumented immigrants who applied for driver’s licenses to federal immigration agents.

“Please understand the world I’m in,” she said in a recent interview at a Greek diner in Lackawanna, noting that Hamburg had been solidly Republican for more than a century. “I was trying to find a way to be a progressive Democrat in a town that is pretty hostile to them.”

Earlier in her term, Ms. Hochul delivered on a local crowd-pleaser: She secured a new stadium for her beloved Buffalo Bills, pushing through $600 million in state funds to build a facility that opened last month with heated seating decks and the largest snow-melting system in the world.

The fanfare greeting the Bills’ home opener did not dampen questions about spending tax dollars on such a project, but Ms. Hochul was undaunted.

“I think there were some other cities that were pursuing the Bills and promising stadiums,” she said in September, just before the Bills played their home opener in the new stadium. “I was a brand-new governor five years ago this month, and I said, ‘No, that’s not happening on my watch.’”

Ms. Hochul is also keen to take credit for Micron’s investment of $100 billion over the next 20 years in the Syracuse region, where it plans to build a huge computer chip factory. The company’s decision was personal for the governor, who expended great energy wooing its leaders with $5.5 billion in state incentives — the largest such package in state history.

The company and the state have committed a combined $500 million for work force training in the region as well.

Over the years, some of the state’s subsidized development projects — like Global Foundries in Malta, just south of Saratoga Springs — have proved successful. At others, like Solar City in Buffalo, Mr. Cuomo’s heady estimates of job growth and economic activity have failed to materialize.

Since the Micron deal was first announced in 2022, the plant’s construction has been delayed, and now it will not open until 2030.

“It’s notable that four years later, we are still several years away from the site producing anything,” said Ken Girardin, a fellow at the Manhattan Institute, who added that cumbersome environmental review processes were part of a reason the project has been delayed.

Ms. Hochul’s enthusiasm has not been dampened. The Micron deal, she says, helps fulfill her goal to create jobs and the kind of hope that seemed to dissipate from upstate communities as the economy sank decades ago.

As a Hamburg Town Board member, Ms. Hochul was asked in 2001 about the local economic mood. She noted that her children — then 11 and 13 — had “already announced they are not staying since western New York has no future and no good jobs.”

Neither of Ms. Hochul’s children — who now have children of their own — live in upstate or western New York, and all five of the governor’s siblings left as well.

She jokes that she is the “only one out of a big Irish Catholic family still left in this area,” directly blaming government for being unprepared for the steep job losses.

“It was painful,” she said in August. “Those scars are still with me today.”

Jeff Ernst and Mark Sommer contributed reporting.

An earlier version of this article misstated which law school Gov. Kathy Hochul attended. She went to the Catholic University of America, not American University.

Benjamin Oreskes is a reporter covering New York State politics and government for The Times.

How Long Will Russians Put Up With War? Here’s What They Told Us.

The New York Times October 23, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

“Everything is fine” is a common refrain in a country used to adapting to a new normal.

By Valerie Hopkins

Reporting from Sofino, in the Moscow suburbs

I always get the same question when I return from reporting in Russia: When will Russians finally be fed up with the war?

They might seem to have good reason now. The war, for years mostly background noise among many Russians, feels more present. The economy is limping. Drivers have to wait in line for gas. Warehouses and data centers are going up in flames. Even Moscow at times comes under heavy attack, as it did on Thursday, when Ukraine launched 630 drones into the region.

One recent morning, I set out to ask Russians what they thought about all this. I went to Sofino, a town about an hour from Moscow, where Ukrainian drones a few days before had struck an industrial area, igniting a fire, and a residential complex, killing two people.

On the way, I pulled over at a Rosneft gas station where waiting cars snaked well past the exit lane. It had no diesel, but gasoline was available for about $3.25 a gallon — a steep price in Russia. A young man named Danya told me he had waited 30 minutes for gas.

He shrugged it off, repeating a refrain I hear all the time from Russians. “Everything is fine,” said Danya, who, like others I spoke with, asked that his last name not be used to avoid trouble with the authorities. He added that fuel shortages were overblown.

The war, he insisted, “doesn’t affect my life at all.”

“Everything is fine,” he said again.

Russians shrug for several reasons. They are silenced by the fear and conformity bred by a repressive government. They feel they have as much influence over their country’s politics as they do the weather. They are used to deprivation from centuries of political and economic crises. They keep their focus, as a coping mechanism, on what hasn’t changed. And they are flooded with anti-Ukraine propaganda from the state.

There is also a more fundamental explanation. Ukraine’s strategy, as it holds Russia to a near deadlock on the front lines, is to make Russians feel the war and demand an end. That includes the strikes on oil refineries that President Trump has pressured Ukraine to stop in recent days as he has openly favored President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

Although the Ukrainian campaign has significantly cut Russian oil production, causing clear economic damage, it has not been enough yet to drastically change life in Russia. Kyiv lacks the ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that Russia fires at Ukrainian cities every day. And Ukraine’s strikes, focused mostly on economic and military targets, do not instill the same fear as Russia’s systematic assaults on Ukrainian civilian targets.

Ukraine’s attacks have politicized some Russians who before now had tried to ignore the war. People have rallied around the flag. In Sofino, outside an apartment building with a gaping hole in the third and fourth floors after the Ukrainian strike, I asked three warehouse workers if they felt angry at the Russian state for starting the war and letting it drag on for nearly five years.

“Quite the opposite, the attacks make people hate them even more, because their homes have been damaged,” one young man said, referring to Ukrainians and their Western backers. He asked that his name be withheld.

Inside the building, a woman named Lusya was dragging a trash bag down the rubble-strewn stairs. She said it was surreal watching television that evening because there was no mention of the attack that had suddenly rendered her homeless. Still, she said she trusted Russia’s leaders.

“I support my president, even more so after all this, because you realize you just have to support the man and consolidate around him,” she said.

“I believe we are very lucky to have Putin,” she added.

Enduring adversity is a source of national pride for Russians. Successive generations have heard tales of the sacrifices of World War II. Waiting in line for basic goods was common during the Soviet era. The war in Ukraine, for many, is just another hardship to bear.

“People get used to a ‘new normal’ again and again,” said Elena Stein of the Berlin-based Center for Independent Social Research, which supports research inside Russia.

Many Russians are just tuning out the war. In a poll last month by the independent Levada Center, nearly 60 percent of respondents said they paid little or no attention to the fighting, the highest level ever recorded. Six in 10 said the country was on the right track, up 10 percentage points from the level in June, just after an earlier drone attack on Moscow.

The reliability of polling data is limited in autocratic Russia. But such numbers indicate that Mr. Putin’s yearslong effort to insulate Russians enough from the war that he can conduct it unimpeded is still largely working, despite mounting challenges.

“The pressure and the problems that are there are, in my view, not intense enough for him to reconsider at this point,” said Janis Kluge, a Russia analyst at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs.

Other analysts have said that the Trump administration’s recent decisions to engage in business deals with the Kremlin while demanding no concessions will only harden Mr. Putin’s resolve to continue fighting until he achieves his objectives in Ukraine.

While polls show that growing numbers of Russians want the war to be over, the vast majority say it should end only on Russia’s terms. Many appear ready to continue deferring to Mr. Putin.

Kirill, 36, a choreographer with a small hoop earring, said that aside from the price of gas, “I don’t feel it at all.”

“I’m not going to complain, because I know that this is my country, I’m going to support it no matter what,” he said. “I know that the people at the top can clearly see the bigger picture.”

As I spoke with Kirill and others at the Rosneft station, the store’s manager, Irina, came to admonish me for interviewing her customers. But soon she was sharing her own story.

Unlike the people in line, Irina did not deny the war’s role in her life.

She said she had told her 11-year-old daughter that if a drone or missile struck the gas station, she risked dying on the spot. Her mother-in-law works as a security guard at a warehouse complex that has been struck. And her brother has been fighting on the front since 2022. She said it was a miracle that he remained alive, adding that he had survived nights when up to 40 people were killed. He told her that he expected the war to continue until 2030.

She voiced the trademark sense of fatalism in Russia. “We’ll just have to endure it,” she said. “If we die, we die. I’ve already made peace with it.”

Irina was not as inclined as others to defer to the government’s approach on the war. She said she felt that officials were not telling the truth about casualties on the battlefield and in long-range strikes on Russian cities.

Eventually, this sort of mistrust, coupled with a worsening economic outlook, could set off more expressions of dissatisfaction, said Jeremy Morris, a sociologist at the University of Aarhus in Denmark who conducts fieldwork in Russia.

While it might not happen soon, he said, most Russians are not apathetic and apolitical, as they are sometimes portrayed. They just lack outlets for action as the government has grown more repressive.

During parliamentary elections last month, I visited the headquarters of Yabloko, Russia’s main antiwar party. I spoke with Maria, 24, one of the approximately 20 percent of Russians who tell pollsters they oppose the war.

She expressed indignation as she described reading English-language posts on social media describing Russians as a “slave nation.” She pointed to comments like one recently by a European Union spokeswoman, who said that “if Russian citizens face the consequences of this war, they have a chance domestically to take action against it.”

Maria described the costs of speaking up in Russia, where 1,856 people are currently incarcerated as political prisoners, according to the banned human rights group Memorial.

“None of you have gone through the experience of the average person living under totalitarianism, repression, total fear and the absence of free speech,” she said. “You can’t demand that we go on strike or turn out for protests, because all we’ll achieve is ending up in prison — or getting killed.”

Valerie Hopkins covers the war in Ukraine and how the conflict is changing Russia, Ukraine, Europe and the United States. She is based in Moscow.

Trump’s Attacks on Voting Raise Fears He Will Try to Challenge Midterm Results

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Election officials say they worry the administration could use its own unsubstantiated claims to contest the vote in November.

By Zolan Kanno-Youngs

Zolan Kanno-Youngs, who covers the White House, has been chronicling President Trump’s efforts to reshape the rules governing elections.

President Trump has warned that the country’s election systems are vulnerable to foreign meddling. Federal agents are scouring state rolls and federal databases to try to find noncitizen voters. And the homeland security chief has asked the Justice Department to examine whether a commonly used voting machine can be trusted.

Just weeks away from the midterm elections, Mr. Trump’s longstanding attacks on the integrity of voting systems are crystallizing into what many election officials and Democrats fear is an attempt to lay the groundwork to challenge the results in November.

So far, the president has been stymied in his efforts to directly assert federal control over elections, which under the Constitution are administered by the states. Last month, the Supreme Court blocked Mr. Trump’s effort to have the U. S. Postal Service screen mail ballots.

Instead, Mr. Trump and his allies across the government have intensified another tactic: systematically laying out unsubstantiated and false claims in an effort to sow doubts about the safety of the country’s decentralized election system.

The result, election officials fear, could be an effort by administration officials to try to contest results that do not favor Republicans by citing their own findings that the vote is tainted.

Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said he had grown increasingly worried that Mr. Trump may claim foreign interference in the election as a reason to seize voting machines, noting that the president made dubious claims about the country’s election defenses in a speech in July.

“President Trump will use any tool, legal or not, to try and make sure he gets the results he wants this year,” Mr. Warner said in an interview, adding that he had reached out to business leaders, former military leaders and veteran federal law enforcement officials to ask them to stand up to Mr. Trump if he contests the results.

“Good people of both parties and independents are going to have to say, ‘No, we’re not going to allow this to take place,’” he added.

White House officials maintain that the administration’s efforts are designed to ensure a fair election. When asked if the president will accept the outcome of the midterms, Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, referred to his recent response to that question.

“Of course I will,” Mr. Trump said earlier this month. “But we don’t want cheating.”

Nearly every day, the president questions the reliability of the vote. At a rally Wednesday in Arizona, a state that was a major focus of his effort to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election, Mr. Trump once again made false assertions about voting machines that year.

“The damn machines were broken in Republican areas,” Mr. Trump said, repeating his lie that the election was stolen from him.

On Thursday, the Justice Department sued the State of California, seeking to temporarily block the state from counting the mail ballots of 20,000 people it claims are “likely noncitizens.”

The administration’s intense focus on potential election issues comes as Mr. Trump has been conferring with outside supporters urging him to consider drastic actions. Last week, Mr. Trump met in the White House with Tina Peters, a former Colorado county clerk who was convicted of tampering with voting machines after the 2020 election, according to two people familiar with their meeting, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation.

Ms. Peters has long pushed the unsubstantiated claim that voting machines are vulnerable to foreign interference and has called for the Trump administration to inspect or take them into custody — a move legal experts say would be an overreach of federal authority.

Ed Martin, a former senior Justice Department official, told Real America’s Voice that Ms. Peters and the president had discussed “election integrity,” saying both are concerned that foreign actors could exploit election vulnerabilities to change votes. That unsubstantiated claim was echoed this summer by Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary.

Ms. Bis declined to comment on the meeting, as did Peter Ticktin, a lawyer who has represented both the president and Ms. Peters.

Despite all the inflammatory rhetoric, it is unclear that Mr. Trump would actually pursue the extreme measures his supporters are seeking. And election experts note that the administration’s attempts to assert more federal control over voting have been repeatedly blocked by the courts.

“There’s been a lot of posturing,” said Lawrence Norden, who oversees the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University, noting that election workers across the country are committed to ensuring a fair vote. “I think mostly election officials are tuning this out. They have elections to run.”

Still, some state and local officials say they are now taking preparations to defend their elections against what used to be a reliable ally: the federal government.

Deidre Henderson, the Republican lieutenant governor of Utah, said that for the first time her state had planned for a situation involving such potential interference, including the prospect of a federal agent showing up to a polling station with a warrant.

“We have had to figure out how to handle some measure of maybe interference from federal officials,” Ms. Henderson said during a George Washington University panel this month. “I don’t think we’ve ever had to think about that before and I don’t necessarily expect it, but right now it would be foolish to not at least think through some scenarios.”

Some voting rights advocates are also worried that a longstanding program by the Justice Department to deploy federal monitors to the polls to protect the civil rights of voters could instead be used to interfere with the elections.

During Wyoming’s primaries in August, two Justice Department monitors tried to interview voters and examine voting machines at polling places, local officials said. Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, called their actions “aggressive, unexpected, disruptive,” saying it “certainly didn’t seem to show respect for the state.”

In an expansion of past efforts, the department plans to have 1,000 monitors in all 50 states this year. The N. A. A. C. P. has sued, seeking information about the deployment. “This administration has made clear its intent to disrupt and interfere with the way elections are run in our country,” said Kristen Clarke, the group’s general counsel.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the program, telling Fox News earlier this month that the monitors “are making sure federal law is being enforced appropriately.”

Mr. Trump has been relentless in his efforts to sow doubts about the integrity of American elections, singling out a variety of issues that he claims are suspicious, whether voting by mail or California’s slow vote counting.

At a rally in Alaska this week, Mr. Trump took aim at the state’s ranked-choice voting system, calling it a “way to cheat.” He said he had instructed the U. S. attorney in Alaska to closely monitor vote tallies there.

Over the last year, his administration has pushed to find evidence to support his claims. Mr. Trump and Mr. Mullin asserted this summer that 278,000 noncitizens were registered to vote across multiple states, a claim that the government has not been able to substantiate. Homeland security officials have mobilized hundreds of agents to try to find noncitizen voters.

Ms. Bis said Mr. Trump’s actions were meant to ensure the country had “free and fair elections.”

“Every American should be asking why the radical left continues to fight against common-sense election integrity measures, like voter ID and citizenship verification, to make sure only Americans decide our elections,” she said.

Mr. Trump has also left open the possibility of taking more extreme steps. He has refused to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act to deploy the military in connection with the elections, a move encouraged by some of his supporters.

“You have the right to declare a national security emergency for elections,” Wayne Allyn Root, a conservative TV and radio host, told Mr. Trump during an interview in August, referring to a legally dubious theory popular among right-wing election activists.

“Let me just say that stranger things have happened,” Mr. Trump responded. “I’ll leave it at that.”

Mr. Ticktin, who took part in the June meeting with the president and Ms. Peters and says he maintains “pretty direct” communication with Mr. Trump, said he believes the president would consider deploying the military in connection with the midterms.

If many Republicans lose their seats “and we can show that there’s something that was wrong with the election, then it could lead to a serious situation such as martial law or something,” he said.

In late August, the president’s top military adviser, Gen. Dan Caine, said there were no plans for the armed forces to deploy troops in relation to the elections.

The president also said earlier this year that he regretted not seizing voting machines in the 2020 election. Ms. Peters, who also met with Mr. Trump in June, has said she has urged Mr. Trump to take possession of voting machines she claims were constructed with foreign-made equipment.

“I said, ‘We are going to lose this country if we don’t get rid of these machines before the midterms,’” she told the pro-Trump outlet Lindell TV. Ms. Peters also said she had urged him to fire members of an independent, bipartisan commission that supports states in administering their elections.

Mr. Trump forced out the panel’s members in July.

The lobbying efforts by election denialists echo the lead-up to the assault by Mr. Trump’s supporters on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, to try to stop the certification of the 2020 election. At the time, a number of conspiracy theorists pressed Mr. Trump on novel ways to try to overturn that election.

Mr. Trump was flanked then by advisers who were willing to push back on such moves. He is now surrounded by loyalists who are judged not so much on their legal assessments, but rather their ability to turn the president’s wishes into action.

They include top policy adviser Stephen Miller, who has been heavily involved in the efforts to assert more federal control over elections, according to people with knowledge of his efforts.

Mr. Miller, who did not return requests for comment, circulated a draft of an executive order to limit mail voting months before Mr. Trump signed a similar version in March. Some of Mr. Trump’s aides initially pushed back on the order because they felt it was too draconian, according to the people familiar with the events.

But Mr. Trump decided to sign the order, which was ultimately blocked by the Supreme Court, once it became clear that his efforts to have the Senate pass legislation that would restrict mail voting were futile.

Maggie Haberman, Devlin Barrett and Julian E. Barnes contributed reporting.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure

Wired October 21, 2026

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.

During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.

Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.

Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.

All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”

Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas, Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.

But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.

In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

Airbnb Hosts Are Furious They Can No Longer Make Guests Do Their Chores

Wired October 21, 2026

Airbnb hosts are melting down over a new policy banning them from making guests complete tasks that “would typically be performed by a cleaner,” like “stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”

The change, which applies to all bookings made on or after November 20, quickly sparked outrage after it was announced in an email to Airbnb hosts on Wednesday. Many began fuming online about losing the right to make their guests clean up after themselves.

“As hosts, we have a responsibility to protect our investments, our homes, and, in many cases, our personal living spaces,” one person wrote in Airbnb’s official forum for hosts. “The problem is that Airbnb increasingly expects hosts to accept the risks while limiting our ability to protect ourselves.”

“Airbnb is like an abusive partner,” wrote one user on the Reddit community r/airbnb_hosts. “I'm alive long enough to recognize how truthful those few words are,” another person replied. “Until and unless I see substantive changes, I'm finally out.”

A different self-described host declared that going forward, the kitchens in their rentals will be “stripped down to only bare essentials.”

Many guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. For years, travelers have complained about having to pay hefty cleaning fees as part of their Airbnb bookings, only to be required to complete a list of chores before checking out.

“The guest experience has become total ass,” one person said in a subreddit for Airbnb hosts. “Clean dishes and run in the dishwasher. Strip the beds, put all linen in the laundry room. Take out all garbage, put in garbage can, take to the curb. Honestly, knock it off.”

Airbnb noted in its Wednesday announcement that hosts can’t get around the new policy by putting cleaning tasks in the “Requests” section of their listings instead. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze tells WIRED that hosts can still make “reasonable” requests, such as asking guests to put dirty dishes in the sink. Other examples Airbnb cites include asking guests to take short showers in areas with drought-related water restrictions, or telling them to place trash in bear-proof containers.

In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted what they claimed was a screenshot of their failed attempt to edit their property’s “Requests” section. They tried to ask guests to wash and air-dry dishes, put dirty towels in the laundry room, and take trash to a dumpster at an RV park they could find using a map on the refrigerator. But they realized they couldn’t hit Save. Airbnb's interface had underlined and highlighted the requests in red and displayed a pop-up that read “Guests shouldn't be asked to do this task.”

Hosts also can’t circumvent the new policy by giving guests a printed list of rules and asking them to sign it when they check in. On November 20, Airbnb is also banning hosts from requiring guests to sign separate contracts, with limited exceptions for local legal requirements, longer stays, or accessing “an optional amenity” like a “golf cart rental.”

If one of these situations applies, hosts have to mention it in the dedicated section of their listing. Airbnb adds that it “doesn’t help enforce the terms of these contracts.” Hosts who violate either policy, Airbnb warns, may receive warnings, or in severe situations, have their listings removed or be banned from the platform entirely.

In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted a letter they claimed to have sent to company executives, demanding the ability to set their own “common-sense expectations” for guests. They encouraged others to send their own versions. Another asked if they should raise their prices, while a third called for hosts to organize a platform-wide strike.

“Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” they wrote. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”

Some hosts haven’t given up on finding a way to ignore or get around the changes. On Reddit, one person said they would simply move their rules to other sections of their listing, like “Guest Access.” (Airbnb did not immediately respond to WIRED’s inquiry about whether this would work.) Another person said they would give the guests a “house manual,” require the guest to read it, and provide a “codeword” as proof. (Several pointed out that this is not only unenforceable but against current Airbnb policy.)

“First sentence of my requests section will now state ‘Here are my house rules!’” another person said, though it’s unclear whether Airbnb’s interface will allow this. They named “not smoking” as an example of one of their house rules, but Airbnb has said it enforces host-imposed smoking bans.

Unwanted smoking and other serious scenarios—like letting dirty dishes become “health hazards,” leaving “permanent stains on sheets,” and creating “mountains of rotting garbage”—were invoked by several hosts. But these policy adjustments, seemingly, will not change how any of these things are treated.

Airbnb already has its own ground rules that all guests must agree to. The general credo is to "treat your host’s home like your own," which translates to things like putting trash in the trash can and not leaving moldy dishes.

If a host finds that anything was damaged or went missing during a stay, guests are expected to pay a “reasonable” amount to repair or replace it. Hosts are also protected through the platform’s protection program, AirCover, which will reimburse up to $3 million for certain property damage caused by guests, including furniture, cars, and other belongings.

Additional cleaning costs, such as performing "smoke odor removal" or handling "pet accidents” are also covered by AirCover. Airbnb notes that the cleaning fees hosts are allowed to set are only meant to cover standard guest turnover tasks like laundry and vacuuming. Hosts can’t “charge guest fees for failing to perform specific cleaning or checkout tasks,” though they can still leave guest reviews “based on cleanliness.”

In the Airbnb Hosts subreddit, a few lurking guests were quick to bring up the cleaning fees, which are famously the subject of their ire. One self-described “mostly guest” said they’re not opposed to running the dishwasher or stripping the bed. “Just don’t charge me a cleaning fee over $100 then,” they said.

“Truth nuke,” another person replied. “Why would I have to pre-game the cleaners?”

‘It’s the President’s Fault’: The White House Blame Game Starts Early Ahead of the Midterms

Wired October 21, 2026

Trump White House aides have started to cast about for a scapegoat to offer the president in the event of bad midterm election losses, as Republicans stare down brutal predictions in key House and Senate races, sources familiar with the matter say.

Republican political operatives say privately that the real blame lies with Trump for starting the Iran war in an election year, causing higher prices across the board and prompting a nationwide voter backlash, the sources say.

“Clearly it's the president's fault,” one operative tells Inner Loop.

But Trump aides also know, for obvious reasons, they cannot say publicly or tell the president behind closed doors that his own policy decisions are at fault as they contemplate losing not just the House majority, but possibly the Senate.

The result has been an unusually early effort to find a scapegoat, and sources say eyes have fallen on deputy chief of staff and political strategist James Blair, who organized the Trump 2024 campaign's turnout strategy and returned to the role for this midterm cycle.

Blair's efforts included a marquee plan for certain states to redraw congressional maps early, which looked likely—though not certain—to yield favorable House seats for Republicans, so long as the coalition that Trump turned out in 2024 came out to support Republicans in 2026.

Even accounting for the Iran war, the redistricting gambit was supposed to bring roughly 10 to 15 pickups for Republicans in the House. After Virginia's top court blocked Democrats from redrawing maps to keep pace in the redistricting battle, Blair wrote on X: “Lord grant me humility.”

But in a remarkable backfire five months later, election forecasters have found that some of the redistricted seats now favor Democrats.

The redrawn map for Florida's 25th congressional district just south of Fort Lauderdale, for instance, is now characterized as "Lean Democrat," and the outlook is so bad that the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House Republican–aligned group, has pulled money out of the race.

Maps that were drawn for Republicans in ruby-red Texas are suddenly also vulnerable, even in seats where the party has incumbents. In Texas' 15th congressional district, GOP candidate Monica De La Cruz's race is now rated a "tossup" by the Cook Political Report.

Blair's allies inside and outside the West Wing say the criticism directed at him is grossly unfair because he could not have foreseen the effects of the Iran war and scandals involving Trump officials undoing his planning.

Blair is also viewed as retaining the confidence of Trump and the White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and he traveled on Air Force One to two rallies within the past week, suggesting any blame that ultimately comes his way could be just symbolic.

After all, when Blair left the White House earlier this year to run Trump's midterm strategy from the outside, the president announced the move as only temporary and said that Blair would return after the election.

Responding to the reporting in this story, Blair said in a statement, “the President, our partners in the House and Senate, and I remain focused on winning in November. All Republicans should be spending themselves equally in our worthy cause.”

“The anonymous ‘sources’ peddling this nonsense are self-serving opportunists focused on themselves. We’re focused on the President and the American people,” White House spokesperson Danielle Alvarez added in a statement.

As for Wiles herself, despite reporting that she has been under fire, sources inside Trump's orbit are adamant that if Wiles leaves after the midterms, it will be purely of her own volition.

Trump aides acknowledge that much of the palace intrigue scapegoating is preemptive. Expectations are so low that if Republicans take some wins—like holding on to the Senate—Blair will be “seen as a savior,” one of the sources added.

But they also say that in many ways Blair has perhaps made it too easy for them to single him out. He explicitly owned the House midterm strategy, and now he may be walked to the gallows with that same rope.

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Trump Isn’t Even Good at TV Anymore

Wired October 21, 2026

Once upon a time, Donald Trump’s talents as a TV personality and pitchman were obvious to everyone—most of all himself.

When he launched his 2016 presidential run, millions of Americans knew him best not from his bankrupt casinos or the gossip pages of the New York Post but as the swaggering host of NBC’s The Apprentice, in which aspiring entrepreneurs competed for a full-time job in his real estate empire.

Trump routinely overstated the primetime dominance of The Apprentice, which was a breakout hit in its debut 2003–2004 season but saw its ratings steadily decline over subsequent years. Nonetheless, his rise as a candidate, propelled by his willingness to say anything to stay in the news cycle, seemed to affirm his on-camera star quality (even if it was actually people behind the scenes of The Apprentice who had edited his unscripted and less-than-coherent bluster to make him sound like a straight-talking businessman).

But where is Trump’s TV firepower today? His latest press secretary, Katie Zacharia, lasted a mere five days in the job, ousted following a disastrous on-camera performance at her first briefing just weeks before crucial midterm elections. Trump’s own media appearances are unhinged and embarrassing even by his standards; when he’s not falling asleep at events or in meetings, he’s claiming that NATO “gave” Greenland to the US and telling rallygoers about how he checked out Senator Jon Husted’s ass.

During Trump’s second term, his administration has done what it can to circumvent existing media and bring its messaging directly to voters with broadcast content that resembles familiar TV formats. It’s not breaking through at all.

On Tuesday, for example, the US Small Business Administration streamed an hour-long special called the Million Dollar Pitch Competition. The premise was that five business owners would appear before three celebrity judges (property investor Grant Cardone, rapper Nicki Minaj, and Airbnb cofounder Joe Gebbia, whose credentials as a member of Elon Musk’s DOGE were not mentioned) to vie for the biggest chunk of a $1 million cash prize supplied by Clover Network, a fintech company that provides point-of-sale platforms.

While the show, hosted by actor Dean Cain, was styled as something like a hybrid of Shark Tank and American Idol, it amounted to an extraordinarily dull attempt to prove that the Trump administration is bringing factory jobs back to the US. For some reason, it featured a short video in which Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, talked to an animated strand of DNA, because “America's DNA is small business.” The judges focused more on how animated the presenters were than the economic fundamentals of their pitch. When Marshall Sasse, the owner and CEO of a pressure valve company based in Wyoming, delivered a solid but subdued presentation, Minaj asked if he had access to any “cowgirls” who could’ve added “more punch to the pitch.”

While Trump himself was not on hand for the pitches, the show featured brief segments in which participants met with Trump in the Oval Office. When the judges asked the president for advice on picking a winner, Trump replied, “You know, it's interesting, because with The Apprentice, I had a very good term that I used: ‘You're fired.’”

A day later, the YouTube stream of the SBA’s Million Dollar Pitch Competition had barely cracked 60,000 views. Even on Trump-friendly X, the reaction to the event was hostile, with users suggesting that the White House cared more about game shows than the cost of living and was taking its cues from dystopian fiction such as The Hunger Games.

Other efforts to supplant mainstream programming have also fared poorly. A month after the White House launched a 24/7 Trump TV streaming channel as part of its ongoing war on news outlets, it’s hard to imagine even the most devoted MAGA disciple watching: on Tuesday, unremarkable B-roll footage from border agents driving alongside the US-Mexico wall segued into a series of testimonials from people describing how their loved ones were raped and murdered by migrants. On Wednesday, the channel showed footage from Trump’s February State of the Union address.

As for Robert F. Kennedy’s The Real Food Show on YouTube, a cooking series in which the health secretary enlists chefs to teach viewers affordable and healthy home recipes, audience has declined since a July premiere, with only six episodes released so far. The most recent segment included Cain as well as actor and ex-bodybuilder Lou Ferrigno, as though to underscore that on the celebrity front, some of Trump world’s biggest names are guys known for playing superheroes on TV in the previous century.

If there has been any sort of a ratings win for MAGA media this year, it would be UFC Freedom 250, the mixed martial arts extravaganza held in June at a ring structure controversially erected on the South Lawn of the White House. Though Ultimate Fighting Championship lost some $30 million on the spectacle, it broke the viewership record for a live event airing exclusively on streamer Paramount+, with an average of 7 million viewers tuned in.

That fell well short of the Super Bowl records that Dana White, CEO of UFC, had promised to break. While he was nonetheless able to declare a victory for his sports organization, White has said that he “can’t afford” to return to Trump’s backyard for an encore. Too bad for the administration, which has yet to capture a real TV audience without significant help from a producer who knows what they’re doing.
